title: Recent advances in functionalized electrospun nanofibers for biomedical and therapeutic applications: A comprehensive review

Nanotechnology has rapidly evolved into a highly impactful research field with significant potential for advancements in healthcare and biomedical sciences. In particular, polymeric micro- and nanofibers (NFs) have attracted increasing attention in biomedical engineering as key building blocks for devices and functional biomaterials [1]. Among various fabrication techniques, electrospinning (ES) has become a leading method for nanofiber production due to its wide applicability in pharmaceuticals and medicine. Through electrostatic interactions, a viscoelastic polymer solution is drawn into continuous fibers, enabling the fabrication of nanoscale structures in a simple and versatile manner [2]. ES is widely valued for its operational simplicity, scalability, and the ability to finely tune fiber diameter, composition, and orientation [3]. ES permits the fabrication of fibers of diameters ranging from the micrometer-to-nanometer scale, utilizing a wide spectrum of materials, including polymers of natural or synthetic origin, ceramics, small molecules, and hybrid systems [2]. In addition, ES allows the fabrication of specialized structures, including porous, hollow, and core-sheath fibers. These structures could be further functionalized by incorporating bioactive agents or nanoparticles (NPs) during or after spinning. Beyond single fibers, more complex architectures, including aligned, layered, and three-dimensional (3D) assemblies, can be achieved through controlled deposition strategies [2], [3], [4], [5]. Owing to these versatile features, electrospun nanofibers (ESNFs) have been widely applied in filtration, catalysis, environmental protection, energy systems, and functional textiles. In biomedical applications, they are particularly important for tissue engineering (TE), wound healing, drug delivery (DD), and regenerative therapies [2].

The development of ES spans several centuries. Early observations of electrostatic effects on liquids were reported by William Gilbert in 1600 [6], [7]. In the 18th century, Stephen Gray and Abbe Nollet described electrostatically driven fluid jets and electrospraying phenomena. A major step toward modern ES occurred in 1902 with Cooley and Morton, who developed early device concepts [7]. In 1914, John Zeleny analyzed fluid behavior under the influence of electric fields using mathematical models. Geoffrey Taylor, in work conducted between 1964 and 1969, provided the theoretical basis for jet formation by describing the “Taylor cone.” Despite these advances, the field saw limited progress for several decades until its revival in 1990 by Darrell Reneker and Gregory Rutledge, who demonstrated the polymer-based fiber production and significantly expanded its application potential [7], [8]. An illustrative overview of this historical development is shown in Fig. 1.

Over time, ES has been exploited with a broad range of natural and synthetic polymers for the fabrication of NFs, including nanocomposites and core-sheath structures. Despite its strengths, ES faces several limitations. A key challenge is the reliance on large amounts of organic or hazardous solvents, especially when processing hydrophobic polymers. Additional issues include difficulties in processing very low- or high-viscosity solutions, limited throughput, and challenges in controlling fiber alignment and uniformity [9]. Common diluents like tetrahydrofuran (THF), dimethylformamide (DMF), and other benzene derivatives raise environmental and safety concerns. Their use limits the integration of sensitive biomolecules like proteins and living cells, thereby restricting their applications in TE. Moreover, residual solvents in the final fibers may impair bioactivity and trigger inflammatory responses in biological systems [10]. These constraints emphasize the need to develop greener and more biologically compatible alternatives. Water-based ES of hydrophilic polymers like PEG, PVA, and PEO offers a promising approach, while solvent blending can further improve spinnability [5], [11], [12], [13]. In contrast, hydrophobic polymers like poly (L-lactic acid) (PLLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), poly lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA), and PAN typically require organic solvents [5], [14], [15], [16]. Efforts are ongoing to optimize ES conditions to produce high-quality fibers suitable for commercial applications [15]. Consequently, the field has experienced rapid advancement, leading to increasingly sophisticated fiber designs and a large range of processing approaches. These developments have led to new ES systems that have significantly expanded the capabilities and impact of this technology.

A standard ES system consists of distinct components including a polymeric solution, a power supply, a spinneret, and a grounded collector [17]. The polymeric solution is delivered through a syringe and subjected to a high electric field, which induces charge accumulation at the needle tip. The resulting electrostatic forces stretch the solution into a jet pointed to the collector [18]. As the jet moves, it elongates and undergoes rapid solvent evaporation, forming solid NFs [17], [19], [20]. Fiber formation is governed by multiple interdependent parameters, including solution properties, process conditions, and environmental factors [21]. Applied voltage typically ranges from a few to 30 kV and influences jet stretching and fiber diameter, with higher voltages generally producing thinner fibers [17], [22]. However, fiber morphology is also strongly affected by viscosity, surface tension, conductivity, and solvent volatility. High viscosity resists elongation and leads to thicker fibers, while insufficient viscosity may cause droplets to form instead of fibers. Beyond viscosity, the solution's conductivity further affects jet stability and fiber morphology [17], [23], [24]. Because these parameters interact nonlinearly, achieving consistent fiber characteristics remains challenging, particularly for scale-up applications [25].

ES parameters are usually divided into three categories: solution properties, operational conditions, and environmental factors [26]. Solution-related variables like polymer concentration, conductivity, surface tension, molecular weight, viscosity, and solvent volatility determine jet stability and fiber formation. Operational parameters like applied voltage, flow rate, and the distance between the collector and tip should be adjusted based on solution-specific characteristics to ensure uniform fibers [27]. Environmental variables, particularly heat and moisture, further affect solvent evaporation and fiber conformation. For example, a stretched working distance extends the time available for jet stretching and solvent evaporation, often producing finer fibers. At the same time, inadequate volatility or low temperature can lead to incomplete drying and fiber fusion. However, excessive distance may destabilize the Taylor cone and reduce uniformity [26], [27]. Overall, ES is governed by a complex interplay of interdependent variables that are difficult to optimize independently. This nonlinear behavior poses a significant challenge for reproducibility, process standardization, and industrial scale-up [26], [27], [28].

The ES process is capable of producing a broad spectrum of nanofiber morphologies, including smooth, branched, core-sheath, porous, ribbon-like, and even fractal-like structures [1], [29]. Over the last twenty years, numerous ES techniques have been introduced to meet diverse application and structural requirements [29]. The growing industrial relevance of ES has driven the establishment of large-scale production systems, making both the technology and nanofibrous products increasingly commercially viable [1], [17]. As a result, a selection of procedures has been recognized to fabricate two-dimensional (2D) and 3D fibrous constructs for specific functional applications. Currently, ES systems are broadly classified into needle-based and needleless approaches [25], [30]. The first ES (needle-based) technique is the most commonly used, in which the polymer is dispensed via a syringe to form fibers. It offers accurate control of fiber structure but often suffers from clogging, particularly when processing highly viscous or particle-loaded solutions [25], [31], [32], [33]. Variants of this approach include side-by-side, blend, and multiaxial (coaxial and triaxial) ES, as shown in Fig. 2 [25]. Needleless electrospinning (NLES) eliminates the use of needles by generating fibers from liquid surfaces or rotating elements such as disks or wires. This approach reduces clogging, increases production rates, and enables the formation of complex fiber morphologies. It also allows management of critical properties such as fiber diameter, porosity, and interface chemistry [25], [34], [35], [36]. However, variations in morphology and mechanical properties are often observed due to differences in materials, solvents, and processing conditions [25], [37]. These tunable features are particularly valuable for biomedical applications, as they influence drug release behavior, targeting efficiency, and tissue compatibility. Consequently, ESNFs are progressively employed in controlled DD, targeted therapy, and TE frameworks [38].

Needle-based ES has provided ample promise in DD and TE applications. ESNFs mimic the structure of the natural extracellular matrix (ECM) and work as effective scaffolds that facilitate cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation. They can also be functionalized with biomolecules like cytokines, growth factors, or genetic material to further enhance their regenerative capacity [8], [25]. In bone and cartilage engineering, electrospun structures provide mechanical reinforcement whilst delivering osteoinductive cues or stem cells to stimulate repair [39]. For wound healing, NFs containing antibacterial compounds or growth factors help maintain moisture and enable controlled drug release, thereby accelerating healing and reducing infection risk. Needle-based ES has also emerged as a promising platform for vaccine delivery [40]. Encapsulation of antigens or adjuvants enables sustained release and enhanced immune responses, with applications in DNA and protein vaccines where fibers act as both delivery vehicles and stabilizing matrices [41]. For infection control, ESNFs incorporating antimicrobial molecules like silver NPs, antibiotics, and antifungals have been developed for wound dressings and implant coatings, providing prolonged antimicrobial protection while supporting tissue regeneration [42]. Overall, needle-based ES offers a versatile tool for modern DD strategies and biomedical instruments. By tuning processing conditions and fiber architecture, it is possible to control drug release profiles, protect sensitive therapeutics, and enable targeted delivery [43]. Continued advances in materials and processing are expected to further expand its applications toward more effective and personalized medical solutions [25].

Blend ES represents one of the simplest and most frequently used strategies for DD, in which both the polymer and the therapeutic compound are mixed in the same solvent solution [44]. This methodology enables the molecule of interest to be evenly distributed and integrated into the polymer matrix during fiber formation. Its effectiveness strongly depends on drug-polymer compatibility, following the “like dissolves like” principle. High compatibility promotes homogeneous drug distribution and sustained release, whereas incompatibility often triggers burst release due to rapid drug expulsion, particularly when hydrophilic drugs and hydrophobic polymers are involved [45]. In biodegradable systems, release mechanisms usually involve diffusion, polymer degradation, or a combination thereof, while in non-biodegradable systems, it is mainly diffusion-controlled [46]. Despite its simplicity, blend ES faces limitations, especially for sensitive biomolecules such as proteins, which may be denatured or damaged when exposed to organic solvents. In addition, polymers with high hydrophobicity often exhibit slow release profiles, making them less suitable for rapid delivery applications [47]. To address compatibility issues, co-solvents like dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) have been used to better drug dispersion and achieve more controlled release behavior [48]. Blend ES has been effectively harnessed for a large selection of therapeutics, including antibiotics [49], cytostatic agents [50], anti-inflammatory drugs [51], and antimicrobial peptides [52], [53]. However, its use for protein delivery remains restricted due to the denaturing effects of organic solvents and most commonly used polymers such as PCL, PLGA, and polyurethane (PU) require them, which can induce protein unfolding and loss of bioactivity [54].

Side-by-side ES is a specialized technique that employs dual parallel nozzles to process two polymer solutions simultaneously, producing multicomponent NFs with distinct compartments. This approach enhances fabrication flexibility and enables the formation of complex fiber architectures with tailored properties in a single step, with applications in biomedical devices, sensors, and advanced functional materials [55]. By tuning spinneret configuration and process parameters, fibers with controlled dimensions and interfacial characteristics can be obtained [56]. In this Janus fiber configuration, two distinct solutions are co-electrospun to form adjacent but separated compartments within a single fiber [57]. A notable benefit of this system is its ability to enable biphasic drug release, where one compartment provides an initial burst release while the other ensures sustained delivery [25]. However, several challenges limit process stability. Interfacial instability between the two phases, differences in solvent evaporation rates, and phase separation can lead to morphological irregularities and altered release behavior [58]. In addition, precise coordination of fluid flow, electrostatic forces, and rheological properties is required to ensure synchronized jet formation from both nozzles [59]. These instabilities make it more difficult to achieve uniform fibers compared with blend ES, although advances in polymer compatibility and solvent selection are gradually improving reproducibility [60].

Coaxial ES is a highly versatile process for producing complex nanofibrous structures with controlled core-sheath architectures, offering enhanced structural and functional design flexibility [61]. It was introduced by Sun et al., in 2003, aiming to overcome conventional blend ES challenges by enabling the fabrication of fibers with distinct internal compartments [62]. This technique involves concurrent electrospinning of multiple polymer solutions via a coaxial spinneret consisting of concentric capillaries. The internal nozzle introduces the core solution, whereas the external nozzle supplies the polymer that forms the shell [25], [26], [62], [63], [64], [65]. During processing, the shell solution encapsulates the core at the spinneret tip, forming a composite Taylor cone under an electric field; subsequently, the solvent evaporation yields continuous fibers with well-defined core-sheath structures [26]. The final fiber properties depend strongly on the interaction between the two solutions, including viscosity, miscibility, conductivity, and interfacial tension. Stable core-sheath formation requires careful control of these parameters and maintenance of a stable Taylor cone throughout the process [26]. Typically, the shell mixture must exhibit higher viscosity than the core to ensure complete encapsulation, while flow rates must be carefully balanced to maintain structural integrity [65]. In addition, the two fluids are ideally immiscible or only partially miscible; otherwise, phase mixing, premature solidification, or structural instability may occur. Interfacial shear forces between core and shell phases also influence fiber morphology and stability [65], [66]. These factors make coaxial ES more complex than single-fluid approaches, as it requires precise optimization of viscosity ratios, flow rates, and interfacial properties. Despite this complexity, the technique is not limited to polymers and has been extended to ceramics, metal oxides, and semiconductors. Recent advances have enabled even more complex architectures, including triple-layer and multichannel fibers [67], [68], [69], [70]. As a result, coaxial ES has found broad uses in biomedicine, energy storage, and environmental fields [71], [72], [73], [74], [75], [76], [77], [78]. In biomedical applications, coaxial fibers are particularly valuable for DD and TE owing to their capacity to combine biocompatibility with mechanical stability. The core-sheath configuration enables precise regulation of drug encapsulation and release, allowing sustained and programmable delivery profiles. Compared with conventional single-jet fibers, coaxial systems offer additional advantages such as hydrophilic-hydrophobic compartmentalization, improved mechanical strength, and tunable release kinetics for bioactive molecules and NPs [26], [71], [79].

Emulsion ES is a versatile and relatively inexpensive technique for encapsulating therapeutic agents within NFs, particularly for generating core-sheath-like architectures. It has been widely used to incorporate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic bioactive compounds, resulting in fibers with distinct internal compartments [80], [81]. The setup is similar to blend ES; however, rather than employing a single homogeneous solution, a multiphase emulsion is prepared and electrospun, as depicted in Fig. 3 [81]. Typically, a water-in-oil emulsion is formed using a surfactant, which disperses an aqueous drug phase within a polymer-containing organic phase [1], [80]. The polymer solution represents the continuous phase, while the active agents are confined to the dispersed droplets. During ES, rapid solvent evaporation increases the viscosity of the organic solution, promoting migration of the aqueous droplets toward the fiber core due to viscosity gradients. Under an applied electric field, droplets align and coalesce due to electrophoresis, forming core-sheath structures [82], [83]. The physicochemical properties of the drug determined the encapsulation behavior: low-molecular-weight compounds are often dispersed within the matrix, whereas higher-molecular-weight molecules are more likely to form well-defined core-sheath morphologies [82], [84]. Despite its advantages, emulsion ES has limitations compared with coaxial ES. Emulsion stability relies on surfactants, which may alter fiber surface properties and reduce cell adhesion. In addition, interfacial tension between phases can affect the structural integrity of sensitive biomolecules, potentially leading to partial degradation during processing [64], [85]. Consequently, this technique may be less suitable for fragile biological molecules that are sensitive to interfacial stress [1], [86].

Triaxial ES is a multiaxial technique that employs a specialized spinneret composed of three concentric capillaries, enabling the simultaneous processing of three distinct fluid streams. As part of the broader multiaxial ES family (including coaxial, quadraxial, and multi-nozzle systems), it allows the fabrication of complex multilayered NFs with enhanced structural and functional control [26]. A typical setup includes three syringe pumps for independent delivery of each solution, a grounded collector, a power supply, and a triaxial spinneret consisting of inner, middle, and outer channels. Under an applied electric field, the three solutions form a compound Taylor cone, resulting in fibers with clearly structured cores, intermediate, and outer layers upon solidification [26], [87], [88]. The primary advantage of triaxial ES is the ability to independently tailor the arrangement and function of each layer, enabling programmable and sequential drug release within a single fiber system [89]. This method is particularly attractive for TE applications, where mechanical support and biological functionality can be decoupled; for example, a mechanically robust synthetic polymer can serve as the core, while bioactive or cell-compatible materials are positioned in outer layers to promote cell adhesion and proliferation [90], [91]. Triaxial fibers are also well suited for the encapsulation of delicate therapeutics like growth factors, proteins, and poorly soluble drugs, as multilayer structures can protect active agents from harsh processing conditions and enable targeted or staged release, including rapid initial release followed by sustained or zero-order kinetics [92], [93]. In addition, these systems have been used to incorporate antimicrobial agents for prolonged antibacterial activity. Despite these advantages, triaxial ES is technically demanding. Careful control of solvent volatility, polymer compatibility, and molecular weight differences is essential, as premature solidification of the outer layer can destabilize fiber formation. In addition, accurate control of flow rates is required to maintain structural integrity and avert nozzle clogging, particularly when processing complex or bioactive core formulations [26], [94].

Multiaxial ES is an advanced ES technique that employs three or more concentric nozzles (spinnerets) to simultaneously process multiple polymer solutions or fluids into a single, structurally complex nanofiber. Extending beyond coaxial (two-fluid) and triaxial (three-fluid) ES, this method enables the construction of fibers with highly precise configurations and multifunctional characteristics by combining multiple layers or compartments within a single fiber [25], [26]. In this process, polymeric solutions are delivered through nested capillaries (e.g., core-sheath-sheath configurations) and subjected to a strong electric field, producing multilayered fibers with structures such as core-double-shell systems and radial multilayer distributions [1], [25], [26]. An important advantage of multiaxial ES is its ability to incorporate different therapeutic agents into individual layers, enabling independent modulation of drug release profiles. This makes the technique particularly attractive for multidrug delivery systems requiring sequential, sustained, or stimuli-responsive release. Notably, antibacterial multiaxial fibers have demonstrated both rapid and prolonged antimicrobial activity, highlighting their promise for extended therapeutic applications [25], [95]. Despite these advantages, multiaxial ES remains technically demanding, requiring careful optimization of processing parameters, solvent systems, and polymer formulations to maintain jet stability and preserve the structural integrity of the resulting NFs [25], [96]. Fiber stability and functionality are strongly affected by factors such as inner-core solvent selection, polymer compatibility, and solvent volatility, all of which affect spinnability and interfacial integrity during fabrication [25], [97]. Consequently, careful selection of compatible solvents and spinnable fluids is essential to ensure robust fiber formation and to support the broader application of multiaxial ES in advanced DD and TE [25].

Needleless electrospinning (NLES) is an innovative nanofiber fabrication procedure that differs from conventional ES by generating fibers straight from the polymer solution's surface rather than through needle-based nozzles. The earliest form of this method was reported by Simm and colleagues in 1979, who used an annular electrode as the spinneret [98]. Nevertheless, the method received little attention until the early 2000s, when Yarin and Zussman introduced a system in which a magnetic field induced surface spikes in the liquid, thereby initiating ES [99]. In 2009, Jirsak and colleagues patented a rotary-cylinder-based NLES device and later commercialized it under the name Nanospider [100]. Since then, numerous alternative NLES configurations have been developed, including systems based on air bubbles [101], conical wire spinnerets [102], flat metal plates [103], splashing spinnerets [104], rotating cones [105], container edges [106], toothed wheels [107], linear flumes [108], and shear-assisted spinnerets [109]. A distinguishing feature of NLES is that jet initiation occurs spontaneously across the polymer solution surface, independent of capillary-driven flow typical of needle-based systems [110]. As a result, spinneret design plays a prominent role in establishing jet stability, fiber morphology, and production efficiency [111]. Over the years, a diverse set of spinneret geometries has been established to improve throughput and fiber quality as shown in Fig. 4 [112].

A major advantage of NLES is its ability to generate numerous polymer drops over a broad surface without relying on individual needles. Under an applied electric field, these droplets form multiple Taylor cones that emit jets toward a conductive collector, producing nonwoven fiber mats [112]. Unlike single- or few-needle systems, the concurrent formation of several jets significantly improves nanofiber production speeds [113]. The success of NLES depends strongly on the polymer solution's conductivity, which governs its interaction with the electric field and promotes stable jet formation, a requirement for continuous, uniform fibers [25], [114]. Because the technique utilizes open liquid surfaces, it is particularly attractive for large-scale production, offering simplified system design, easier maintenance, and greater flexibility in material processing [113], [114]. These features have supported its application in wound dressings, TE scaffolds, DD, biosensors, and filtration systems, where diverse polymer systems can be incorporated to produce functional NFs for biomedical and environmental uses [25], [115]. Despite these advantages, NLES still faces important challenges, including inconsistent jet formation, sensitivity to solution properties, and difficulties in controlling surface tension, all of which can contribute to variability in fiber morphology and reproducibility across batches or experimental conditions [25].

A range of NLES techniques have been developed, including corona, bubble, roller, high-speed, and alternating current (AC) ES [25]. These methods promote simultaneous multi-jet formation, significantly increasing fiber productivity compared to conventional needle-based systems. In roller ES, a rotating cylinder is partially immersed in a polymer blend solution, with an electric field applied between the roller surface and the collector. Rotation generates a thin liquid film that is subsequently stretched into NFs under the applied electric field. Although this configuration enables continuous and scalable fiber production, accurate control over fiber width and morphology remains difficult [116], [117], [118]. Bubble ES relies on gas flow to generate bubbles at the polymer surface. In the presence of a strong electric field, Taylor cones form on the bubble surface, leading to jet initiation and fiber formation. This technique enables high-throughput production and can yield hollow fiber structures; however, it is highly susceptible to solution and gas-flow parameters, which can negatively affect fiber uniformity and reproducibility [119], [120], [121]. In corona ES, a high-voltage electrode positioned close to the polymer solution induces corona discharge, generating a strong electric field that triggers Taylor cone formation and fiber discharge. The procedure is rather straightforward and easy to execute, allowing production of fibers with varying diameters, but maintaining consistent fiber alignment and uniformity remains a key limitation [122], [123]. High-speed ES employs rapidly rotating disks or similar elements to generate fibers through combined centrifugal force and shear stress. This approach can generate fibers with high aspect ratios and enhanced mechanical characteristics; however, the process needs dedicated equipment and precise adjustment of operational conditions [25], [124]. AC ES utilizes a periodically reversing electric field to induce cyclic deformation of the polymer solution surface, enabling multi-jet formation without needles. Unlike direct current systems, AC ES reduces charge accumulation on deposited fibers, resulting in more voluminous, highly porous, and 3D nonwoven structures [125], [126]. These characteristics make AC ES especially favorable for large-scale fabrication and applications that require a large interfacial surface and increased porosity. However, the oscillatory characteristic of the electric field introduces challenges to jet stability and trajectory control, making the achievement of fiber uniformity and alignment more difficult. Consequently, careful optimization of parameters such as frequency, voltage amplitude, and solution properties is essential for consistent fiber morphology [125], [126], [127].

Modifying or functionalizing the surface of ESNFs is a widely used strategy to enhance key surface features like wettability, surface charge, and roughness, thereby improving their performance in biomedical applications. The integration of biological molecules including nutrients, proteins, growth factors, and other bioactive or biomimetic materials into or onto nanofiber matrices, can create a favorable microenvironment that facilitates stem cell adhesion, differentiation, and proliferation. This, in turn, enhances the bioactivity of the platforms and broadens their applicability in regenerative medicine and related fields [128], [129], [130]. Surface modification strategies are generally categorized into two main approaches: (i) physical methods, such as adsorption or non-covalent functionalization, and (ii) chemical methods, including plasma treatment and graft polymerization [128], [129]. Physical modification is often preferred for its simplicity and for preserving the intrinsic structure of NFs, as it does not involve chemical reactions that may alter bulk properties [130]. This approach relies on weak, non-covalent interactions (e.g., van der Waals interactions, electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonding, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic effects) [131]. However, these interactions are typically less stable over time, which may limit long-term functionality. In contrast, chemical modification involves covalent bonding and permanent alteration of the nanofiber surface through the addition or activation of functional groups, thereby enhancing surface hydrophilicity and enabling stable biomolecule immobilization. This process is typically initiated by activating reactive groups on the nanofiber surface, such as -COOH, -NH2, or -OH, followed by their reaction with bioactive molecules to form stable covalent linkages [128], [132]. Because these bonds are chemically stable, functionalization achieved through this route is generally more durable than that achieved through physical adsorption. A key advantage of chemical surface modification is the creation of robust and long-lasting bioactive sites that significantly improve cell-material interactions, thereby promoting efficient cell adhesion and growth on the nanofiber scaffold [129], [133]. A schematic overview of common surface functionalization strategies for biomedical applications is presented in Fig. 5 [128].

Wet-chemical treatment is a widely used functionalization strategy for ESNFs, involving chemical reactions conducted under acidic or basic conditions or in the presence of nucleophiles such as diamines. These reactions typically lead to selective cleavage of polymer chains at labile sites, such as ester bonds commonly present in polyester-based NFs [129]. Unlike purely physical modification methods, which are largely confined to the surface, wet chemical approaches can introduce hydrophilic functional groups both at and beneath the fiber surface, thereby enabling more extensive surface activation. The degree of modification depends on several parameters, including reaction time, reagent type and concentration, and the polymer's intrinsic chemical composition. Careful optimization of these conditions is therefore essential to avoid excessive degradation of the polymer backbone, which may adversely influence the mechanical durability and overall stability of the NFs structure [133], [134]. Through controlled reactions, functional groups such as amine (-NH2), carboxyl (-COOH), and hydroxyl (-OH) can be added onto the nanofiber surface, enhancing its chemical reactivity and suitability for further biofunctionalization. Among the most commonly employed wet chemical approaches are hydrolysis and aminolysis. The efficiency and outcomes of these processes are strongly influenced by reagent type and concentration, as well as exposure duration, all of which govern the degree of surface modification and its compatibility with biomedical applications such as DD and TE [135].

Aminolysis is a prominent surface functionalization procedure used to graft free -NH2 groups onto nanofiber surfaces by covalently linking diamine molecules to reactive ester groups within the polymer, enabling the formation of -NH2-functionalized surfaces [136]. Common diamines used for this purpose include N-aminoethyl-1,3-propanediamine, ethylenediamine, and 1,6-hexanediamine, which have been applied to both aromatic and aliphatic polyesters [137]. Successful aminolysis depends on multiple reaction parameters, including diamine concentration, solution pH, treatment duration, and reaction temperature. The process generally enhances wettability through the introduction of -COOH, -NH2, and -OH groups, while increased surface roughness may improve biomolecule immobilization and cellular adhesion [129]. Because of its relatively rapid reaction time, often less than 1 h, aminolysis is frequently employed as a preparatory strategy for immobilizing growth factors and other bioactive agents.

Despite these advantages, the literature presents a less consistent picture than is often implied. While many studies report improved hydrophilicity and bioactivity following aminolysis, considerable variability exists in the reported extent of amine grafting, preservation of fiber morphology, and resulting biological outcomes. These discrepancies often stem from methodological differences, including the choice of diamine, solvent system, treatment severity, and characterization technique. For example, ninhydrin assays, Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and contact angle measurements are frequently used to assess functionalization efficiency. Yet these methods probe different aspects of surface modification and are not always directly comparable [129], [132]. In some cases, improved wettability has been interpreted as evidence of successful amination even when direct quantification of surface amine density was lacking, potentially overstating functionalization efficiency [135], [136], [137], [138], [139], [140], [141], [142], [143], [144].

A notable unresolved issue concerns the role of polymer crystallinity in governing aminolysis efficiency. Several studies identify crystallinity as a major barrier, particularly in PCL, where highly ordered regions and a low ester-to-alkyl ratio may restrict nucleophilic attack [129], [132], [143]. However, interpretation of these findings remains complicated because many reports treat crystallinity as a bulk property measured by Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) or X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), whereas aminolysis is inherently a surface-limited reaction. As suggested by Jeznach et al. [132], ESNFs may possess a highly crystalline skin layer distinct from the fiber core, and this radial distribution may exert greater control over aminolysis than bulk crystallinity alone. Yet few studies systematically distinguish surface crystallinity from overall crystallinity, raising the possibility that conflicting reports regarding polymer responsiveness to aminolysis may reflect unaccounted structural heterogeneity rather than intrinsic differences in polymer chemistry. This methodological limitation complicates cross-study comparisons and may partly explain why some investigations report minimal modification of PCL surfaces, whereas others observe substantial amine incorporation under ostensibly similar conditions [132], [133], [135].

Conflicting observations are also evident regarding the effect of aminolysis on NF structure and mechanics. For example, Yaseri et al. [135] proposed PCL ESNFs surface modification with relatively minor morphological changes after aminolysis compared with hydrolysis, whereas Jeznach et al. [143] reported fiber fracture (Fig. 6) under harsh aminolysis conditions. In the study by Yaseri et al., the modified surfaces supported fibroblast adhesion and spreading, with cells exhibiting a spindle-shaped morphology. Enhanced cell proliferation was also reported, suggesting that aminolyzed and hydrolyzed PCL NFs may serve as promising structures for TE applications [135]. Similarly, in the work of Jeznach et al., improved cell spreading was observed for both L929 and MG63 cells even at low amine concentrations, indicating sufficient bioactivity enhancement without significant polymer degradation [143]. Other studies have intentionally exploited extensive fragmentation to generate nanocylinders or nanofibrils. These divergent outcomes suggest that the boundary between beneficial surface modification and detrimental polymer degradation remains poorly defined and likely depends strongly on polymer microstructure, solvent-mediated swelling, and reaction kinetics [144], [145]. However, these variables are not consistently controlled or reported, limiting reproducibility. Likewise, while some authors associate increased amine density with improved cell adhesion and proliferation, others report enhanced bioactivity even at low amine concentrations [143], indicating that biological responses may not correlate linearly with functional group density. These results raise questions about whether observed cellular improvements arise from surface amine density itself, secondary changes in roughness and wettability, or other confounding factors.

Studies involving dendrimer-mediated aminolysis and secondary functionalization strategies further illustrate both opportunities and uncertainties. Approaches involving polyamidoamine (PAMAM) and polypropylene imine dendrimers, graphene oxide deposition, or hyaluronic acid immobilization have demonstrated improved hydrophilicity, enhanced cell interactions, and even antibacterial effects in surface-functionalized ESNFs [138], [140], [141], [142], [143], [144], [145]. However, in many such studies, the contributions of aminolysis cannot be readily isolated from those of subsequently immobilized coatings or additives. As a result, improvements in biological performance are sometimes attributed broadly to aminolysis, despite likely arising from synergistic or even dominant effects of secondary modifications. More rigorous controls are needed to distinguish the role of initial amine functionalization from that of downstream bioactive modifications. Another underexamined issue concerns the long-term stability of aminolyzed surfaces. Zhu et al. [146] suggested that aminolyzed polymers may lose surface functional groups during storage at physiological temperatures or upon immersion in PBS due to chain rearrangement and burial of amines beneath the surface. Although frequently cited as a concern, this phenomenon has been investigated in only a few systems, and systematic aging studies across different polymers remain scarce. Consequently, the extent to which amine instability poses a universal barrier to translation remains uncertain.

Overall, while aminolysis remains a versatile and widely used surface modification technique, the field contains significant unresolved questions regarding reaction mechanisms, structure-reactivity relationships, reproducibility, and long-term functional stability. Future studies would benefit from standardized characterization protocols, clearer differentiation between surface and bulk crystallinity effects, and better-controlled comparisons that isolate aminolysis-specific contributions from those of subsequent functionalization steps. Addressing these methodological weaknesses is essential for resolving conflicting findings and improving the reliability and translational potential of aminolyzed nanofiber scaffolds [129], [132], [135].

Hydrolysis-based surface modification can be broadly classified into acidic and alkaline hydrolysis. This technique involves cleavage of ester bonds in polyester-based materials, generating -COOH and -OH groups on the surface [133]. The reaction mechanism depends on whether acidic or basic conditions are applied. As with aminolysis, hydrolysis must be carefully controlled for temperature, pH, and reaction time, which can range from minutes to several hours depending on the material and conditions [147]. Surface hydrolysis has been widely used to enhance surface functionality of aliphatic biodegradable polyester films and scaffolds, particularly wettability. This effect arises from random cleavage of ester linkages on outer polymer chains, producing functional groups from partially decomposed, water-insoluble residues. The efficiency of hydrolysis depends strongly on reaction time and reagent concentration; in many cases, low concentrations are sufficient to accomplish surface modification, ensuring that the bulk properties or structural integrity remain unaffected [128], [137].

Acid hydrolysis proceeds via an electrophilic mechanism in which high-energy protons interact with polymer chains. This can result in carbon-centered radical formation and subsequent reactions involving unstable -OOH intermediates, producing -OH, -COOH, and ether (-R-O-R) groups [148]. Because such transformations are not easily achieved under mild conditions, acid hydrolysis typically requires strong acids, elevated temperatures, and longer reaction times [137]. Common reagents comprise hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), perchloric acid (HClO4), and organic acids such as lactic and acetic acid [147], [149], [150]. Several studies demonstrate its effectiveness. For example, HCl treatment of polyglycolic acid (PGA) scaffolds improved surface functionality, resulting in enhanced cardiac fibroblast adhesion and proliferation after 96 h [147]. Similarly, treatment with a perchloric acid/potassium chlorate system improved adhesion and growth of chondrocytes and fibroblasts, correlating with increased wettability [148]. However, acid hydrolysis can also introduce drawbacks; H2SO4 treatment of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) has been shown to reduce thermal stability and cause uncontrolled acid release during heating [150]. Due to such limitations, its application is relatively restricted.

Alkaline hydrolysis, in contrast, is a nucleophilic process driven by hydroxide ions (OH−) from bases such as sodium or potassium hydroxides (NaOH, KOH). These ions attack electrophilic sites on the polymer surface (e.g., carbonyl and ester groups), cleaving polymer chains and generating hydrophilic functional groups [151]. The extent of modification depends on hydroxide concentration and treatment conditions; higher concentrations increase surface activation but may also risk excessive degradation, including mass loss and thickness reduction [151]. Because it is easier to control and generally less damaging to bulk properties, alkaline hydrolysis is more widely used for nanofiber functionalization in biomedical applications. It is often employed as a pre-treatment step for biomolecule immobilization. For instance, NaOH-treated PLGA NFs have been successfully activated for collagen attachment using EDC/NHS chemistry as demonstrated in Fig. 7 [152]. This modification significantly improved wettability and supported enhanced cell viability in keratinocyte and fibroblast cultures over extended periods, demonstrating its suitability for skin tissue engineering (STE) [152].

In another study, PCL ESNFs were treated with varying NaOH concentrations and exposure times to optimize flow behavior and enhance detection sensitivity in nucleic acid-based lateral flow assays (LFAs) [153]. The results showed that NaOH treatment had minimal effect on fiber diameter, pore size, and overall porosity. However, surface wettability improved significantly, as shown by a pronounced drop in water contact angle. This increase in hydrophilicity was linked to the formation of -OH and -COOH groups on the NF surface, with higher NaOH concentrations producing a more pronounced effect. Morphologically, hydrolyzed NFs exhibited a flatter and more compact structure compared to untreated PCL fibers. At higher NaOH concentrations, slight fiber erosion was observed, contributing to increased surface roughness. Notably, exposure to 2.0 M NaOH resulted in a substantial reduction in membrane thickness, possibly due to peeling under strongly alkaline conditions [135]. Despite these structural changes, the modified NFs demonstrated enhanced analytical performance, achieving a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.5 nM for synthetic Zika viral DNA. These findings highlight the potential of PCL NFs as a cost-effective and tunable alternative to conventional nitrocellulose membranes in LFA systems [153]. In a related work, Mobarakeh et al. functionalized PCL nanofiber membranes (NFMs) with Matrigel following alkaline hydrolysis [154]. The electrospun mats were first mixed with NaOH solution to expose reactive surface groups. Subsequent activation with 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDAC) enabled covalent linkage between the activated surface and -NH2 groups of Matrigel. This modification significantly enhanced hydrophilicity, as well as cellular proliferation and adhesion, indicating strong potential for TE purposes [154], [155].

Chemical grafting is a widely used surface modification strategy where polymer chains or functional groups are covalently attached to electrospun substrates. This approach enables precise tuning of surface features by adding specific functional groups onto nanofiber surfaces. Chemical grafting is generally grouped into two main strategies: “grafting to” and “grafting from.” In the “grafting to” approach, pre-synthesized polymers with reactive end groups are covalently linked to functional sites on the nanofiber surface through coupling reactions. This method supports various polymerization techniques, including atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP), controlled free-radical polymerization (CFRP), and anionic polymerization by employing various monomers like acrylonitrile, acrylates, and acrylamides [156], [157], [158], [159]. A key benefit of this strategy is the capability to fully characterize the polymer before grafting, allowing accurate control over distribution and molecular weight [160]. However, grafting density is often limited due to steric hindrance, which results in a non-uniform layer thickness and a self-limiting growth process. Additionally, thorough control of reaction conditions is necessary to avoid undesirable changes in nanofiber morphology or bulk mechanical properties [160], [161].

In contrast, the “grafting from” approach (i.e., surface-initiated polymerization) enables polymer chains to grow in situ directly from reactive sites present on the substrate surface [160], [161]. This method enables higher grafting densities and more precise control over brush thickness at near-molecular resolution [161]. Typically, reactive functional groups are first added onto the nanofiber surface, and initiators are subsequently immobilized through post-polymerization modification, copolymerization, or polycondensation. Polymer chains then propagate outward from these surface-bound initiators [162], [163]. A representative example is the use of atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) treatment to introduce reactive groups onto nanofiber surfaces. In this approach, argon plasma facilitates the deposition of 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES), enriching the surface with amino functionalities [164]. These groups can later covalently bind to biomolecules, such as aldehyde-functionalized peptides. This strategy has been described to increase osteoblast adhesion and migration, demonstrating the effectiveness of surface-initiated grafting for biomedical applications [164]. Overall, chemical grafting provides a versatile platform for tailoring surface charge, wettability, and biocompatibility of ESNFs. A wide selection of biological molecules (e.g., proteins, antibodies, peptides, and enzymes) can be immobilized through covalent attachment [161], [165], [166]. Typically, this involves a two-step process: (i) introduction of reactive functional groups and (ii) coupling reactions such as amidation, esterification, or click chemistry [167]. Grafting techniques have proven effective for modifying diverse polymer substrates, including synthetic polymers like PET, PCL, and PLA, as well as natural polymers like cellulose, chitin, and chitosan [167], [168], [169], [170]. For example, HA grafted onto PCL ESNFs via carbodiimide chemistry resulted in improved mechanical properties, enhanced cell adhesion, and increased proliferation [171]. Similarly, poly (2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine) (PMPC)-grafted chitosan (CS) NFs synthesized via ATRP demonstrated superior cell attachment and uniform spreading. These improvements are attributed to synergistic interactions between functional groups on the grafted polymers and cellular components. Collectively, these findings highlight chemical grafting as a powerful and adaptable strategy for engineering nanofiber-based scaffolds with tailored functionalities for advanced biomedical applications [172].

Qin et al. [173] developed an effective strategy to modify hydrophobic PCL scaffolds by introducing an azide-terminated amphiphilic polymer, followed by conjugation with growth factor-loaded nanocapsules functionalized with dibenzocyclooctyne (DBCO). This approach utilized azide-alkyne click chemistry to enable controlled delivery of bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2). The BMP-2-containing nanocapsules were constructed via in situ polymerization around the protein core, forming a protective and degradable shell. The formulation included acrylamide (AAm) and N-(3-aminopropyl) methacrylamide (APm) in addition to the crosslinkers glycerol dimethacrylate (GDMA) and PLA-PEG-PLA dimethacrylate, which were described as biodegradable crosslinkers [173]. Following encapsulation, the nanocapsules were functionalized with DBCO-PEG-NHS, enabling bioorthogonal azide group conjugation to the PCL surface to form DBCO-n(BMP-2). Surface functionalization of the PCL scaffold was achieved via a simple one-step reaction based on non-covalent interactions between oleylamine (OA) chains and the polymer matrix resulting in the formation of an azide-presenting coating (OA-PLL-PEG-N3), which served as a reactive platform for subsequent click chemistry conjugation [173]. The nanocapsules were designed to degrade gradually under physiological conditions, allowing sustained BMP-2 release through hydrolysis of GDMA and PLA-PEG-PLA crosslinkers. Importantly, the encapsulated BMP-2 remained protected within the polymer shell and securely anchored to the scaffold surface, preserving its bioactivity. This surface modification strategy substantially enhanced the biocompatibility of the PCL scaffold, promoting enhanced cell proliferation and adhesion. Moreover, the sustained and localized release of BMP-2 effectively guided osteogenic differentiation of stem cells, demonstrating strong potential for bone tissue engineering (BTE) applications [173].

Although chemical grafting plays a pivotal role in nanofiber surface modification, it is associated with several limitations. One major challenge is achieving a uniform grafting density across the nanofiber surface. Variations in graft distribution can lead to inconsistent physicochemical properties and compromised performance; thus, precise control of grafting density is essential to ensure homogeneous functionalization and minimize surface defects [174]. In addition, harsh reaction conditions, such as the employment of strong oxidizing agents or high incubation temperatures, may disrupt NFs structure, thereby negatively affecting their mechanical characteristics and functionality [167]. However, careful optimization of reaction parameters, including treatment time and coupling agent concentration, has been shown to mitigate such damage and preserve nanofiber morphology [175]. Scalability and reproducibility also remain significant challenges. Small variations in reaction conditions during scale-up can lead to batch-to-batch inconsistencies, underscoring the need for process standardization and tighter control over reaction environments [167]. Furthermore, the utilization of hazardous chemicals and organic solvents raises concerns for human health and the environment, underscoring the importance of developing more sustainable and environmentally friendly grafting strategies [176]. Overall, precise tuning of grafting parameters is crucial for attaining the required surface functionality while maintaining the structural integrity and bulk properties of NFs [177], [178].

Chemical crosslinking is a key strategy for the functionalization of ESNFs, forming inter-chain bonds with the polymeric chains thereby enhancing mechanical robustness, heat resistance, environmental stability, and biocompatibility [155], [179], [180]. Crosslinking can be accomplished through physical, chemical, or biological mechanisms, each using different agents or stimuli, including glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde, enzymes, UV irradiation, or thermal treatment [181], [182]. Physical crosslinking is based on non-covalent interactions including hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic attractions which are widely reported in the literature [179], [183], [184], [185]. For example, blending oppositely charged polymers can induce electrostatic crosslinking, while thermal treatment may promote conformational changes in polymer chains. In protein-based systems, heating can cause partial unfolding, exposing hydrophobic domains that facilitate intermolecular interactions. Dehydration during thermal processing further enhances chain proximity and interaction [179], [186], [187]. This approach avoids toxic chemicals but often requires precise optimization to ensure sufficient stability and durability [188]. Chemical crosslinking, in contrast, involves the formation of covalent bonds using reactive agents such as glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde, or genipin [179], [182], [189], [190]. This method significantly improves mechanical integrity and resistance to environmental degradation. However, residual crosslinking agents or side reactions may introduce cytotoxicity, necessitating careful post-treatment and biocompatibility evaluation, especially for biomedical applications [179], [190]. Biological crosslinking offers a safer alternative by employing naturally derived enzymes or biomolecules. Enzymes such as cellulase, transglutaminase, laccase, and β-galactosidase can catalyze bond formation under mild conditions [179], [191]. For instance, transglutaminase catalyzes the covalent linkage of lysine and glutamine residues in proteins [192], [193]. This approach enhances structural stability while promoting desirable biological responses, including improved cell adhesion, angiogenesis, and reduced inflammation [194], [195]. The selection of a crosslinking strategy depends on the polymer composition, the required material characteristics, and the intended application. Achieving a balance between functionality and biocompatibility is particularly critical in fields such as TE, DD, and wound healing.

Crosslinked ESNFs have garnered substantial attention in biomedical applications due to their improved performance [179], [196], [197], [198]. Crosslinking can reduce cytotoxicity and inflammatory responses while enhancing cell attachment and proliferation. For example, acid-oxidized xanthan gum has been used to crosslink gelatin NFs, improving their biocompatibility [199]. Similarly, cold plasma-treated gelatin NFs exhibited enhanced cell adhesion and growth [200], while enzymatic crosslinking using horseradish peroxidase (HRP) enabled efficient plasmid DNA delivery [201]. Crosslinking also facilitates the design of multifunctional scaffolds. For instance, genipin-crosslinked coaxial NFs composed of gelatin and PLA have been developed for combined anticancer therapy and bone regeneration, incorporating bioactive agents such as doxorubicin (DOX) and icariin (ICA) [202]. In another study, CS-based NFs functionalized with fucoidan and copper sulfide NPs via polyelectrolyte complexation and genipin crosslinking demonstrated enhanced stability, antibacterial activity, and bone regeneration potential [203]. Additionally, physical crosslinking of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/gelatin NFs using methanol produced denser, water-resistant structures that supported osteoblast adhesion and proliferation [204].

Advanced crosslinking approaches have also been explored. Radiation-induced crosslinking of PLLA NFs using triallyl isocyanurate (TAIC) and gamma irradiation yielded stable networks with good cell compatibility and no cytotoxic effects [205]. Similarly, genipin-crosslinked PCL/gelatin membranes demonstrated enhanced osteogenic differentiation in pre-osteoblast cells [206]. Hybrid CS/calcium phosphate (CaP) NFs crosslinked with vanillin and incorporating silver ions exhibited antibacterial activity, sustained ion release, and excellent compatibility with bone marrow stromal cells [207]. Collectively, these studies highlight crosslinking as a versatile and powerful approach for reinforcing the structural integrity, functional properties, and bioactivity of ESNFs. When carefully optimized, crosslinking enables the development of novel scaffolds that maintain structural integrity while delivering tailored bioactivity for a wide panel of biomedical applications.

Plasma treatment is a widely used post-modification procedure for modulating the surface features of ESNFs, including adhesion, roughness, and wettability [155], [208]. It is considered a cost-effective, environmentally friendly, and solvent-free approach that offers advantages over conventional modification procedures, particularly in terms of energy efficiency, short processing times, and the absence of hazardous chemicals [209], [210]. In contrast to many chemical treatments, plasma modification is rapid, typically requiring only seconds to minutes to achieve the desired surface changes [129]. A key advantage of plasma treatment is its ability to selectively alter the nanofiber surface without modifying the bulk structure or generating harmful byproducts [155], [211]. By carefully selecting the plasma source and optimizing operational parameters, such as working pressure, applied voltage, and gas flow rate, it is possible to add functional groups, generate radical sites, and induce limited chain scission on the fiber surface. These modifications enhance surface reactivity, improve biocompatibility, and facilitate subsequent covalent immobilization of biomolecules [210], [211]. Fig. 8 illustrates various plasma sources used for nanofiber surface modification and the interaction of plasma gases with the fiber surface [212]. Several types of gases, including oxygen, hydrogen, argon, ammonia, nitrogen, helium, and carbon dioxide, are commonly used in plasma treatment. Adjusting the gas composition allows the incorporation of specific functional groups; for instance, oxygen or air plasma promotes the formation of oxygen-containing groups (e.g.,-COOH), while ammonia plasma introduces amine functionalities. These changes significantly increase surface energy, wettability, and roughness [155], [213], [214]. In addition to surface activation, plasma techniques can additionally be employed for thin polymer coating deposition, further enabling the attachment of proteins and other biomolecules onto nanofiber structures [215]. Despite its advantages, plasma treatment is limited by the shallow penetration depth of reactive species, which is governed by exposure time and plasma power [216]. To address this limitation, plasma-treated NFs are generally further functionalized with ECM proteins such as gelatin, collagen, and fibronectin. significantly promotes cell–material interactions and boosts biological functionality, with notable relevance to TE [213], [217], [218].

Chen et al. [213] improved the compatibility of PLLA NFs with chondrocytes by functionalizing their surface with cationized gelatin (CG) for cartilage tissue engineering (CTE) applications. Oxygen plasma treatment was first applied to introduce -COOH onto the NF surface, creating reactive sites for subsequent covalent grafting of CG. Physicochemical characterization confirmed the successful immobilization of CG on the plasma-treated PLLA NFs. Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that chondrocytes cultured on CG-modified PLLA NFMs maintained high viability, exhibited a rounded morphology, and formed cartilage-like tissue enriched in sulfated glycosaminoglycans (sGAG) and type II collagen. These findings underscore the effectiveness of plasma-assisted functionalization in improving cell-material interactions and support the potential of CG-modified PLLA scaffolds for cartilage regeneration [213]. In a related study, Tabaei et al. [219] demonstrated the synergistic effects of coral incorporation and plasma treatment on CS/polyethylene oxide (PEO) NFs for BTE. Coral, a calcium-rich component, was integrated into electrospun CS/PEO NFs, which were subsequently treated using medium-pressure dielectric barrier discharge plasma with argon (Ar), nitrogen (N2), or air (Fig. 9) [219]. Plasma exposure introduced O2- and N2-based functional groups on the NF surfaces, thereby improving wettability and surface reactivity. This modification promoted osteoblast activity, while the presence of coral further supported initial cell adhesion. The biomineralization capacity of these scaffolds was evaluated by immersion in simulated body fluid (SBF). Plasma-treated CS/PEO NFs resulted in globular carbonate apatite nanocrystals formation. In contrast, coral-containing composites showed a denser and more uniform deposition of flake-like nanocrystals, resulting in a thicker mineralized layer while preserving interfibrous porosity and structural integrity. These results demonstrate that combining plasma treatment with bioactive fillers is an efficient approach to enhance the biological and physicochemical performance of nanofiber structures for bone regeneration applications [219].

Plasma treatment is a powerful way for altering the physicochemical features of biomaterials, thereby influencing cell-material interactions and cellular behavior [220], [221], [222]. For instance, Nandakumar et al. [220] utilized radio-frequency (RF) oxygen plasma to modify ESNFs composed of polybutylene terephthalate (PBT)/polyethylene oxide terephthalate (PEOT) copolymers. The treatment produced nanoscale surface roughness and increased oxygen content, thereby enhancing hydrophilicity. This modification also promoted greater bovine serum albumin (BSA) adsorption after 15 and 30 min of exposure. After 21 days of culture, plasma-treated nanofiber meshes supported more extensive cell growth compared to untreated controls. Gene expression analysis further revealed upregulation of bone-related glycoproteins, indicating that oxygen plasma can promote osteogenic differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) [220]. In another work, ES PCL nanofiber meshes were modified using RF plasma with argon or oxygen at varying power levels and exposure times [221]. Plasma treatment significantly improved surface hydrophobicity, as demonstrated by reduced water contact angles. Among the cell types evaluated (chondrocytes, fibroblasts, and osteoblasts), osteoblast-like cells displayed the greatest enhancement in adhesion and proliferation on treated scaffolds. Similarly, biodegradable NFs composed of PGA, PLLA, and PLGA were modified via O2 plasma followed by in situ acrylate attachment. This dual modification introduced -COOH groups, increasing hydrophilicity and significantly improving fibroblast adhesion and proliferation [222]. Jiang et al. [65] demonstrated the versatility of plasma treatment by combining air plasma activation with polydopamine (PDA) coating on PCL NFs. The resulting scaffolds enabled pH-responsive loading and release of DOX. Under acidic conditions, enhanced drug release led to increased cytotoxicity against cancer cells, underlining the potential of plasma-modified NFs for targeted DD applications, including gastric cancer therapy and localized treatments [65].

Plasma treatment can also be integrated with other modification strategies to enhance stem cell differentiation. Kooshki et al. [223] combined oxygen plasma treatment with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) preconditioning of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) on PLLA NFs. This approach improved surface hydrophilicity and cell attachment and significantly enhanced osteogenic differentiation, as confirmed by alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, calcium deposition, gene expression, and immunostaining analyses. In another research, Asadian et al. [224] proposed a two-step modification strategy for PCL ESNFs. Initially, plasma polymerization of acrylic acid introduced -COOH groups onto the surface. After that, post-plasma grafting of ethylenediamine via EDC/NHS coupling was performed, yielding -NH2-functionalized NFs as illustrated in Fig. 10 [224]. Surface characterization confirmed successful modification, including reduced negative charge and altered wettability. These changes significantly enhanced bone marrow stem cell adhesion and proliferation, which is believed to be due to the mutual effects of surface roughness, tailored chemistry, and optimized surface charge [224]. Overall, these studies demonstrate that plasma treatment (either alone or in combination with other modification techniques) offers a greatly adaptable route for enhancing the biological performance of ESNFs. Its ability to precisely tailor surface chemistry and functionality makes it particularly beneficial for regenerative medicine, TE, and targeted therapeutics.

Onak et al. [225] elaborated a surface functionalization strategy for PLGA ESNFs by conjugating biomimetic peptides rich in aspartic acid (ASP) and glutamic acid (GLU). This was achieved using EDC/NHS coupling chemistry following cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) treatment. The approach aimed to enhance osteoinductive properties and assess the ability of the modified structure to support osteogenic differentiation of human bone marrow-derived hMSCs. Comprehensive surface characterization using contact angle measurements, FTIR, XPS, and SEM, demonstrated that CAP treatment significantly improved surface hydrophilicity and increased the density of -COOH groups, enabling efficient peptide conjugation. Biological evaluations revealed that ASP-functionalized NFs (ASP-pNF) outperformed both GLU-functionalized (GLU-pNF) and untreated CAP NFs. Specifically, ASP-pNF scaffolds exhibited higher ALP activity, increased calcium mineral deposition, and upregulated expression of key osteogenic biomarkers such as osteocalcin (OC), osteopontin (OP), and collagen type I (Col-I). These findings underline the strong potential of ASP-conjugated NFs for biomimetic scaffold design in bone regeneration applications [225]. Furthermore, multiple studies [226], [227], [228], [229] have consistently demonstrated that plasma-based surface treatments significantly improve cell adhesion and proliferation on ESNFs. Overall, plasma treatment represents a versatile and tunable strategy for introducing functional groups onto nanofiber surfaces, enabling their optimization for various biomedical applications [208], [212], [213], [214], [215], [216], [217], [221], [230].

Ultraviolet (UV) treatment is one of the simplest and most affordable approaches for surface modification of ESNFs, as it eliminates the need for chemical reagents or vacuum systems [231]. UV irradiation alters surface chemistry by inducing polymer chain scission and generating functional groups, while largely preserving nanofiber morphology and alignment [232], [233]. Additionally, UV exposure produces surface-bound free radicals that act as reactive sites for subsequent modifications, including grafting, crosslinking, and covalent immobilization of biomolecules [234], [235]. These modifications enhance surface hydrophilicity, tailor chemical functionality, and significantly improve cell adhesion and proliferation [236], [237]. Moreover, UV-induced crosslinking can be applied to both hydrophilic and hydrophobic polymeric NFs to improve water resistance and structural stability, resulting in insoluble polymer networks suitable for long-term biomedical applications [238]. Tort et al. [239] studied the effect of UV exposure time on nanofiber-based wound dressings. They reported that 2 h of irradiation achieved effective sterilization without compromising fiber morphology, wettability, mechanical properties, or bioadhesion. Khosravi et al. [240] demonstrated the covalent immobilization of silk fibroin (SF) onto PCL NFs using UV-ozone activation, followed by acrylic acid grafting to introduce -COOH groups. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 fibroblasts proved enhanced cytocompatibility, cell adhesion, and proliferation compared to untreated scaffolds. In a related approach, UV photolithography was employed to fabricate microporous electrospun scaffolds, in which patterned UV exposure generated ∼100 μm pores that facilitated directional muscle cell migration, underscoring the significant potential of UV-based patterning for 3D TE [240]. Similarly, Asadi et al. [241] utilized UV treatment to immobilize enzymes on PAN/PVA NFs, preserving structural integrity while enabling controlled enzyme release. Andrews et al. [242] compared UV-ozone and ethylene oxide sterilization of Tecoflex® SG-80A PU NFs, finding that UV-ozone treatment reduced surface roughness via photo-oxidative effects and improved cell coverage through favorable topographical changes. Mohsen et al. [243] developed UV-treated PVA/CS NFs for wound healing, demonstrating broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, high cell viability (96.9% at 2000 mg/mL), and complete wound closure within 72 h. Collectively, these studies establish UV treatment as a safe, efficient, and versatile strategy for tailoring the surface properties of ESNFs, enabling their application across a wide span of biomedical fields.

Physical adsorption is one of the most straightforward, cost-effective, and non-destructive strategies for functionalizing the surface of ESNFs. This method relies on non-covalent interactions to enable molecular attachment onto nanofiber surfaces [244]. A significant advantage of this method is its capability to introduce functional moieties without altering the bulk properties or structural integrity of the NFs [167]. Typically, the process involves spraying or immersing NFs in biomolecule-containing solutions, allowing spontaneous adsorption driven by intermolecular interactions [129]. Physical adsorption is applicable to various electrospinnable polymers such as PLLA, PLGA, PCL, PVP, PVA, and PEG [245], [246], [247], [248]. Commonly adsorbed biomolecules include peptides, proteins, enzymes, polysaccharides, growth factors, antibacterial agents, and vitamins [128], [249], [250], [251]. This strategy enhances cellular recognition of surface cues, promotes cell adhesion, and improves overall biocompatibility without compromising scaffold architecture [129], [252]. Furthermore, it enables rapid immobilization of bioactive molecules and helps preserve their bioactivity by avoiding harsh processing conditions such as organic solvents, elevated temperatures, or high-voltage conditions during ES [247], [253].

Casper et al. [245] incorporated low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) conjugated with polyethylene glycol (PEG-LMWH) into PEO/PLGA NFs to enhance their bioactivity for tissue regeneration and DD. The modification preserved fiber morphology while improving binding affinity for fibroblast growth factors. Similarly, Patel et al. [246] combined surface adsorption of ECM proteins and growth factors with fiber alignment to mimic native tissue architecture. Their results showed that aligned NFs significantly enhanced neurite outgrowth, while biochemical functionalization further amplified this effect, underscoring the synergistic role of physical and biochemical cues. Shitole et al. [247] demonstrated the functionalization of core-sheath ESNFs composed of a poly (vinyl pyrrolidone)-iodine (PVP-I) core and a PCL shell using Poly-L-lysine as a surface modifier. The modified NFs exhibited significantly enhanced protein adsorption, with higher affinity for BSA and fibrinogen than pristine PCL. Cytocompatibility studies confirmed non-toxicity at an optimized PVP-I concentration (3.0 wt%), while poly-L-lysine-functionalized NFs showed enhanced cell viability after 7 days of culture. Additionally, the scaffolds demonstrated strong antimicrobial activity against both S. aureus and E. coli, highlighting their potential as multifunctional wound dressings that promote early-stage healing and prevent infection.

Chen et al. [254] functionalized silica/PVP composite NFs with laminin, a key ECM matrix protein. The modified scaffolds exhibited excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and structural stability for up to 18 days. Notably, neurite extension was markedly greater on covalently functionalized fibers as opposed to both unmodified and physically adsorbed laminin-coated fibers, indicating that while adsorption is simple, covalent strategies may provide stronger and more stable biofunctional effects in certain applications. Ye et al. [255] reported a facile adsorption-based modification of thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) NFs using cellulose nanofibrils under ultrasonication. This treatment resulted in uniform surface coating, enhanced hydrophilicity, and improved mechanical properties. Importantly, the modified NFs significantly promoted adhesion and proliferation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), demonstrating their suitability for vascular tissue engineering (VTE).

In DD applications, Kim et al. [256] encapsulated the hydrophilic antibiotic cefoxitin sodium (Mefoxin®) onto PLGA NFs. While initial drug release was rapid, the incorporation of PEG-b-PLA enabled sustained release over seven days, with antimicrobial activity exceeding 90% inhibition of Staphylococcus aureus. Similarly, Bolgen et al. [257] developed PCL NFMs loaded with Biteral®, which significantly reduced postoperative adhesions and supported tissue healing in vivo. In a related work, Xiao et al. [258] engineered a 3D PCL NF scaffold through sequential surface hydrolysis, biomimetic mineralization, and SF coating as demonstrated in Fig. 11. This process generated a -COOH -rich, bone-mimicking architecture that supported directional cell growth and enhanced proliferation. In vivo studies further confirmed improved tissue organization and accelerated bone regeneration [258]. Overall, physical adsorption represents a resourceful and useful surface modification strategy for ESNFs. Despite its simplicity and preservation of biomolecule activity, its relatively weak interaction strength compared to covalent methods may limit long-term stability, highlighting the need to tailor the approach to specific biomedical applications.

Layer-by-layer (LBL) assembly is a highly adaptable surface modification procedure that enables precise control over film thickness, spanning the nanometer-to-micrometer scale [259], [260], [261], [262], [263]. The method relies on the sequential attachment of negatively charged species to a substrate, resulting in a well-ordered multilayered coatings or freestanding films. Electrostatic attraction is the main driving force; however, additional interactions such as covalent and non-covalent bonding, metal-ligand coordination, and specific biomolecular recognition can also contribute to film assembly [264], [265], [266]. Between successive deposition steps, intermediate rinsing (and typically drying) was performed to remove loosely bound species and prevent cross-contamination, thereby preserving layer integrity. The total number of layers can be simply tuned by adjusting the amount of deposition cycles, while film features like composition, thickness, morphology, and porosity can be precisely adjusted by controlling solution parameters (e.g., concentration, pH, ionic strength) and processing conditions (e.g., temperature and deposition time) [267].

LBL assembly is widely regarded as an affordable, environmentally friendly technique that does not require harsh organic solvents or high-temperature processing. It offers exceptional tunability in terms of film architecture, porosity, and mass loading, and is compatible with various substrates and biomolecules due to its mild processing conditions [128], [268], [269]. In addition, its scalability and ability to incorporate multiple functional components render it highly appropriate for creating responsive, multifunctional materials. A rich selection of building blocks, including natural and synthetic polymers, proteins, lipids, DNA, NPs, and supramolecular complexes, can be integrated using this approach, allowing the design of innovative functional coatings for various application fields, like biomedicine, catalysis, energy storage, optics, and filtration [270]. Several LBL deposition strategies have been developed, including dip-coating (immersion), spin-assisted deposition, spray-assisted assembly, electromagnetic-assisted assembly, and microfluidic-based assembly [270]. Each technique offers distinct advantages and constraints regarding deposition speed, uniformity, structural control, and scalability, making method selection critical for application-specific design [271].

In biomedical engineering, LBL assembly has materialized as a powerful strategy for functionalizing electrospun NF membranes without significantly altering their intrinsic porosity or morphology. Its ability to uniformly coat complex 3D fibrous structures has enabled broad applications in TE, bone regeneration, controlled DD, wound healing, and biosensing [272], [273], [274], [275], [276], [277], [278]. For example, Ma et al. functionalized SF ESNFs using LBL deposition of CS and PDA, resulting in enhanced antibacterial activity and improved cytocompatibility [279]. Similarly, Zhou et al. constructed multifunctional antibacterial NFMs by combining ES and LBL deposition of quaternized chitin (QC) and tannic acid (TA), thereby achieving improved wettability, antibacterial performance, antioxidant activity, and hemocompatibility for wound-healing applications [280].

LBL assembly has also been intensively applied in BTE through biomimetic mineralization strategies.
