For example, Zheng et al. developed apatite-coated PCL NFs using LBL assembly of collagen and chondroitin sulfate followed by mineralization, resulting in enhanced osteogenic differentiation and in vivo bone formation. The fabrication procedure for biofunctional bone scaffolds using the LBL approach is depicted in Fig. 12 [281]. Similarly, Wang et al. constructed a tissue-engineered periosteum by integrating PCL, nano-hydroxyapatite (nHAp), and collagen with bone marrow-derived stem cells, promoting efficient osseointegration and reducing fibrotic encapsulation [282]. Further advancing multifunctional scaffold design, Cheng et al. developed core-sheath nanofibrous mats with spatially controlled delivery of BMP2 and CTGF using LBL functionalization, achieving temporally regulated growth factor release and enhanced bone regeneration outcomes [272]. In another study, PLLA NFs functionalized with CS, heparin, and graphene oxide via LBL assembly exhibited increased surface roughness, hydrophilicity, mechanical strength, and improved endothelial cell compatibility, while also reducing inflammatory responses [283].

The aforementioned discussion of the different functionalization strategies for ESNFs emphasizes that no single strategy is universally superior; rather, each involves a balance among biological advantages, material performance, process complexity, and translational feasibility. Table 1 provides a concise comparative analysis of the major functionalization strategies discussed earlier in this manuscript, highlighting their key advantages, limitations, and most suitable biomedical applications. From a translational perspective, the most promising functionalization strategies should therefore be selected not solely on the basis of their ability to enhance biological performance, but also on whether the resulting improvements provide a meaningful therapeutic advantage that justifies the additional material, processing, manufacturing, and regulatory complexity.

Nanofiber technology has rapidly emerged as a key focus in biomedical research, offering promising solutions to major clinical challenges, including wound and burn care, osteoporosis treatment, organ regeneration, and the management of various diseases [284], [285], [286]. ESNFs are particularly attractive due to their exceptionally high surface area relative to bulk materials, which improves the adhesion of cells, proteins, and therapeutic agents. Additionally, these NFs can be assembled into complex 3D architectures, enabling their use in diverse biomedical applications [284], [285], [286], [287], [288]. The large interfacial surface of NFs contributes to improved cellular interactions, enhanced drug loading volume, and tunable drug release profiles. Furthermore, optimization of ES parameters, such as polymer type, solution properties, and fiber alignment, allows accurate modulation of cell differentiation and DD behavior. Consequently, the combination of high surface area, mechanical elasticity, and adaptable surface chemistry makes ESNFs highly valuable in biomedical applications [284], [285], [286], [287], [288], [289], [290], [291]. Importantly, the properties of ESNFs can be further tailored through surface functionalization using various chemical groups and bioactive molecules. Such modifications significantly influence both physicochemical and biological characteristics. For instance, surface treatments can alter wettability, thermal features (including melting and glass transition temperatures), and overall stability of the NFs [43], [285], [289]. Simultaneously, biological properties such as biocompatibility, cell adhesion, and cell proliferation can be markedly enhanced. A wide range of materials (polymers, metal and magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs), carbon-based nanomaterials, functional groups, proteins, and peptides) have been employed for nanofiber surface modification [43], [285], [289]. These innovations have led to extensive integration of functionalized ESNFs across domains such as regenerative medicine, TE, wound healing, targeted DD, biosensing, and cell imaging. Overall, surface-functionalized ESNFs represent a powerful tool for next-generation biomedical technologies. The following sections will discuss their applications in greater detail across various biomedical domains.

TE and regenerative medicine sit at the intersection of biology, clinical medicine, and materials science, with the primary goal of restoring or replacing damaged tissues and organs. Given the structural intricacy of the human body and the interdependence of its tissues, biomaterials should be carefully designed to ensure mechanical integrity, biocompatibility, and chemical compatibility with the physiological microenvironment. In this context, NFs have emerged as a critical class of biomaterials due to their structural resemblance to the ECM, which enables dynamic cell-material interactions and supports tissue regeneration [292], [293], [294]. For instance, Zheng et al. [295] developed functionalizable nanostructured scaffolds by combining PCL with 4-dibenzocyclooctynol via chemical polymerization. This strategy enabled the synthesis of adaptable arrangements suitable for various TE purposes. Their design leveraged the interplay between sol and gel states, emphasizing the importance of rheological transitions from injectable sol phases to mechanically stable gel networks. Similarly, Doench et al. [296] engineered a nanostructured system based on nanofibrillated cellulose for nucleus pulposus regeneration. In vivo studies using porcine and rabbit spinal models demonstrated that injectable cellulose nanofibril/CS formulations improved biomechanical performance of intervertebral discs, highlighting their potential in spinal tissue repair.

A crucial aspect of successful tissue regeneration is the promotion of angiogenesis, particularly in hard-tissue repair such as bone regeneration. Kuttappan et al. [297] demonstrated that ESNF membranes can serve as carriers for the localized and controlled delivery of key signaling molecules like vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), and BMP-2. These biomolecules perform complementary roles: VEGF stimulates vascularization in MSCs, BMP-2 promotes osteogenic differentiation [298], and basic FGF (bFGF) enhances endothelial cell migration and proliferation, particularly in HUVECs [299]. The controlled and sequential release of these factors from NF-based systems was shown to substantially accelerate the formation of vascularized bone tissue, a major objective in advanced regenerative therapies.

Cell-material interactions are central to scaffold performance and directly influence cellular behavior. Cho et al. [145] investigated the metabolic outcome of cells cultured on different NF systems (aNFs, HA0@NFs, and HA5@NFs) using WST-1 assays. While aNFs initially supported higher cell viability during the first three days, a decline was observed by day 5, likely due to cell overcrowding and the scaffold's structural instability as depicted in Fig. 13a [145]. In contrast, HA-modified NFs, particularly HA5@NFs, maintained superior cell viability, attributed to HA's stabilizing effect. DNA quantification further confirmed enhanced cell proliferation on HA-functionalized NFs, with HA5@NFs showing the highest proliferation rates throughout the culture period (Fig. 13b) [145]. In addition to proliferation, HA functionalization significantly influenced cell morphology as depicted in Fig. 13c [145]. NIH 3T3 fibroblasts cultured on HA-modified NFs exhibited a more elongated morphology with enhanced actin filament organization, whereas cells on unmodified NFs displayed a rounded shape with weaker cytoskeletal development [145]. These findings highlight the importance of surface-mediated cell adhesion, particularly for anchorage-dependent cells such as fibroblasts. Enhanced ECM protein adsorption on HA-functionalized surfaces further enhances cell adhesion and proliferation [300]. These results are consistent with previous studies demonstrating that HA incorporation promotes cytoskeletal organization and strengthens cell-material interactions, underscoring the critical role of ECM-mimetic cues in TE applications [301].

Nanofibrous scaffolds can be specifically engineered for targeted clinical applications, including ocular wound healing. Yan et al. [42] designed a PLA electrospun scaffold functionalized with silver nanoparticle/cellulose nanofiber (AgNPs/CNF) hybrids to create a multifunctional system with enhanced antibacterial and cell-supportive properties. The fabrication process of PLA-based electrospun fiber mats (EFMs) incorporating CNF and AgNPs is illustrated in Fig. 14 [42]. This study represents an early effort to design ocular bandages with intrinsic antimicrobial activity, potentially reducing the need for repeated topical antibiotic administration. In this system, cellulose NFs (CNFs) served as anchoring platforms for silver NPs at very low loading levels, simultaneously improving scaffold hydrophilicity and imparting antibacterial functionality. In vitro co-culture studies demonstrated excellent biocompatibility with ocular epithelial cells, with CNF-coated scaffolds significantly enhancing cell proliferation. The scaffolds exhibited strong antimicrobial activity, achieving over 95% inhibition against E. coli and S. aureus, as well as notable antifungal activity against Fusarium species. Although silver NPs are often associated with cytotoxicity concerns [302], [303], the modified scaffolds (PLA-1 and PLA-2) maintained normal cell morphology and proliferation comparable to pure PLA, indicating that the AgNP concentrations used were within a safe range. Live/dead staining assays (Fig. 15a1-a4 and 15b1-b4) revealed minimal cell death, further confirming the non-toxic nature of the scaffolds [42].

Effective ocular bandages must also promote rapid wound healing by facilitating cell movement and proliferation [304]. Consistent with this requirement, BrdU-based proliferation assays (Fig. 15c1-c4 and 15d1-d4) showed a higher proportion of proliferating cells on PLA-1 and PLA-2 scaffolds compared to tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS) and non-modified PLA. Both conjunctival epithelial cells (CjECs) and corneal epithelial cells (CECs) exhibited the highest viability on the modified scaffolds, confirming their aptitude to support cell growth. Enhanced cell viability over 48 and 72 h further highlighted the beneficial effect of CNF incorporation on scaffold cytocompatibility. This improvement was primarily attributed to enhanced surface hydrophilicity, as demonstrated by a reduced water contact angle, which created a more beneficial environment for cell adhesion and proliferation. Additionally, CNF incorporation contributed to collagen-like fibrillar features within the scaffold, which may further influence cellular responses [305]. Overall, the combined mechanical and biological enhancements of these PLA-based nanofibrous scaffolds underscore their strong potential as ocular wound-healing materials. The incorporation of CNF promotes epithelial regeneration, while AgNPs provide effective antimicrobial protection, making these scaffolds promising candidates for advanced ocular therapies [42].

In the pursuit of multifunctional scaffolds for bone repair, Cheng et al. [272] developed core-sheath structured SF/PCL/PVA NF constructs using coaxial ES combined with LBL assembly, as shown in Fig. 16. In this design, BMP-2 (10 μg/mL) was integrated into the nanofiber core. In contrast, connective tissue growth factor (CTGF, 10 μg/mL) was immobilized on the surface, enabling a double DD construct with temporally controlled release profiles. Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that the dual-functioning system successfully promoted osteogenesis and angiogenesis. A sequential release behavior was observed: BMP-2 exhibited a sustained, nearly linear release over 30 days, while CTGF showed a relatively faster release over approximately 40 days. When implanted into cranial defects of mice, the BMP-2/CTGF-loaded SF/PCL (1:5)/PVA-LBL20 scaffolds achieved extensively enhanced bone formation (∼43%) as opposed to structures delivering BMP-2 alone. After eight weeks, the dual-delivery system maintained the highest bone volume and area, along with increased expression of angiogenic indicators such as VEGF and CD31. These findings highlight the effectiveness of time-controlled release enabled by core-sheath NF architectures in coordinating osteogenic differentiation and vascularization, thereby accelerating bone regeneration and microvascular development [272]. In a complementary strategy, Oliveira et al. [306] developed injectable composite scaffolds based on organically modified glass (ormoglass) particles enriched with calcium and phosphorus (CaO: P2O5:Na2O: TiO2 molar ratio of 44.5:44.5:6:5). These particles were synthesized via a partially hydrolyzed alkoxide sol-gel process, subsequently coated with PLA fibers, and uniformly dispersed in a 40% (w/v) hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) hydrogel matrix. Upon implantation into the femoral condyles of Wistar rats, the scaffolds promoted both angiogenesis and bone regeneration within 3-6 weeks. This outcome was primarily attributed to the controlled release of Ca2+, which plays a critical role in bone remodeling and vascularization [306].

Bone, a dense connective tissue, plays a fundamental role in sustaining structural integrity and supporting vital organs [307]. However, traumatic injuries, infections, and pathological conditions often result in bone defects that are difficult to repair using conventional grafting techniques [308]. Consequently, BTE has become a multidisciplinary field that combines biomaterials, cells, and bioactive signaling molecules to restore bone function more effectively than traditional grafts or implants [309]. Among the various biomaterial strategies, nanofibrous scaffolds and membranes functionalized with bioactive agents have shown significant promise. Their structural similarity to the native ECM offers an ideal microenvironment for cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation [310], [311]. In particular, 2D NFMs are designed not merely to fill bone defects but to guide and regulate new bone tissue formation in a controlled manner [293]. Beyond bone regeneration, nanofibrous systems have also demonstrated considerable potential in VTE. Jia et al. [312] investigated tissue-engineered blood vessels (TEBVs) fabricated from collagen and chondroitin sulfate-collagen (ChS-COL) NFs, which were implanted into unilateral carotid arteries of New Zealand white rabbits (Fig. 17A-B). Of the six animals used in the study, one animal died due to postoperative complications. At the same time, the remaining grafts were explanted after 10 days for evaluation of early endothelialization and thrombosis. SEM analysis revealed that collagen-based TEBVs exhibited extensive blood clot formation, indicating significant thrombosis (Fig. 17C) [312]. Histological assessments, including hematoxylin-eosin and Masson's trichrome staining, further confirmed lumen occlusion in these grafts, characterized by dense platelet aggregation and the absence of a functional endothelial layer (Fig. 17D-E) [312]. In contrast, ChS-COL nanofiber-based grafts displayed a smooth, thrombus-free lumen. They were covered by a uniform monolayer of endothelial-like cells expressing PECAM and ICAM markers, confirming successful endothelialization (Fig. 17F) [312]. These results emphasize a critical role of surface composition and biofunctionalization in modulating blood compatibility and cellular responses, underscoring the significant potential of nanofibrous scaffolds in both BTE and VTE.

Electrospun SF/Poly(L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone) (SF/PLCL) scaffolds have demonstrated significant potential in promoting bone tissue regeneration. When cultured with human adipose-derived stem cells (hADSCs), SF/PLCL (50:50) scaffolds exhibited an optimal tensile strength of about 6 MPa and an enhanced ALP activity (∼150 absorbance units), compared to ∼80 for pure PLCL, indicating improved osteogenic differentiation [313]. Similarly, Zhu et al. [314] incorporated adenoviral vector-encoded BMP-2 into electrospun PLGA NFs with fine diameters (∼140 ± 40 nm), which supported bone marrow stromal cell adhesion and proliferation. After 14 days, the expression of key osteogenic markers, including collagen type I, Runx2, and ALP, was markedly increased. In another study, Dhand et al. [315] developed collagen-based ES scaffolds incorporating calcium and catecholamines, resulting in mechanically robust constructs (Young's modulus ∼675.8 ± 81 MPa) that closely simulate the configuration of natural bone. These scaffolds significantly enhanced osteoblastic differentiation, with ALP activity per cell reaching 0.12 on day 14 compared to 0.075 for the tissue culture plastic (TCP) control. Karaman et al. [316] further demonstrated that MSCs cultured on PLGA NFs functionalized with glutamate-rich peptides retained osteoblast-like morphology under osteogenic conditions, confirming enhanced differentiation. Osteogenic differentiation is a multistep process involving cell adhesion, proliferation, ECM deposition, and mineralization. While synthetic scaffolds are typically bioinert, they can be rendered osteoinductive by incorporating ECM-mimetic peptide motifs that activate relevant cellular signaling pathways [317]. The evaluation of osteogenesis commonly relies on markers such as ALP activity, Ca2+ accumulation, and osteogenic protein expression [318], [319]. Consistent with this, immunofluorescence analyses after 28 days of culture revealed that hMSCs grown on ASP-functionalized NFs exhibited significantly higher expression of collagen type I (COL-I), OP, and OC compared to those cultured on GLU-functionalized or unmodified NFs [225]. These findings suggest that while both ASP and GLU peptides promote osteogenic differentiation, ASP exerts a more pronounced inductive effect.

Beyond regeneration, nanofibrous systems are also being investigated for the treatment of bone-related cancers such as osteosarcoma (OS), where surgical resection often results in large, difficult-to-repair defects. Conventional allogeneic grafts are associated with risks including infection, immune rejection, and disease transmission (e.g., HIV, hepatitis) [320], [321]. To address these challenges, current strategies focus on integrating therapeutic agents into biodegradable polymeric systems, such as hydrogels, microspheres, NPs, and electrospun fibers, to create multifunctional implants [322]. Electrospun membranes are particularly attractive due to their increased interfacial area, drug-loading capacity, and ECM-mimicking structure. The development of coaxial ES has enabled the fabrication of core-sheath NFs capable of dual or sequential drug release. For example, He et al. [323] engineered a core-sheath membrane with naringenin-loaded PVP in the core and metronidazole-loaded PLGA in the shell, achieving both rapid and sustained drug release. However, single-drug systems often fall short in addressing the multifaceted requirements of cancer therapy [324], [325]. To overcome this limitation, Cao et al. [326] elaborated a multifunctional coaxial nanofibrous membrane co-loaded with DOX, nHAp, and ICA, a flavonoid known to promote osteogenesis. In this system, DOX and nHAp were incorporated into the shell, while ICA was embedded in the core, enabling sequential release to achieve combined antitumor and bone regenerative effects.

Building on this concept, Liu et al. [202] demonstrated that such composite membranes possess sufficient flexibility to conform to irregular bone defects, making them proper for guided bone regeneration (GBR) applications (Fig. 18). Their biological evaluations revealed strong cytotoxic effects against MG-63 OS cells, particularly in higher DOX-loading formulations (2% and 4% DHGIP), as evidenced by extensive cell death (Fig. 19A). The two-stage release mechanism (i) initial diffusion of DOX followed by (ii) gradual release from nHAp ensured sustained antitumor activity. Importantly, the same scaffolds supported the viability and proliferation of MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts, with relative growth rates exceeding 90% in most formulations and surpassing 95% in lower DOX-content samples after 168 h. Morphological analyses using SEM and fluorescence imaging confirmed healthy, elongated cell morphology and strong adhesion to the nanofibrous matrix (Fig. 19B-C). Overall, these findings demonstrate that multifunctional electrospun nanofibrous scaffolds can simultaneously inhibit tumor growth and promote bone regeneration, offering a promising strategy for GBR following OS resection [202].

Building on the incorporation of bone-mimetic inorganic phases, Gao et al. [327] co-electrospun nHAp platelets into PCL NFs, resulting in enhanced osteoconductivity and mechanical stiffness. These composite structures promoted osteogenic differentiation of hMSCs in vitro and significantly improved in vivo bone formation. Similarly, hydroxyapatite (HA)/poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) NFs were shown to support the differentiation of hADSCs while also improving mechanical performance, with increases in elastic modulus (12.7%), stress at break (25.7%), and elongation at break (52%) [328]. Ko et al. [329] further advanced this strategy by functionalizing electrospun SF scaffolds with HA distributed throughout both the inner and outer regions, thereby markedly accelerating mineralized tissue formation in a critical-sized calvarial defect model. In another approach, CaP deposition onto hydroxyethyl cellulose/PVA (HEC/PVA) NFs significantly improved osteoconductivity, increasing the elastic modulus from 355 ± 10 MPa to 412 ± 12 MPa [330]. Additionally, magnetically functionalized organic-inorganic hybrid NFs have emerged as promising multifunctional scaffolds, offering enhanced osteogenic potential and antimicrobial properties, thereby broadening their applicability at implantation sites [285].

Beyond BTE, nanofibrous scaffolds have also shown promise in cartilage regeneration. In one study [213], cartilage-oriented constructs were evaluated histologically to assess chondrocyte morphology, cell distribution, and ECM formation. After 14 days, PLLA NFMs predominantly exhibited spindle-shaped, fibroblast-like cells, whereas chondroitin sulfate-grafted PLLA (CG-PLLA) NFMs displayed round or oval cells characteristic of chondrocytes. Alcian blue and Safranin O staining confirmed the existence of sulfated proteoglycan-rich ECM in both systems; however, CG-PLLA NFMs showed more intense and uniform staining, indicating higher glycosaminoglycan (GAG) accumulation and the formation of lacunae-like structures resembling native hyaline cartilage. Further in vivo analysis compared unseeded control CG-PLLA NFMs with cell-seeded constructs using histological staining methods, including hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Alcian blue, and Safranin O (Fig. 20a–g) [213]. Control samples showed minimal tissue infiltration and only a slight inflammatory response, suggesting limited host interaction. In contrast, by week 4, cell-seeded constructs exhibited rounded cells maintaining a chondrocyte phenotype, along with abundant pericellular GAG deposition, as evidenced by Alcian blue and Safranin O staining. Immunohistochemical investigation further confirmed cartilage-specific matrix formation, with positive staining for type II collagen observed throughout the CG-PLLA scaffolds (Fig. 20h) [213]. Overall, these discoveries reiterate the versatility of ESNFs structure in both BTE and CTE, where the incorporation of inorganic phases and biofunctional modifications can significantly enhance mechanical performance, cellular response, and tissue-specific regeneration.

From a broader regenerative medicine perspective, replacing allografts or xenografts requires biomaterials that do more than simply avoid adverse host responses; they must actively regulate cell-material interactions in a manner that recapitulates the native ECM, while maintaining appropriate biodegradation kinetics, mechanical integrity, and mass transport properties. ES has therefore emerged as a key fabrication strategy, enabling precise control over fiber diameter, alignment, and porosity to mimic the fibrillar architecture of ECM across a range of tissues, including bone, skin, and nerve [331], [332]. However, many synthetic polymer-based scaffolds inherently lack bioactive surface cues [333], necessitating extensive surface modification to introduce cell-recognizable ligands and biomolecules [128]. The primary objective of such modifications is to promote integrin-mediated adhesion through defined biochemical motifs, thereby enhancing the survival, proliferation, and function of both transplanted and infiltrating cells [334]. For example, dextran grafted biodegradable PCL NFs were studied for TE applications [335]. Gelatin, a commonly used bioactive coating, was also applied to PCL NFs to improve endothelial cell spreading and proliferation, enhance cell orientation, and support the development of new materials for blood vessel engineering [336], [337]. Another example involves the use of mussel-inspired PDA coatings to convert hydrophobic nanofibrous surfaces into highly cell-adhesive substrates [338]. The authors experimentally validating the finding that a conformal PDA coating on 3D PCL nanofibrous meshes significantly enhances endothelial cell adhesion (Fig. 21A). In their approach, PCL NFs were fabricated via ES and subsequently immersed in an aqueous dopamine (DA) solution, where in situ oxidative polymerization led to the formation of a uniform PDA layer. Morphological analysis revealed that all scaffolds retained a non-woven nanofibrous architecture with a highly porous structure suitable for nutrient transport and ECM mimicry [338]. SEM imaging confirmed that fiber diameters were comparable across the various treatment groups, indicating that macroscopic fiber diameter alone is insufficient to confirm successful PDA deposition (Fig. 21B) [338]. Nevertheless, further analysis divulged that the PDA layer formed a uniform coating with an approximate width of ∼40 nm after 16 h of incubation, consistent with previously reported values [339], [340].

Mammalian cells typically undergo a sequential adhesion process involving cytoskeletal organization, substrate attachment, and cell spreading [296]. To visualize these events in HUVECs cultured on unmodified and surface-modified PCL NFs, rhodamine-phalloidin staining was employed to label filamentous actin [338]. Analysis of cytoskeletal organization and cell morphology revealed that HUVECs on pristine PCL NFs remained predominantly spherical or weakly elongated, indicating limited adhesion and restricted spreading (Fig. 22A) [338]. In contrast, PDA-coated PCL NFs supported a well-spread, fibroblast-like morphology characterized by extensive cytoskeletal organization. Gelatin-coated fibers exhibited an intermediate response, with a heterogeneous population containing both spread and rounded cells. This difference is probably due to the distinct interfacial chemistries of the coatings. In the case of PDA, spontaneous oxidative polymerization generates a bioactive surface capable of covalently interacting with serum proteins via Schiff-base formation and Michael-type addition reactions involving amine and thiol groups [288]. These adsorbed proteins retain their native conformation and biological activity, thereby providing stable and functionally active adhesion sites for cells [297]. By contrast, gelatin attachment to PCL is predominantly driven by weak physical adsorption, resulting in reduced stability and lower surface density of bioactive ligands, ultimately limiting sustained cell adhesion and spreading [298]. Immunofluorescence analysis further supported these observations. The endothelial junctional marker PECAM-1 was primarily localized at cell-cell interfaces in PDA- and gelatin-coated samples, indicating enhanced intercellular connectivity. In contrast, in unmodified PCL, it was largely restricted to isolated cells with poor junction formation (Fig. 22B) [338]. Consistent trends were observed on non-adherent control substrates. In the absence of surface modification, HUVECs displayed poor attachment and a diffuse cytoskeletal structure lacking well-defined stress fibers (Fig. 23A) [338]. Although gelatin coating modestly improved cell spreading, substantial heterogeneity in morphology remained across different substrates. In contrast, PDA modification promoted uniform adhesion and robust stress fiber formation across all underlying materials, indicating strong, substrate-independent bioactivity. Metabolic activity assays further corroborated these morphological findings. MTT analysis demonstrated that PDA treatment significantly enhanced HUVEC viability, increasing metabolic activity by approximately 7.5-fold on PDMS, 8.8-fold on SR, and 2.7-fold on PE compared to unmodified controls, whereas gelatin produced only marginal improvements (Fig. 23B) [338]. Overall, these results demonstrate that PDA serves as a versatile, broadly effective surface modification strategy applicable to both flat films and 3D nanofibrous scaffolds, significantly enhancing endothelial adhesion and functionality in VTE applications [338].

A wide range of cell types benefit from nanofibrous meshes, including keratinocytes, hepatocytes, MSCs, and embryonic stem cells, largely due to their high interface-to-volume proportion and ECM-mimetic topography [341]. In liver TE, for example, acrylic acid has been photo-grafted onto thermoplastic NFs to introduce -COOH functionalities, which are subsequently conjugated to galactopyranoside. The resulting galactosylated, highly porous poly (ε-caprolactone-co-ethyl ethylene phosphate) (PCLEEP) scaffolds supported rat hepatocyte adhesion in vitro and promoted spheroid formation with enhanced hepatic function [339]. Fiber architecture has also been shown to strongly influence cellular behavior. Electrospun meshes fabricated in both random and aligned configurations and subsequently coated with collagen supported human coronary artery endothelial cell proliferation along the direction of the underlying fibers, while maintaining characteristic endothelial morphology independent of alignment [341]. In cartilage bioreactor systems, nanofibrous grids have enabled long-term stem cell expansion and chondrogenic differentiation over 42 days, resulting in elevated expression of key cartilage-specific ECM components like aggrecan and type II collagen [341]. More generally, surface immobilization of adhesive ligands, including collagen, fibronectin, and RGD peptides, leverages the high-aspect-ratio nanofibrous architecture to increase ligand density relative to conventional flat substrates, thereby enhancing initial cell adhesion and accelerating proliferation [341].

Electrospun meshes have also been extensively explored for epithelial TE. Through glutamate-mediated crosslinking, fibronectin was successfully grafted onto PLLC NFs without altering fiber morphology. Although a slight reduction in tensile properties was observed due to mild polyester aminolysis, SEM imaging, immunohistological analysis, and protein quantification confirmed significantly enhanced proliferation and adhesion of porcine esophageal epithelial cells. Besides the structural support, ESNFs have served as efficient platforms for drug and gene delivery, benefiting from rapid fluid uptake at mucosal surfaces driven by nanoscale porosity and strong mucoadhesive properties. Collagen functionalization further enhances stem cell attachment and proliferation, with dose-dependent increases in neural stem cell growth and differentiation attributed to improved initial adhesion and sustained viability on the nanofibrous interface [225]. In parallel, hybrid electrospun systems composed of biodegradable polymers, PLGA beads, and PLLA have been used to expand mouse MSCs, although translating high in vitro cell yields into stable in vivo engraftment remains a key challenge [342].

Chemically modified CNFs provide an additional class of bioactive scaffolds. For example; 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine 1-oxyl (TEMPO)-oxidized CNFs (TOCNFs), which contain C6-COOH groups, support adhesion and proliferation of mouse fibroblasts and myoblasts even in the absence of protein coatings, highlighting the role of charge-mediated cell-material interactions [343]. Further surface phosphorylation of CNFs has been demonstrated to directly induce osteogenic differentiation and matrix mineralization in osteoblast-like cells without the need for exogenous growth factors or collagen supplementation [343]. These findings emphasize that nanoscale crystallinity and surface chemistry are key determinants of cellular response at the biomaterial interface. In the context of xeno-free and serum-free culture systems, recent studies have explored ECM-mimetic alternatives such as polyuronates and sulfated glycosaminoglycan (sGAG)-like materials to replace animal-derived collagen [343], [344]. Combining TOCNFs with polyuronate motifs and newly developed sulfated CNFs (S-CNFs), which mimic GAG sulfate groups, has enabled adhesion and proliferation of primary human MSCs under serum-free conditions. A graphic overview of this strategy is shown in Fig. 24 [344]. Importantly, stem cell multipotency was preserved across multiple CNF-based substrates (TOCNF, TS11, and S-CNF0.64). Immortalized hMSCs expanded for 3 passages retained their differentiation potential, as confirmed by effective induction into osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic lineages. As shown in Fig. 25 [344], chondrogenic induction produced spheroidal cell aggregates within 24 h that stained positively with Alcian Blue after cryosectioning, whereas non-induced controls remained flattened with minimal staining. Adipogenic differentiation resulted in intracellular lipid droplet formation observed by Oil Red O staining, in contrast to undifferentiated spindle-shaped cells. Overall, these results demonstrate that surface-engineered CNFs can sustain stem cell growth and preserve multipotency under serum-free conditions, highlighting their strong potential for clinically relevant, xeno-free regenerative medicine applications [344].

For soft-tissue repair, nanofiber-hydrogel composite systems have demonstrated particular promise in skin regeneration, where mechanical demands are lower than in load-bearing tissues. Liu et al. [345] established an alginate-based hydrogel reinforced with PCL NFs as an implantable skin substitute. The system was further functionalized with an amino-terminated hyperbranched polyamide to impart antimicrobial activity. The resulting composite exhibited high tensile strength, favorable water uptake, and appropriate water vapor permeability, leading to effective performance in an in vivo skin defect model. Similarly, protein-based photocrosslinked hydrogels incorporating NF dispersions have been reported as efficient wound dressings [346]. In this approach, gelatin and decellularized dermal matrix were chemically modified to form gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) and methacrylated decellularized dermal extracellular matrix (ddECMMA), respectively. PCL NF suspensions and thioglycolic acid-modified chitosan (TCS) were incorporated into the precursor solutions, followed by photocrosslinking to generate four hydrogel systems: GelMA, GTP4, DP, and DTP4. These hydrogels exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, excellent biocompatibility, and negligible cytotoxicity. In a full-thickness skin defect model in Sprague-Dawley rats, all hydrogel-treated groups showed significantly enhanced wound healing compared to untreated controls. Histological analyses using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome staining further confirmed improved tissue regeneration, particularly in hydrogels containing both PCL NFs and TCS (GTP4 and DTP4). Among these, the GTP4 formulation demonstrated the most pronounced regenerative effect, highlighting its strong potential for advanced STE applications [346]. Overall, nanofiber reinforcement provides a practical strategy for hydrogel-based wound dressings by improving mechanical stability without requiring excessive crosslinking density. In addition, the embedded nanofibrous network introduces interfacial porosity, enhancing mass transport and providing structural cues that support cell adhesion, migration, and alignment [346]. Beyond skin applications, nanofiber-hydrogel composites incorporating HAp or HAp-like structures have shown strong potential in bone regeneration due to the osteoconductive nature of CaP phases [308], [347]. For instance, Wang et al. [348] fabricated high-aspect-ratio HANFs and integrated them into GelMA hydrogels to form m-HANFs/GelMA composites. Subsequent biomineralization in SBF induced the formation of spherulitic HA structures resembling native bone mineral, which significantly enhanced the proliferation and osteogenic maturation of MC3T3-E1 cells [348].

The literature increasingly highlights drug-eluting nanofiber layers integrated into implants and stents, enabling medical devices to function as localized DD platforms. In a representative study, a urethral stent was wrapped with an ESNF membrane designed for sustained nitrofurantoin delivery, a commonly used antibiotic for urinary tract infections [349]. Drug-free NFs were first fabricated, followed by deposition of drug powder onto the membrane surface, after which the assembly was stretched over the stent to form a multilayer stent-drug-nanofiber construct. In vitro release studies conducted in PBS buffer (0.1 M PBS, pH 6.8; 50 mL) demonstrated near-zero-order release kinetics over 28 days, with cumulative drug release of about 82.8 ± 1.75%. Importantly, in vivo results confirmed the system's ability to deliver prolonged, localized antimicrobials and to improve infection control [349]. Surface-modified, prefabricated nanofibrous meshes are particularly advantageous for drug immobilization on high-surface-area interfaces. Given their exceptionally high interface-to-mass ratio, these meshes can achieve higher drug loading than conventional carriers. They can be engineered for rapid, localized “on-demand” release, making them especially suitable for post-operative antimicrobial prophylaxis [257]. More advanced hierarchical strategies further expand their functionality. For example, drug-loaded NPs can be adsorbed onto nanofiber surfaces to generate composite delivery systems capable of multi-phase or sequential release profiles that are difficult to achieve using homogeneous fiber matrices alone [350], [351]. Three commonly employed physical loading strategies for ESNF surfaces are summarized in Fig. 26 [128]. For sensitive molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, surface immobilization offers a key advantage over bulk encapsulation, as it avoids exposure to harsh ES conditions and the solubility limitations of high-molecular-weight biomolecules in organic solvents. Consequently, biologically active macromolecules can be selectively or non-selectively immobilized on engineered nanofiber surfaces, enabling localized and sustained release while preserving their functional integrity [352].

Nanofiber-coated implants have demonstrated strong potential for localized and sustained DD in ophthalmic applications. For instance, Guerra et al. [353] developed an intravitreal ESNF system co-delivering bevacizumab (50 μg) and dexamethasone (300 μg) from a biodegradable implant. In this system, PLGA degradation primarily governed dexamethasone release, which initiated around day 7 and peaked between days 10-15, whereas bevacizumab exhibited a sustained release profile reaching approximately 88% cumulative release by day 48 [353]. The dual-DD platform was well tolerated when administered intravitreally, highlighting its potential for long-term ocular therapy. More broadly, nanofiber processing parameters can be systematically tuned to regulate drug loading and release kinetics. Kersani et al. [352], for example, proposed a stent-based strategy for preventing post-angioplasty restenosis using simvastatin-loaded electrospun coatings. Dynamic flow studies showed that coating time (10, 30, and 60 min) had minimal influence on burst release for CS-only NFs; however, when CS was combined with cyclodextrin, coating duration significantly modulated release behavior. The time required to reach 90% drug release increased from approximately 15 min to 120 min and 300 min with increasing coating times, respectively, demonstrating the strong influence of processing conditions on drug release kinetics [352]. While short-term in vivo studies confirm the therapeutic efficacy of nanofiber systems for up to 14 days [353], potential systemic drug exposure at higher doses remains a concern [354], underscoring the importance of careful dose optimization. In addition to process-controlled release, pH-responsive nanofiber systems provide an additional mechanism for spatiotemporal control. PLA/CS@ZIF-8 (PLA/CS@ZIF-8) nanofibrous film layers have been shown to exhibit increasing drug loading capacity (DLA) and encapsulation efficiency (EE) with higher 2-methylimidazole (2-MIM) concentrations, attributed to enhanced ZIF-8 crystal growth on the nanofiber surface [355]. For camptothecin (CPT) and artemisia polysaccharide (APS), DLA/EE values reached approximately 32%/91% and 36%/93%, respectively. In vitro release experiments showed distinct release profiles for the two drugs. APS, being hydrophilic, exhibited rapid diffusion, with more than 50% released within 8 h, whereas CPT showed a slower release of approximately 30% over the same period (Fig. 27a and b) [355]. This behavior is consistent with the higher aqueous solubility and diffusion rate of hydrophilic compounds compared to hydrophobic molecules [356], [357], [358]. Release profiles gradually plateaued at approximately 90% for APS and 50% for CPT as diffusion became rate-limiting. Environmental pH further modulated release behavior (Fig. 27c and d) [355]. At physiological pH (7.4), both drugs exhibited sustained release, whereas under acidic conditions (pH 5.5), cumulative release increased to approximately 75% within 10 h. This acceleration is attributed to acid-induced degradation of the ZIF-8 framework into zinc ions and organic ligands [359]. Despite this enhancement, CPT continued to exhibit slower release than APS, reaching only ∼50% under acidic conditions due to diffusion limitations associated with its hydrophobic nature. Overall, these findings demonstrate that PLA/CS@ZIF-8 NFMs function as versatile pH-responsive DD systems, making them particularly suitable for targeted delivery in acidic tumor microenvironments [355].

For applications requiring rapid and localized drug administration, fast-dissolving electrospun systems offer significant advantages. Eudragit-based vancomycin-loaded NFs (E-VAN) have been shown to provide sustained antibiotic release for at least 7 days, with an initial faster release phase attributed to increased hydrophilicity and improved wetting behavior [360]. Such characteristics make these systems suitable for loco-regional therapies, including intravaginal DD [361], intraoral anti-inflammatory treatment [362], anticancer applications [356], and rapid infection control in wound environments [363]. Sustained and tunable drug release from Eudragit matrices can be further achieved through polymer blending or crosslinking strategies [364]. For example, blending E-VAN with the cationic polymer EE100 (25:75, E-VAN1) resulted in pH-responsive release behavior, with the quickest release observed at pH 5.5. In contrast, blending with the ionizable polymer ES100 (25:75, E-VAN2) produced an inverted pH response, showing minimal release at pH 5.2 and accelerated release at pH 8.8, reflecting the solubility profile of ES100 above neutral pH [360]. These tunable behaviors have important practical implications. Specifically, E-VAN2 formulations can function as “smart” wound dressings that enhance drug release in alkaline conditions typically associated with infected wounds, while maintaining reduced release under mildly acidic conditions characteristic of healthy skin [360]. A ternary blend system (E-VAN/ES100/ERL100; 25:40:35) showed intermediate behavior, with relatively faster release at acidic pH (pH5.2) and more sustained release at physiological pH (pH7.4) compared to E-VAN2. Formulations with higher ES100 content (E-VAN4 and E-VAN5) enabled more refined control of release near physiological pH. Overall, these differences are primarily governed by electrostatic interactions between vancomycin and the polymer matrices (EE100-ES100 and VAN-ES100 interactions). Importantly, vancomycin stability remained high throughout the release period, with approximately 96.9%, 97.1%, and 81.5% of the drug remaining after 7 days at pH 5.2, 7.4, and 8.8, respectively [360].

Beyond polymer blending systems, hierarchical “nano-in-nano” architectures further expand control over DD. As illustrated in Fig. 28 [365], capsaicin-loaded alginate NPs (CAP ALG NPs) were embedded within PCL-CS ESNFs to create a composite delivery platform designed to stabilize the drug, regulate release kinetics, and enhance anticancer efficacy. Within alginate NPs, CAP achieved an exceptionally high encapsulation reaching 98.7%, primarily driven by hydrogen bonding between CAP functional groups and the -OH and charged moieties of alginate, Tween 80, and the cationic gemini surfactant, consistent with previously reported high encapsulation efficiencies in alginate-based systems [365]. In vitro release assessment demonstrated a biphasic release pattern. An initial burst phase within approximately 30 min released ∼20% of CAP from free NPs and ∼35% from nanoparticle-loaded NFs, attributed to surface-associated drug on high-area interfaces. Subsequently, free CAP ALG NPs released nearly 100% of their payload within 120 h (5 days), whereas nanoparticle-embedded NFs extended release to over 500 h (approximately 21 days). These results clearly demonstrate that integrating NPs within electrospun fiber matrices provides a powerful strategy for substantially prolonging and modulating drug release profiles [365].

Hydrogels have been widely explored as DD matrices due to their high water content, biocompatibility, and adjustable physicochemical properties. However, drug release from conventional hydrogels is primarily diffusion-controlled, making precise regulation of release kinetics difficult and limiting their suitability for long-term therapeutic delivery. To overcome these limitations, incorporating NFs into hydrogel systems has emerged as a promising approach to modulate drug transport and enhance release performance [366]. NFs can modify the mechanical properties of the hydrogel network, alter diffusional pathways, and simultaneously function as independent drug reservoirs. This dual functionality enables orthogonal engineering of both hydrogel and fiber components, thereby facilitating synergistic control over mechanical behavior and therapeutic release.

Several studies have demonstrated the versatility of nanofiber-hydrogel composite systems for coordinated DD. For example, Nakielski et al. proposed a thermoresponsive poly(NIPAM) hydrogel containing gold nanorods (AuNRs) and embedded drug-loaded PLA NFs [367]. Upon near-infrared irradiation, the plasmonic resonance of the AuNRs generated localized heating, increasing the temperature to approximately 42 °C and inducing hydrogel deswelling. The resulting water expulsion, combined with mild thermal stimulation, accelerated drug release from the NFs. In another study, Liguori et al. prepared a gelatin hydrogel reinforced with PEO/PBT NFs, in which diclofenac was encapsulated within the fibers and chlorotetracycline within the hydrogel matrix [368]. Drug release behavior was strongly influenced by laminate architecture, with double-layer constructs containing an additional hydrogel layer exhibiting more gradual release profiles than monolayer systems. Similarly, Zare et al. designed multilayer laminates composed of alginate hydrogel sheets, PLA nanofiber mats, and PLGA NPs loaded with kartogenin [369]. In this system, the increased diffusion pathway length and nanoparticle encapsulation synergistically contributed to prolonged and sustained drug release.

NF-based systems have also been studied for wound-healing applications, where DD is combined with structural and biological support. β-cyclodextrin-grafted CS/PVA) (β-CD-g-CS/PVA) NFs loaded with indomethacin represent one such example [370]. CS contributes intrinsic hemostatic activity comparable to collagen-, fibrinogen-, and thrombin-based materials while also promoting cellular attachment. In these systems, indomethacin was dispersed separately within CS and β-CD-g-CS matrices before ES. Both preparations showed a distinct biphasic release profile involving a preliminary fast phase followed by a prolonged near-linear release phase, a behavior generally observed in blend-electrospun systems [370], [371]. The initial fast phase, typically observed within the first day at physiological pH and temperature, was attributed to molecules localized near the fiber surface during fabrication and storage. The rapid diffusion of these molecules into the release medium was driven by thermodynamic partitioning and their high aqueous solubility [370]. The subsequent sustained-release phase was primarily governed by matrix swelling and degradation. Native CS fibers degraded slowly, resulting in an approximately linear release profile. In contrast, β-CD-g-CS systems demonstrated swelling-mediated release that accelerated as degradation progressed [370]. The incorporation of β-cyclodextrin increased hydrophilicity, swelling capacity, and drug-loading efficiency, resulting in faster and more complete drug release. Indomethacin release from β-CD-g-CS fibers reached equilibrium after approximately 125 h and continued gradually until nearly 300 h, indicating sustained diffusion from deeper regions of the hydrated matrix. The close correspondence between swelling and release profiles suggested that swelling dominated transport at early stages, whereas diffusion-controlled release became more significant over time. Notably, CS fibers released only approximately 20% of the encapsulated drug over 12 days, whereas β-CD-containing systems achieved nearly complete release, facilitated by cyclodextrin cavities that facilitate drug transport [370]. Compared with CS/PVA fibers, β-CD-g-CS/PVA fibers also exhibited faster initial release because of enhanced drug dispersion, increased hydrophilicity, and improved solubility. In contrast, bead formation within CS/PVA fibers reduced the fraction of surface-accessible drug [370]. Overall, these systems demonstrated prolonged local DD behavior, which may be further improved through the integration of biomolecules like nerve growth factors.

Surface modification strategies have additionally been employed to optimize nanofiber-mediated drug release. In a recent study, CAP treatment was applied to quercetin (QU)-loaded PCL NFs to enhance their DD performance [372]. CAP exposure for 0.5, 1, and 3 min induced morphological alterations in NFs, resulting in changes in fiber diameter and surface characteristics. These modifications significantly influenced release kinetics and loading efficacy. The cumulative release of QU increased from 29 ± 1.8% in untreated PCL/QU fibers to 56 ± 2.2% following 0.5 min CAP treatment, while longer treatments of 1 and 3 min reduced release to 48 ± 4.2% and 44 ± 3.9%, respectively, as shown in Fig. 29 [372]. Similarly, loading efficiencies improved following short-duration CAP exposure, reaching a maximum of 88 ± 4.4% after 0.5 min treatment. These findings indicate that moderate CAP treatment enhances drug diffusion and loading capacity, whereas prolonged exposure may induce surface densification or structural rearrangement that impedes molecular transport [372], [373]. Collectively, these studies emphasize the significant potential of nanofiber-based composite and surface-engineered systems for achieving tunable, sustained, and multifunctional DD.

Collectively, these studies highlight the magnitude of controlling the release kinetics of NF-based DD systems to achieve effective therapeutic outcomes. Drug release must provide appropriate concentrations over clinically relevant durations [374]. Recent advances summarized in Table 2 continue to leverage the many advantages of ESNFs, including their high surface area-to-volume ratio, interconnected porosity, ECM-like structure, flexible processing, and ability to incorporate diverse therapeutics such as peptides, proteins, antibodies, and small molecules [373], [375], [376], [377], [378], [379], [380]. ES remains one of the most versatile NF fabrication techniques for DD systems. Increasing commercial availability and the development of advanced ES variants have helped overcome limitations of conventional systems, as summarized in Table 3 [381], [382], [383], [384], [385].

Skin is the largest organ of the human body and functions as the primary barrier against pathogens, chemical agents, physical trauma, and environmental contaminants [386]. In addition to its defensive role, the skin contributes to vitamin D synthesis, thermoregulation, moisture retention, and sensory perception [387]. Structurally, the skin is composed of three major layers: the epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis. The outermost layer is the epidermis, which prevents transepidermal water loss, maintains internal homeostasis, and protects against external insults [388]. Keratinocytes comprise approximately 80% of epidermal cells, alongside melanocytes, Merkel cells, and tissue-resident immune cells [389]. Under the epidermis lies the dermis, a collagen- and elastin-rich connective tissue layer that provides mechanical strength, elasticity, and nutritional support [390], [391]. The dermis is subdivided into a superficial papillary layer, containing loosely organized collagen fibers, and a deeper reticular layer, characterized by dense collagen bundles aligned parallel to the skin surface. Although less cellular than the epidermis, the dermis contains fibroblasts, fibrocytes, mast cells, dermal dendritic cells, macrophages, innate lymphoid cells, and extensive vascular, lymphatic, and neural networks. The innermost hypodermis primarily consists of adipose tissue arranged in lobules parted by fibrous septa containing blood vessels and nerves. This layer functions as an energy reservoir, thermal insulator, and mechanical cushion [391].

Cutaneous wound healing is a highly coordinated biological process involving numerous cell types, ECM components, and signaling mediators. Regardless of injury etiology, wound healing is generally separated into four temporally overlapping phases: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling, as illustrated in Fig. 30 [390]. The hemostatic phase begins immediately after injury and is characterized by vasoconstriction and platelet activation at sites of vascular damage. Von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen through interactions with platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX/V receptors, triggering platelet activation and degranulation. Simultaneously, tissue factor-mediated thrombin generation promotes fibrin formation, while activated factor XIII stabilizes the fibrin network through covalent crosslinking. The resulting platelet-fibrin clot not only limits blood loss but also provides a provisional matrix enriched with growth factors and complement proteins that support subsequent cellular recruitment and immune activation [392].

The inflammatory phase overlaps with hemostasis and functions to eliminate pathogens and remove damaged tissue. Neutrophils are amongst the first recruited immune cells to the damaged site, where they perform phagocytosis, release antimicrobial peptides and proteolytic enzymes, generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), and form neutrophil extracellular traps [393]. As inflammation progresses, macrophages become the dominant cell population. These cells exhibit phenotypic plasticity and are often broadly categorized into pro-inflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative M2 phenotypes [394]. M1 macrophages (CD86+) contribute to pathogen clearance in response to stimuli such as LPS and interferon-γ [395], [396], whereas M2 macrophages (CD206+) secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-10, along with growth factors that promote angiogenesis, fibroblast activation, and re-epithelialization [397]. Proper macrophage recruitment and phenotypic transition are critical for successful healing; as impaired macrophage function is associated with delayed tissue repair [398].

The proliferative phase is characterized by active tissue reconstruction. Keratinocytes at the wound margins migrate and proliferate to restore epidermal continuity, while fibroblasts infiltrate the wound bed and synthesize a provisional ECM. Cytokines and growth factors transform fibroblasts into α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-expressing myofibroblasts, which mediate wound contraction. Concurrently, angiogenesis restores vascular supply by forming new capillaries from endothelial cells. Epidermal stem cells originating from basal epidermal layers and hair follicle niches further contribute to tissue regeneration. Collectively, re-epithelialization, neovascularization, matrix deposition, and wound contraction re-establish tissue integrity during this stage [399], [400].

The final remodeling phase may continue for months or even years following injury. During this period, granulation tissue is gradually reorganized into mature scar tissue through continuous matrix synthesis, degradation, and remodeling. Type III collagen deposited during earlier phases is progressively replaced by mechanically stronger type I collagen, leading to increased tensile strength [401], [402]. However, healed skin rarely regains the structural organization of native tissue. Scar tissue typically lacks appendages such as hair follicles and sweat glands, exhibits reduced elastin content, and displays collagen fibers aligned in parallel rather than the basket-weave architecture of normal skin. Consequently, the tensile strength of healed tissue generally reaches only 50-80% of that of uninjured skin [403], [404]. Myofibroblasts remain important regulators during this stage by controlling collagen fibrillogenesis through ECM-associated molecules such as decorin. Prolonged inflammation, particularly in burn injuries, can further delay remodeling and contribute to excessive scar formation [403]. Overall, wound healing is a complex, immensely controlled process that functions through coordinated interactions among immune cells, stromal cells, signaling molecules, and ECM components. A deeper understanding of these processes is critical for developing advanced biomaterials and regenerative therapies to improve tissue repair outcomes [405], [406], [407], [408].

Recently, a rapid and practical approach for generating aggregation-induced emission luminogen (AIEgen)-based nanofibrous dressings directly at the wound site has been reported for the treatment of postsurgical and trauma-related infections [409]. Using a handheld ES device, N, N-diphenyl-4-(7-(pyridin-4-yl) benzo[c] [1,2,5] thiadiazol-4-yl) aniline functionalized with 1-bromoethane (TBP)-loaded PCL NFs were deposited in situ onto skin wounds as shown in Fig. 31, forming a conformal and adhesive dressing that adapts to irregular wound geometries while providing immediate protection. The portable system integrates a miniaturized high-voltage source and syringe pump, enabling on-demand fabrication of personalized dressings without conventional laboratory equipment [409]. TBP, the incorporated AIEgen, exhibits a strong antibacterial effect against Gram-positive bacteria, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), without inducing resistance. Photophysical analysis confirmed its aggregation-induced emission behavior, with enhanced fluorescence observed at higher toluene fractions due to aggregate formation. When embedded in PCL NFs, TBP exhibited loading-dependent fluorescence and efficient ROS generation under visible light irradiation, indicating potent photodynamic antibacterial activity [409]. The resulting NFs were uniform and defect-free, and cytocompatibility tests using HUVEC and NIH 3T3 cells confirmed good biocompatibility. In vitro antibacterial experiments demonstrated significant reductions in the viability of S. aureus and MRSA, accompanied by membrane disruption. In vivo, in situ-deposited AIE nanofibrous dressings hastened wound healing, reduced inflammation, and promoted tissue regeneration compared with control groups [409]. Overall, this work highlights handheld ES of AIEgen-loaded NFs as a rapid, customizable, and effective strategy for managing infected wounds.

In parallel, TA has been widely explored as a supramolecular cross-linker for assembling LBL block copolymer micelle (BCM)/TA films with swelling-deswelling behavior capable of regulating small-molecule release [410]. TA is particularly attractive due to its intrinsic pro-healing, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties, including suppression of TNF-α, a key cytokine elevated in chronic wound environments [411], [412]. These characteristics make TA-based systems highly promising for wound healing applications. For instance, Albright et al. [413] developed BCM/TA coatings on PCL/collagen (PCL/Coll) NFs to create bioactive surfaces that enhance fibroblast adhesion, proliferation, and spreading, thereby accelerating wound closure. The BCM/TA layer can also be loaded with antibiotics, enabling infection control governed by swelling-dependent release kinetics. As illustrated in Fig. 32 [413], the system is modular and can be combined with TGF-β1-loaded PCL/Coll fibers to achieve antimicrobial properties and enhanced tissue regeneration simultaneously. In vitro wound-closure assays using normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDFs) further confirmed the efficacy of this approach. Bare PCL/Coll NFs showed limited migration, with approximately 20% and 50% closure at 24 and 72 h, respectively. In contrast, BCM/TA-coated NFs achieved ∼60% and ∼80% closure over the same time points. This improvement was attributed to the synergistic effects of BCM/TA-induced surface topography and increased cell attachment, which together promoted fibroblast migration and proliferation, key processes in effective wound healing [413].

Electrospun dressings have been extensively explored as wound management tools, as their nanofibrous architecture provides both mechanical support and interconnected transport pathways that facilitate cell infiltration and signaling [414]. However, even with standard care, early-stage infection and dysregulated inflammation can impair healing, driving the engineering of multifunctional dressings that combine physical support with localized delivery of anti-infective and anti-inflammatory agents [415]. Various approaches have been explored, including antibiotic-loaded fibers [416], silver nanoparticle-based composites with broad antimicrobial activity [417], [418], and gold (Au) NPs functionalized with small molecules like 6-aminopenicillanic acid for combating multidrug-resistant bacteria [419]. In vivo studies have shown that PCL-gelatin NFs decorated with surface-modified Au NPs significantly reduce bacterial load and improve healing outcomes in infected wound models [419]. In addition, local delivery of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., naproxen, ibuprofen, and ketoprofen) has been incorporated into NFs to modulate excessive inflammation [420].

In a related study, the in vivo efficacy of coaxial nanofiber dressings was assessed in a diabetic wound model [421]. Macroscopic analysis showed progressive wound closure in all groups, with both coaxial blank PVP/PLA and AS/PVP/PLA functional dressings outperforming conventional medical gauze (Fig. 33a). From day 6 onward, the AS/PVP/PLA group exhibited the fastest healing, accompanied by minimal edema, erythema, and inflammation, whereas the gauze group showed mild exudation and irritation. Quantitative analysis confirmed this trend: on day 3, wound closure rates were 10.84 ± 1.80% (gauze), 14.27 ± 0.96% (blank PVP/PLA), and 18.76 ± 1.82% (AS/PVP/PLA) (Fig. 33b), with significantly higher healing rates observed in the functional dressing group at subsequent time points. By day 14, the AS/PVP/PLA group achieved 96.54 ± 0.29% wound closure [421]. Histological analysis further supported these findings. H&E staining on day 7 revealed inflammation, localized hemorrhage, and limited collagen deposition across all groups. By day 14, the gauze-treated wounds demonstrated incomplete re-epithelialization and sparse collagen production, whereas the blank group exhibited partial closure but persistent hemorrhage and reduced collagen density. Nevertheless, the AS/PVP/PLA group demonstrated a fully re-formed epidermis, a markedly thicker granulation layer, and substantially enhanced collagen deposition. Masson's trichrome staining confirmed denser and more organized collagen fibers in the functional dressing group, along with increased fibroblast presence and alignment (Fig. 34) [421]. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that coaxial nanofiber dressings significantly accelerate wound closure and improve tissue regeneration in diabetic wounds.

Chen et al. [422] prepared a curcumin-loaded sandwich-like NF membrane (CSNM) using sequential ES, as depicted in Fig. 35, for hemostasis, antibacterial activity, and accelerated wound healing. Both in vitro and in vivo hemostatic assays demonstrated that CSNM exhibited excellent blood-clotting performance. DPPH-based evaluation of the antioxidant activity showed that CSNM possessed strong free radical scavenging activity. In addition, antibacterial testing using the disk diffusion method confirmed its effective antimicrobial properties. In a rat dorsal skin defect model, CSNM significantly promoted collagen deposition, granulation tissue formation, and epithelial tissue remodeling. Immunohistochemical analysis further revealed that CSNM enhanced early expression of CD31 and TGF-β, thereby facilitating angiogenesis and accelerating wound closure [422]. In another work, the therapeutic effect of SMGT on diabetic wounds was evaluated using a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model [423]. Progressive hyperglycemia was observed, with blood glucose levels reaching approximately 28 mM by week six (Fig. 36a). Wound regions were photographed on a specific schedule (0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 days), and contraction rates were quantified from the images (Fig. 36b). As expected, severe hyperglycemia disrupted skin histoarchitecture and significantly delayed wound closure, whereas treatment with SMGT-NFM accelerated healing and improved tissue regeneration (Fig. 36c and d) [423]. The expression of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), a marker of myofibroblast activity and neovascular maturation, was assessed by immunohistochemistry. Because timely activation and subsequent resolution of myofibroblasts are critical to preventing fibrosis, α-SMA expression provides important insight into wound remodeling. In the high-glucose (HG) group, SMGT combined with NFM restored more normal cutaneous architecture and promoted appropriate spatial localization of α-SMA within regenerated tissue, indicating improved wound maturation and controlled repair [423].

Hyaluronic acid, a major component of the ECM, plays a key role throughout all phases of the wound-healing process. Throughout the hemostatic and inflammatory phases, it contributes to provisional matrix formation that stabilizes the wound and supports early fibrin-based scaffold formation [424]. In the earliest and mid-stages of healing, hyaluronic acid facilitates leukocyte and fibroblast infiltration, enhances clearance of necrotic tissue, and suppresses excessive inflammatory signaling by modulating macrophage phenotype and TLR4 activity [425]. In the proliferative phase, it promotes keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation and stimulates ECM synthesis, thereby increasing collagen and elastin deposition to support granulation tissue formation and angiogenesis [426]. During the remodeling phase, hyaluronic acid regulates matrix turnover by interacting with TGF-β and matrix metalloproteinases, contributing to balanced collagen organization rather than directly inducing myofibroblast differentiation [427]. Despite these beneficial roles, native hyaluronic acid exhibits weak tissue adhesion, limited antimicrobial activity, and insufficient intrinsic regenerative capacity, which has motivated the development of hyaluronic acid -based composite dressings and cross-linked hydrogels to enhance its stability and bioactivity [428].

DA, a catecholamine neurotransmitter involved in vasodilation, insulin regulation, and immune modulation, offers complementary advantages. Its catechol structure enhances tissue adhesion, improves antioxidant capacity, and increases biocompatibility [429]. To overcome the limitations of hyaluronic acid, DA was grafted onto hyaluronic acid, followed by amidation with gelatin (GEL) after acetic acid removal, enabling the fabrication of DA-modified hyaluronic acid (OHDA)/GEL-based nanofiber dressings [430]. This strategy produced multifunctional scaffolds with antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and pro-healing characteristics for diabetic wound management, as shown in Fig. 37 [430]. In the diabetic wound environment characterized by hyperglycemia, high bacterial load, and elevated levels of inflammatory mediators, untreated wounds initially exhibited larger areas with delayed contraction [430]. By day 7, wounds treated with OHDA/GEL or cordycepin (COR)/OHDA/GEL NF membranes displayed wound contraction, whereas control wounds remained inflamed with visible exudate. After two weeks, the control group showed only limited healing, while both treatment groups exhibited substantial closure, with COR/OHDA/GEL performing best. By day 21, large unhealed regions persisted in the control group, whereas complete wound closure was noted in the COR/OHDA/GEL group. The histological analysis further supported these findings. In the control group, a thin epidermis, sparse collagen deposition, and delayed granulation and re-epithelialization indicated impaired fibroblast activity and matrix formation. In contrast, both OHDA/GEL and COR/OHDA/GEL groups showed well-developed granulation tissue, increased and well-organized collagen fibers, complete re-epithelialization, and partial regeneration of skin appendages, including hair follicles. The COR/OHDA/GEL group demonstrated the most advanced tissue remodeling, indicating superior collagen organization and more effective functional skin regeneration [430].

Despite their advantages, many electrospun membranes are dense 2D structures with limited pore size, poor interconnectivity, and low fluid absorption capacity, which can restrict 3D cell infiltration and biofluid transport [431]. Gas-foaming has been employed to convert these structures into 3D nanofiber sponges and to incorporate functional agents such as TA, curcumin, and Ag-metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), thereby enhancing porosity, water uptake, and ECM-like behavior [431], [432]. Owing to their greater structural similarity to native tissue, 3D sponges better support cell adhesion, proliferation, and migration than conventional 2D mats [433]. To address MRSA-infected wounds, a layered electrospun 3D nanofiber sponge (3D-ZnMOF) was developed from CS, pullulan, and citric acid, with in situ incorporation of ZnMOF (Fig. 38) [434]. An MRSA-infection wound model in rats was used to compare gauze (control) with three nanofiber-based dressings. Wound images recorded on days 0, 3, and 9 demonstrated progressive contraction and infection status (Fig. 39A-C) [434]. On day 3, wound closure rates were 21.7% (control), 37.9% (2D-T/D/P/C), 47.4% (3D-T/D/P/C), and 53.8% (3D-ZnMOF). By day 9, closure increased to 82.46 ± 5.28% (control), 92.99 ± 1.25% (2D-T/D/P/C), 94.7% (3D-T/D/P/C), and 97.4% (3D-ZnMOF), indicating that all nanofiber dressings significantly improved healing, with 3D-ZnMOF performing best. Bacterial load analysis from wound exudates cultured on agar showed abundant colonies in the control and 3D-T/D/P/C groups on day 3, fewer colonies in the 2D-T/D/P/C group, and the lowest bacterial burden in the 3D-ZnMOF group, consistent with in vitro antibacterial performance (Fig. 39B) [434]. Histological evaluation further supported these findings. H&E staining at day 9 revealed minimal inflammatory infiltration in the 3D-ZnMOF group, whereas numerous neutrophils persisted in the control and, to a lesser extent, in the 2D- and 3D-T/D/P/C groups (Fig. 39D, E) [434]. Evidence of neovascularization was observed in all groups (blue arrows), while newly formed mature vessels and hair follicles were more evident in the 3D-T/D/P/C and 3D-ZnMOF groups (green arrows). Masson's trichrome staining demonstrated the highest collagen deposition and most organized fiber alignment in the 3D-ZnMOF group, followed by 3D-T/D/P/C and 2D-T/D/P/C, with the lowest levels in the control group. Quantitative analysis of collagen coverage on day 9 showed values of 51.6% (control), 57.3% (2D-T/D/P/C), 64.3% (3D-T/D/P/C), and 70.1% (3D-ZnMOF) (Fig. 39 F, G) [434]. Overall, nanofiber-based dressings enhanced wound healing and collagen regeneration, with the 3D-ZnMOF system exhibiting the most pronounced therapeutic effect, whereas commercial gauze led to more pronounced scarring. Moreover, rapid hemostasis remains a critical clinical challenge [434].

Rathinavel et al. studied the in vivo wound-healing functionality of PVA NFs integrated with amine-modified mesoporous silica (NH2-SBA-15) and curcumin [435]. Using Albino Wistar rats, they compared electrospun PVA/NH2-SBA-15 (5.0 wt%) and PVA/NH2-SBA-15 (5.0 wt%)/curcumin NFs over days 0, 4, 10, 14, and 18. Their earlier work had also evaluated PVA, saline controls, and SBA-15-loaded PVA/curcumin systems. In the early stage (day 4), wound closure was limited; by day 10, noticeable improvement in healing was observed. At day 14, curcumin-loaded NFs exhibited pronounced tissue regeneration. By day 18, the PVA/NH2-SBA-15/curcumin group achieved nearly complete wound closure (∼98% reduction in wound area) along with healthy hair regrowth, outperforming the curcumin-free NH2-SBA-15/PVA system. No evidence of inflammation, infection, or allergic response was detected, confirming good biocompatibility and suitability for skin applications. The synergistic effect of PVA, NH2-modified SBA-15, and curcumin contributed to accelerated healing. SBA-15 provided a high-surface-area, porous structure with strong drug-loading capacity, serving as an efficient curcumin carrier. At the same time, surface amine groups enhanced bioactivity and supported cellular processes involved in tissue repair [435]. To further evaluate macroscopic healing, Liao et al. analyzed wound images collected on days 3, 7, and 14 after dressing removal (Fig. 40A) [436]. Image analysis was used to quantify residual wound area relative to baseline, enabling comparison between nanofiber membrane (NFM) treatments and gauze controls. In diabetic wounds, PCH and PC NFs promoted faster healing than PLGA and gauze, with PCH showing the best performance, consistent with the superior efficacy of curcumin-based NFMs observed in vitro. By day 3, wound areas were already reduced in PCH (58.3%) and PC (58.1%) compared with gauze (66.2%) (Fig. 40B) [436]. On day 7, all NFM-treated groups significantly outperformed the control, with PCH beginning to show clear superiority over PLGA. By day 14, the curcumin-heparin composite (PCH) achieved the most rapid closure, reflecting synergistic anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic effects. Final wound-area reductions were lowest with PCH (13.9%) and highest with gauze (37.1%), followed by PC (20.5%) and PLGA (27.4%). Overall, these results confirm that dual-component NFMs significantly enhance wound contraction and accelerate tissue regeneration, particularly in diabetic wound environments [436].

ESNFs are a highly versatile tool for antibacterial applications given their large interfacial surface area, adjustable porosity, and easily modifiable surface chemistry, which enable the efficient incorporation of diverse antimicrobial agents [437], [438]. CS, a derivative of chitin, is one of the most extensively studied natural polysaccharides owing to its intrinsic antimicrobial activity and biocompatibility. However, its poor solubility and limited stability in aqueous media can restrict processing and practical applications [439]. Similarly, cellulose and its derivatives represent another important class of biopolymers for antimicrobial NFs. Native cellulose is difficult to electrospin because of its low solubility; therefore, CA, which is soluble in solvents such as DMF and acetone, is commonly used instead [438]. To overcome limitations in spinnability and functionality, CS and related biopolymers are often blended with synthetic polymers, NPs, or biomolecules to improve physical features and introduce multiple antibacterial mechanisms [437], [440]. Current strategies increasingly focus on functionalizing NFs with metallic NPs (e.g., ZnO, TiO2), antibiotics, natural antimicrobial agents, engineered nanostructures, or multilayer coatings. These systems typically act through contact killing, oxidative stress generation, and controlled drug release [441]. Such modular designs enable precise tuning of antimicrobial activity, release kinetics, and cytocompatibility for biomedical and environmental applications [442].

Evaluation of antibacterial performance in ESNFs is commonly performed using standardized assays, including direct-contact, dynamic-contact, and agar-diffusion methods, which simulate different bacterial-material interaction scenarios. The most frequently used bacterial strains are S. aureus (Gram-positive) and K. pneumoniae or E. coli (Gram-negative), with E. coli often preferred due to its lower biosafety requirements and wide availability [443], [444]. These assays are primarily conducted in vitro using bacterial cultures in agar or liquid media to assess inhibition zones, colony reduction, or minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). However, in vivo evaluations remain limited, especially in biomedical applications such as wound dressings, sutures, implants, and filtration systems, where physiological complexity and immune responses significantly influence performance [445]. In this context, the following section highlights representative functionalization strategies and their antibacterial performance, focusing on material integration approaches, synergistic nanostructures, and both in vitro and in vivo studies relevant to wound healing and antimicrobial barrier systems.

Antimicrobial functionality typically requires incorporation of active agents such as metallic NPs or photosensitizers [446]. Huang et al. reported electrospun PVP/CNC/Ag NFs with tunable morphology and strong antibacterial activity [447]. The addition of CNCs and silver NPs (AgNPs) increased solution conductivity, resulting in uniform, thinner fibers.
