The PVP/CNC/AgNO3 NFs exhibited clear inhibition zones against both E. coli and S. aureus, whereas CNC-only mats showed no antibacterial activity (Fig. 41) [447]. This effect was attributed to Ag+ release and nanoparticle interactions with bacterial membranes, leading to disrupted permeability and impaired respiration. Similarly, He et al. developed AgNP-loaded feather keratin (FK)/PVA/PEO NFs with strong antibacterial performance mediated by silver-induced membrane disruption [448]. Increasing AgNP content (0.6-3%) progressively enhanced antimicrobial activity against both E. coli and S. aureus, whereas Ag-free pads showed no inhibition zones. At optimal loading, the NFs produced clear inhibition halos, with larger zones observed for E. coli than for S. aureus, suggesting higher sensitivity of Gram-negative bacteria [448].

Beyond AgNPs, a range of metal-based NPs, including zinc, titanium, copper, cobalt, and hybrid systems such as Zn/Ti, have been explored for antibacterial applications via contact-killing mechanisms and ROS-mediated activity similar to silver-based systems [449], [450], [451], [452]. For example, Kenawy et al. [450] developed ZnO-loaded PVA/SA NFs exhibiting strong antimicrobial performance, particularly when combined with glycine. Their optimized formulation (AS 3.3: 10% PVA/1.5% SA/10% CA/0.75% ZnO/0.5% glycine) produced the largest inhibition zones against multiple multidrug-resistant pathogens, reaching 23.15 ± 2.34 mm for Bacillus cereus and 22.22 ± 2.65 mm for Staphylococcus aureus. Gram-negative strains also showed significant susceptibility, with E. coli exhibiting inhibition zones up to 17.45 ± 3.21 mm. Glycine-containing NFs consistently outperformed control formulations, and biofilm assays confirmed inhibition rates exceeding 97% for Gram-positive bacteria. In addition, time-kill kinetics demonstrated nearly complete eradication of B. cereus and S. paratyphi within 48 h, highlighting the synergistic antibacterial impact of ZnO NPs and glycine [450]. Similarly, Devi et al. revealed the potent antibacterial action of metal nanoparticle-doped polyacrylonitrile (PAN) NFMs [452]. ZnO-based (PZCR) and Cu-based (PCCR) NFs, both functionalized with CS and the thiourea-derived antimicrobial compound R1, achieved up to 95% reduction in bacterial growth against E. coli and S. aureus. The zones of inhibition reached 12-13 mm for E. coli and 20-22 mm for S. aureus, indicating particularly strong activity against Gram-positive bacteria. The enhanced antimicrobial performance is attributed to the combined effects of (i) electrostatic membrane disruption by cationic CS, (ii) intrinsic antibacterial activity of R1, and (iii) ROS generation induced by ZnO and Cu NPs [452]. In another work, PLGA/CuO hybrid nanofiber scaffolds were engineered to impart strong antimicrobial activity to otherwise inert PLGA mats [453]. While pristine PLGA produced no inhibition zones, CuO-loaded NFs generated clear bactericidal halos against both S. aureus and E. coli. Optical density measurements further confirmed pronounced growth suppression, with E. coli showing the greatest reduction in turbidity over 24 h. The antibacterial activity was attributed to sustained Cu2+ ion release, which reached 1.6 ppm by day 10 and correlated with the inhibition trend. These results demonstrate that CuO incorporation effectively transforms PLGA NFs into potent antimicrobial scaffolds suitable for wound care applications [453].

Cobalt-based fibers have also demonstrated strong antimicrobial performance, as reported for cobalt-MOF/PVA-PVP-based NFs [454]. These MOF-loaded fibers inhibited all seven tested pathogens, with MIC values ranging from 8 to 64 μg/mL, including Salmonella enterica (8 μg/mL), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (16 μg/mL), and E. coli (32 μg/mL). Their bactericidal activity was similarly strong, with MBC values as low as 16 μg/mL for S. enterica and P. aeruginosa. The NFs achieved complete bacterial clearance against E. coli, outperforming both pristine PVA-PVP fibers and amikacin, which was ineffective against Legionella and Giardia. This broad-spectrum efficacy was attributed to the high specific surface area (2415 m2/g), which enhances microbial interaction with cobalt MOF active sites [454]. Titanium-based NFs, particularly electrospun PVP/TiO2 systems, have also shown strong antibacterial performance [455]. Across all tested concentrations (0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 mg/mL), TiO2 NFs inhibited both Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains, including E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella typhimurium, Bacillus subtilis, and Staphylococcus aureus. The highest activity was observed at 1.0 mg/mL, where S. aureus exhibited an inhibition zone of 21 mm, outperforming both TiO2 NPs and PVP-only controls, which showed no inhibition. This enhanced efficacy is attributed to the higher surface area of TiO2 NFs, which promotes stronger bacterial membrane disruption and more efficient interaction with bacterial cell walls [455].

In another study, functionalized electrospun polyamide NFMs were developed as antibacterial microfiltration media, achieving high pathogen removal in water treatment applications [456]. Among the tested biocides, poly[(dimethylimino)(2-hydroxy-1,3-propanediyl) chloride] (WSCP) at 5 wt% showed the strongest performance, removing 5.2 log10 colony forming units (CFU)/100 mL of hospital wastewater in short-term tests. Long-term filtration maintained high disinfection efficiency, achieving 5.6 log10 removal for Staphylococcus aureus and 4.0 log10 for Escherichia coli, demonstrating greater efficacy against Gram-positive bacteria. WSCP-functionalized NFs consistently outperformed silver, bronopol, 2,2-dibromo-3-nitrilopropionamide (DBNPA), and 2-(thiocyanomethylthio)benzothiazole (TCMTB). Although approximately 10% of WSCP was leached during operation, the membranes retained over 90% of the active agent and maintained full antibacterial performance [456]. In a related study, Nageh et al. prepared ZnO-loaded polyvinylidenefluoride (PVDF) NFs that exhibited strong antiviral activity, transforming otherwise inert PVDF into a functional antiviral platform [457]. Increasing ZnO content from 2.0% to 5.0% significantly enhanced activity; at 5% loading, ZnO/PVDF NFs completely suppressed human adenovirus type-5 (ADV-5), with viral copies reduced to undetectable levels as quantified by real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in both adsorption and virucidal assays. Pristine PVDF showed no antiviral activity, while 2% ZnO/PVDF was effective only in the virucidal mode. All nanofiber formulations remained non-toxic to Vero cells (70-80% viability), confirming that antiviral effects originated from ZnO rather than cytotoxicity. The activity was attributed to Zn2+-mediated viral neutralization, membrane interactions, and oxidative stress mechanisms [457].

Boron nitride (BN) has also been explored in antimicrobial NFs, as demonstrated by Doğan et al., who incorporated hydroxylated BN (mBN) into PVA/PAA electrospun mats [458]. While pristine PVA/PAA exhibited limited antibacterial activity, mBN addition significantly improved bacterial reduction, achieving 68.8% inhibition against E. coli and 75.1% against S. aureus after 24 h of dynamic contact. Antibacterial activity increased with BN loading, with Gram-positive S. aureus showing higher susceptibility than E. coli. This difference is attributed to variations in cell wall structure, hydrophilicity, and aggregation behavior. The antimicrobial mechanism is associated with BN-induced oxidative stress, membrane disruption, and electrostatic interactions with bacterial cell walls [459], [460].

LBL micellar coatings provide a modular strategy for antibiotic loading and controlled release from fibrous scaffolds [461]. For example; BCM/TA coatings on PCL/Coll NFs were evaluated against S. aureus using zone-of-inhibition (ZOI) assays as shown in Fig. 42 [413]. Before testing, both bare and BCM/TA-coated fibers were UV-sterilized and loaded with clindamycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg/mL, pH 7.5) at 4 °C for 20 h. The MIC of clindamycin was 0.25 μg/mL, while BCM/TA-coated fibers produced larger ZOIs than bare fibers (32 ± 6 mm vs. 23 ± 9 mm) and absorbed approximately ten times more antibiotic by mass. Notably, clindamycin-loaded BCM/TA coatings retained antibacterial activity after 20 weeks of storage at 5 °C, with ZOIs comparable to those of freshly prepared samples. In liquid culture, these fibers reduced bacterial CFU by approximately two orders of magnitude within 5 h, similar to free clindamycin [413].

Antimicrobial screening is essential in diabetic wounds because patients with diabetes are at increased risk of infection. Wang et al. [430] demonstrated that COR/OHDA/GEL NFMs provide strong antimicrobial activity against both E. coli and S. aureus. In vitro assays showed that COR-loaded NFs achieved 71.2% inhibition of E. coli and 95.6% inhibition of S. aureus, outperforming the OHDA/GEL control membranes. As illustrated in Fig. 43A and 43B, bacterial colonies were markedly reduced around COR/OHDA/GEL samples, confirming their enhanced bacteriostatic effect. The differential activity between the two species is attributed to Gram-positive bacteria's greater sensitivity to COR. Overall, these findings indicate that COR/OHDA/GEL NFs can effectively suppress early-stage infection in diabetic wounds, creating a cleaner microenvironment that supports subsequent healing [430]. Puigmal et al. evaluated fucoidan (FUC)-loaded PVA/CS NFs as antibacterial scaffolds for skin tissue applications and demonstrated that fucoidan significantly enhanced antimicrobial performance [462]. While PVA and PVA/CS control mats produced only modest inhibition zones (7-8 mm), the incorporation of fucoidan increased antimicrobial effect against E. coli and S. aureus, with the 30 mg FUC formulation reaching up to 10 mm for E. coli and 9 mm for S. aureus. The inhibition areas increased progressively with higher fucoidan loading, confirming a dose-dependent effect. This improvement was attributed to the underlying antimicrobial activity of fucoidan, which synergizes with CS to disrupt bacterial membranes and inhibit growth. Overall, fucoidan-enriched NFs exhibited the strongest antibacterial response among all tested formulations, highlighting their suitability for infection-prone wound environments [462]. Another approach involved the development of chitosan-thiourea/PVA (CST/PVA) NFs incorporating Ag NPs and coated with polyhexamethylene biguanidine (Ag/PHMBG), leading to a highly effective antibacterial wound-healing scaffold. The optimized formulation containing 3.0% Ag/PHMBG (PCT3) achieved 95% inhibition of S. aureus and P. aeruginosa within three days, significantly outperforming CST/PVA controls. As illustrated in Fig. 44, time-kill assays showed a sharp and sustained reduction in bacterial optical density over 72 h, confirming continuous bactericidal activity [463]. This strong antimicrobial effect is attributed to the synergistic action of thiourea-modified CS, which enhances electrostatic interactions with bacterial membranes, and PHMBG-stabilized Ag NPs, which provide controlled silver ion release [463].

Building on these antibacterial nanofiber strategies, Soo et al. demonstrated that silver-doped titanium dioxide (Ag-TiO2) NFs can deliver exceptionally strong antibacterial activity, far surpassing that of intrinsic TiO2 [464]. Their optimized formulation containing 2.0% Ag achieved the highest bactericidal performance, achieving a 5.92 log CFU reduction against Salmonella Albany and a 1.38 Log CFU reduction against S. aureus after only 60 min of contact. Ag-TiO2 consistently outperformed pure TiO2 across multiple Gram-negative strains, with log reductions exceeding 4-5 logs for several E. coli pathotypes. The study attributed this enhancement to the synergistic interaction between Ag NPs and photocatalytic TiO2, which increases ROS generation and suppresses electron-hole recombination, thereby intensifying membrane damage and bacterial inactivation [464]. Extending this antimicrobial nanofiber framework, CA membranes loaded with metal-doped silica nanohybrids were developed and exhibited exceptionally broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity [465]. Among all formulations, the trimetallic Ag-Si + Cu-Si + Co-Si nanohybrid membrane produced the largest inhibition zones, outperforming all monometallic counterparts against S. aureus, MRSA, S. pneumoniae, K. pneumoniae, E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and multiple fungal strains. The inhibition zones were consistently wider for the trimetallic system, confirming a strong synergistic effect. This enhanced activity was attributed to visible-light-activated ROS generation, facilitated by the lowest band gap energy, along with the combined bactericidal effects of Ag, Cu, and Co [465]. Overall, ES combined with diverse biocidal agents provides a highly flexible platform for antimicrobial NFs. In addition to the studies discussed above, many other reports in the literature have explored similar systems, some of which are listed in Table 4.

Compared to a uniform film, an ESNF network offers a dramatically higher surface-to-volume ratio, allowing extensive interaction with solutes and tumor cells and thereby improving drug loading and interaction efficiency [477]. Drugs can be embedded within or onto NFs for localized, sustained delivery, allowing chemotherapeutic agents to act directly at the tumor site while minimizing general toxicity [478]. This spatial control over drug release is particularly beneficial in solid tumors and in sensitive regions such as the brain. ESNFs fabricated from synthetic, natural, or hybrid polymers have therefore been widely applied in cancer therapy, 3D tumor modeling, and diagnostics. For instance, they serve as delivery vehicles for small molecules, genes, or stimuli-responsive agents in tumor-targeted therapy [479] and as scaffolds to recreate tumor microenvironments for high-throughput drug screening and disease modeling [480]. Nanofiber meshes have also been functionalized for cancer diagnostics, including the detection and identification of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and the recognition of tumor biomarkers, thereby playing a key role in cancer research and diagnosis as tools for therapeutic applications [481], [482].

Zhang et al. examined how fibrillar ECM cues regulate cell migration by patterning polystyrene fibers into linear, curved, looped, and grid-like arrays (3 μm diameter) using continuous ES with reduced power [483]. Cells adjusted their shapes and migration routes according to local microfibrillar geometries; however, the global pattern had little effect on mean migration speed. A behavioral shift emerged when feature dimensions approached the cell's minor-axis limit, suggesting that the short axis of the cell body constrains rerouting along a given fiber track [483]. Estabridis et al. cultured U251 glioblastoma cells on suspended NFs (approximately 400 nm) to compare 1D and 2D migration. Cells adhered to single, dual, or orthogonal fibers; migration was faster on parallel fibers than on single fibers, and 1D guidance resulted in more persistent and rapid movement than 2D surfaces [484]. In another study extending capture-based approaches, Ma et al. reported a 3D fibrous network that demonstrated a “trap” effect for the efficient isolation and capture of cancer cells [485]. Compared with an anti-epithelial-cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM)-functionalized smooth polystyrene control that captured fewer than 40% of MCF-7 cells, the 3D micro- and nanofibrous interfaces captured 67-82% of MCF-7 cells within 30 min. They selectively enriched EpCAM-positive cell lines (MCF-7, PC3) over EpCAM-negative lines (Daudi, Jurkat, HeLa), attributed to the elastic 3D network topology [485].

Drug-loaded nanocarriers such as mesoporous silica NPs, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and polymeric micelles have been co-electrospun into fibers to enhance local therapy, improve retention, enhance tumor accumulation, and sustain drug release [486], [487], [488], [489]. Local recurrence following cancer surgery is still an important clinical issue. To enhance antitumor efficacy while maintaining acceptable toxicity for the prevention of local recurrence, Zhang et al. [490] demonstrated a dual-drug-loaded multilayered fiber mat approach, in which dichloroacetic acid (DCA) and oxaliplatin were co-spun into specific layers of the fabricated scaffold. The oxaliplatin-loaded fiber layer was sandwiched between a base film layer and two outer fiber layers, yielding multilayered mats with dual-release capability and synergistic anticancer activity. DCA, with its relatively low toxicity, promoted apoptosis in cancer cells through metabolic modulation, whereas oxaliplatin, at low concentrations, eliminated remaining cells. When applied at the resection margin in a murine cervical carcinoma model, these dual-drug multilayered mats demonstrated superior anti-recurrence efficacy and reduced systemic toxicity over 30 days compared with single-layer counterparts. Such time-programmed DD highlights the potential of multilayered nanofiber scaffolds for localized post-surgical cancer treatment [490].

Another investigation reported a novel strategy for developing simultaneously photo-cleavable and activatable (SPCA) prodrug-backboned block copolymer micelles using a Pt(IV)-azide complex. These Pt(IV)-azide complexes functioned as anticancer prodrugs, stimuli-responsive groups, and co-monomers, enabling the construction of a new class of macromolecular prodrugs and drug carriers for mono- or multi-drug cancer therapy [491]. Building on these findings, Zhang et al. exhibited an implantable nanofiber system loaded with a prodrug micelle/small-molecule for improved localized therapy [492]. In this approach, amphiphilic Pt(IV) prodrug-backbone micelles ((PEG2k-Pt(IV))n) were synthesized via copper-free click chemistry and co-electrospun with DCA into PVA NFs to achieve localized combination therapy, as illustrated in Fig. 45 [492]. In U14 tumor-bearing mice, the combination micelle/DCA fiber system suppressed tumor growth more effectively than single-agent fiber systems. Also, it outperformed systemic (intravenous) administration of micelles plus DCA, particularly beyond day 7, consistent with sustained high local drug exposure and gradual cellular uptake of micelles. Body weight increased steadily in all fiber-treated groups, whereas intravenous treatment initially decreased, followed by recovery. Survival was improved relative to controls, and histological analysis revealed extensive tumor necrosis with pyknotic or absent nuclei in the combination-fiber group (Fig. 46) [492]. Furthermore, histological assessment revealed that all major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, remained healthy without visible inflammation or lesions after treatment, as shown in Fig. 47A [492]. The excellent biocompatibility of PVA has been demonstrated in previous research. Although PVA is not readily degradable in vivo, the fibrous matrix can gradually dissolve in body fluids and subsequently removed. At the same time, systemic toxicity was markedly decreased by local fiber delivery. The potential adverse effects in mice were further evaluated using biochemical blood markers estimation. The results shown in Fig. 47B indicated that kidney and liver functions remained normal compared with the control group. These findings suggest that the M/DCA-fiber system may serve as an implantable tool for effective therapy of advanced tumors while reducing possible adverse effects [492].

NFs can also enable selective detention and slow release of CTCs. For example, Wang et al. grafted thermoresponsive poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm) brushes onto CS NFs by ATRP and later introduced a poly (methacrylic acid) linker to anchor a DNA aptamer-based capture agent [493]. At low temperature, the PNIPAAm chains extended, rendering the surface hydrophilic and facilitating the release of non-target white blood cells (WBCs), thereby increasing purity. In spiked human whole blood (10-1000 MCF-7 cells/mL), the aptamer-PNIPAAm-modified CS fibers efficiently captured cancer cells while minimizing WBC carryover [493]. In another study, SF/gelatin (SF/GL) NFs functionalized with Pd and Pt NPs exhibited cytotoxic effects against A549 lung cancer cells, with IC50 values of 32.8 μg/mL (SF/GL), 30.3 μg/mL (SF/GL/Pd), 30.2 μg/mL (SF/GL/Pt), and 28.8 μg/mL (SF/GL/Pd-Pt), with the bimetallic system showing the strongest activity [494]. The proposed mechanism involves close contact between NFs and cells, followed by gradual ion release and ROS generation, resulting in damage to cellular membranes and nucleic acids, in agreement with previous reports [495], [496], [497]. Additionally, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis showed downregulation of Hsp90 after SF/GL/Pd-Pt exposure (−0.70 at 100 μg/mL), consistent with the literature linking reduced Hsp90 expression to favorable cancer prognosis [494], [498].

Magnetic hyperthermia can sensitize tumors to chemotherapy [499]; however, free MNPs raise safety concerns in vivo, including DNA damage and mitochondrial dysfunction [500], [501]. Embedding MNPs within NFs provides a more controllable and implantable platform while preserving their nanoscale functionality. For example, Kim et al. [502] demonstrated a smart hyperthermia nanofiber system that integrates both heat generation and controlled drug release. In this design, MNPs and DOX were incorporated into a chemically crosslinked, thermoresponsive poly (N-isopropylacrylamide-co-N-hydroxymethyl acrylamide) [poly(NIPAAm-co-HMAAm)] nanofiber matrix. When an alternating magnetic field (AMF) is applied (“on” state), the MNPs generate localized heat, inducing collapse of the polymer network and triggering an on-demand burst release of DOX. When the AMF is turned off, the system returns to its swollen state, thereby suppressing further drug release. This mechanism was further validated in vitro, where human melanoma (COLO 679) cells exhibited minimal cytotoxicity in the absence of AMF, confirming stable drug retention within the fibers [502]. Upon AMF exposure, a pronounced decrease in cell viability was observed. MNP-only fibers reduced viability by approximately 20% via hyperthermia alone, whereas DOX/MNP-loaded fibers achieved a greater reduction of about 30%, demonstrating a synergistic effect between thermal ablation and chemotherapeutic release [502]. Overall, ESNFs offer multiple convergent advantages in oncology: ECM-mimetic guidance for migration studies and CTC capture, high-capacity localized drug depots enabling synergistic combination therapies and prodrug systems, and implantable hyperthermia platforms that couple thermal effects with stimulus-triggered drug release. Moving forward, improved in vivo pharmacokinetic characterization at tumor margins, standardized reporting of drug loading and release parameters, and harmonized cytotoxicity assessment frameworks will be crucial to hasten the clinical translation of these nanofiber-based therapeutic strategies [502].

Another study reported that DOX released from DOX/MNP-loaded NFs induces apoptosis through synergy with magnetic hyperthermia. In contrast, short exposure to an AMF produced only a mild anticancer effect when hyperthermia was applied alone [503]. Notably, although the cumulative amount of DOX released from DOX/MNP-NFs was comparable to that of free DOX, the combined modality resulted in higher cell death than chemotherapy alone. In contrast, DOX/MNP-NFs without AMF exposure exhibited no intrinsic cytotoxicity. These findings support a trigger-on-demand mechanism that is superior to conventional systemic drug administration [503]. In other studies, apoptosis staging was confirmed using annexin V (early apoptosis) and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick end labelling (TUNEL) (late apoptosis) assays [502], [504], [505]. MNP-only NFs showed annexin V positivity without TUNEL staining, consistent with membrane perturbation as the primary effect under brief AMF exposure. In contrast, DOX/MNP-NFs and free DOX induced both annexin V and TUNEL signals by day 5 (but not day 4), indicating progression to late-stage apoptosis [502].

Beyond therapeutic applications, nanofiber-enabled CTC capture systems have demonstrated strong translational potential. For example, a microfluidic platform containing an electrospun interface functionalized with a melanoma-specific anti-CD146 coating was developed for the efficient capturing and separation of circulating melanoma cells (CMCs) [506]. In this study, a PLGA nanofiber-containing NanoVelcro chip (Fig. 48a and b) was designed to achieve high-efficiency CMC capture while allowing highly precise isolation of single CMCs immobilized on the nanosubstrate without contamination from WBCs. A custom-built ES system was used to deposit PLGA NFs with a thickness of 130.6 ± 62.7 nm (Fig. 48c) over a laser microdissection (LMD) slide, thereby generating transparent PN-NanoVelcro substrates. These substrates were subsequently functionalized with streptavidin-conjugated melanoma-specific anti-CD146 antibodies. To facilitate covalent streptavidin attachment, N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) chemistry was employed to activate the -COOH groups present on the PLGA nanofiber surface (Fig. 48d). The PN-NanoVelcro chip consisted of a transparent PN-NanoVelcro substrate overlapped with a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) chaotic mixer (Fig. 48e), both assembled within a plastic container and secured with four screws. A 22 cm-long microchannel with herringbone microfeatures was fabricated within the PDMS mixer to enhance cell-substrate interactions by increasing the frequency of cell-capture surface contact. Importantly, integrating PLGA NFs with the LMD slide enabled precise single-cell isolation (Fig. 48f). For performance optimization and validation, PN-NanoVelcro chips were tested with suspensions of the M229 human melanoma cell line, prepared at 100 cells mL−1 in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) which served as a model system. The effect of different ES deposition times on CMC capture efficiency was evaluated at a flow rate of 1 mL h−1, and the optimized deposition time was 180 min, yielding an approximate capture efficiency of 87% (Fig. 49a). Furthermore, the use of PLGA NFMs (3 μm) and application of a reduced flow rate of 0.5 mL h−1 further enhanced cell capture efficiency (Fig. 49b). The distribution of captured cells along the 22 cm channel was also investigated, revealing that approximately 68% were localized within the initial 8 cm, indicating that the explored length was sufficient for effective cell capture (Fig. 49c). To further evaluate device performance, four control experiments were conducted in parallel using PN-NanoVelcro chips without anti-CD146 coating, PN-NanoVelcro chips lacking herringbone microfeatures, anti-CD146-coated PLGA films without nanostructures, and anti-CD146-coated silicon nanowire (SiNW) substrates. The comparative results demonstrated that the capture antibody, chaotic microfluidic mixer, and nanostructured substrate each contributed significantly to the enhanced cell capture efficiency observed in the PN-NanoVelcro system (Fig. 49d). The dynamic detection range of the chips was subsequently evaluated using artificial CMC samples (DiO-stained M229 cells spiked into either healthy blood or DMEM medium) at concentrations ranging from 10 to 1000 cells mL−1. The data showed that the device possessed sufficient sensitivity and performance for clinically relevant samples, which typically contain only a few to several hundred CMCs per milliliter (Fig. 49e). Finally, the specificity and broader applicability of the developed chips for capturing CD146-positive melanoma cells were assessed using three cell lines known to express the antigen (M229, M229R, and M202), two CD146-negative cancer cell lines (Jurkat leukemia and PC3 prostate cancer cells), and freshly isolated human WBCs. The findings confirmed that the PN-NanoVelcro chips selectively captured melanoma cells with high specificity (Fig. 49f). In contrast, nonspecific binding of other cell types was effectively minimized through subsequent immunocytochemistry (ICC) and fluorescence-guided LMD analysis [506].

Core-sheath and multilayer designs provide additional control over drug localization and leakage. For example, Yang et al. demonstrated an implantable active-targeting micelle-in-nanofiber system for effective and safe cancer therapy, as shown in Fig. 50 [507]. First, folate (FA)-conjugated PCL-PEG (FA-PCL-PEG) copolymers were used to incorporate DOX via self-assembly into active-targeting micelles (FM). Folate ligands can specifically bind to folic acid receptors, which are overexpressed on many solid tumors. These micelles were subsequently inserted into the core of core-sheath NFs via coaxial ES, in which the inner phase consisted of an aqueous PVA solution containing micelles and the outer phase consisted of a gelatin solution [507]. In vitro release studies showed that free FM exhibited a fast ∼60% release within the initial 12 h, followed by a cumulative ∼75% release at 48 h and ∼98% at 288 h. In contrast, FM-loaded NFs showed a reduced initial burst and a slower cumulative release, reaching ∼40% at 48 h and just over 80% at 288 h [507]. The faster release from free micelles was attributed to their limited thermodynamic stability in aqueous environments [508]. In vivo fluorescence imaging (4T1 tumor model) at 6, 24, and 48 h showed weak tumor signals in all groups receiving 1.0 mg DOX/kg, consistent with rapid micelle clearance and the lower dose compared with 5.0 mg/kg used in previous studies [509], [510]. In contrast, implantable DOX-nanofiber, M-nanofiber, and FM-nanofiber groups exhibited strong and sustained tumor-localized fluorescence over time (Fig. 51a) [507]. Following implantation near tumors, micelles initially remained stable due to immobilization within the nanofiber matrix, preventing rapid systemic clearance. As the NFs gradually degraded in vivo, embedded micelles were slowly released and accumulated at tumor sites through interstitial passage, including diffusion through the ECM and entry into circulation via lymphatic pathways, followed by enhanced permeability and retention (EPR)-mediated accumulation and cellular uptake via endocytosis [507]. Among implantable systems, FM-nanofiber and M-nanofiber groups showed stronger tumor-associated fluorescence than DOX-nanofiber alone, indicating that micelle incorporation, particularly folate-targeted micelles, enhanced tumor accumulation. Ex vivo imaging at 48 h further confirmed higher tumor fluorescence in the FM-nanofiber group than in the DOX-nanofiber group, indicating improved carrier-mediated delivery and receptor-assisted internalization. Quantification of DOX levels by fluorescence spectroscopy (Fig. 51b) showed that, at 1, 6, 24, and 48 h post-administration, tumor accumulation in the FM and FM-nanofiber groups was significantly higher than in the free DOX group. This was attributed to the PEGylated micellar shell, which reduces recognition by the reticuloendothelial system (RES) [511], the EPR effect in tumor vasculature [512], and folate-mediated active targeting [513]. Finally, DOX accumulation in normal tissues was primarily observed in the heart, lung, liver, and kidney. Importantly, the FM-nanofiber showed decreased drug accumulation in these organs compared with free DOX and FM, confirming that this implantable system effectively limits off-target distribution and reduces systemic toxicity [507].

Another study demonstrated that integrating DOX-loaded vanadium MOFs (DOX@V-MOFs) into CS/PVA ESNF membranes can yield a unique multifunctional and stimuli-responsive DD platform [514]. The resulting membrane exhibited a dual response to pH and heat cues, substantially enhancing content release under simulated tumor environment (pH5) and high temperatures (37 °C −42 °C). Drug release profiles were consistent with zero-order, Higuchi, and Korsmeyer-Peppas models, suggesting that diffusion-driven mechanisms dominanted release behavior. The DOX@V-MOF membranes also demonstrated strong cytotoxic effect against several cancer cell lines, including liver cancer (HepG-2) and breast cancer (MCF-7), as well as notable antioxidant and antimicrobial activities against S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans. Optimization using a Box-Behnken design further uncovered that temperature, pH, and time were important factors influencing drug release dynamics [514]. Babadi et al. [515] fabricated piperine (PIP)-loaded electrospun PCL NFs as an implantable anticancer controlled-release platform for postsurgical breast cancer treatment and also investigated the effect of collagen (Coll) integration into the structure. The fabricated NFs were evaluated for shape, drug content, hydrophilicity, release behavior, mechanical features, cytotoxicity, and the underlying anticancer mechanisms in two breast cancer cell lines (MCF-7 and 4T1). The inclusion of collagen decreased the hydrophobicity of the PCL matrices, while the formulation containing 25% collagen exhibited favorable mechanical properties [515]. An in vivo antitumor study was conducted in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice, and among the tested formulations, the PIP-PCL75-Coll25 nanofiber was identified as the optimal combination because of its stable PIP release, suitable mechanical properties, and enhanced cancer toxicity. Fig. 52A illustrates the surgical procedure, during which all mice survived successfully. Photographs of tumors collected from the different experimental groups are also presented in Fig. 52B. Both surgical procedures and treatments were tolerated by animal as demonstrated by the minimal fluctuations in body weight (Fig. 52C) [515]. Efficacy results showed that tumors in both the control and PCL75-Coll25 groups grew similarly, reaching approximately 4000 mm3, corresponding to nearly a 10-fold increase over baseline size, as shown in Fig. 52D. Additionally, implanting the PIP-PCL75-Coll25 membrane suppressed tumor growth during the first 9 days, maintaining tumor volumes at approximately 700 mm3, comparable to those with PIP suspension treatment. Thereafter, the PIP-PCL75-Coll25 nanofiber exhibited significantly greater tumor inhibition, with a final tumor volume of approximately 1280 mm3 compared to approximately 2550 mm3 in the PIP suspension group. This corresponded to tumor volume increases of roughly 3-fold and 7-fold relative to the initial tumor size, respectively. Overall, the in vivo antitumor efficacy study confirmed the superiority of the PIP-PCL75-Coll25 NF compared to other groups. In contrast to the restricted PIP alone effect, these findings highlight the importance of sustained, controlled drug release to maintain appropriate drug concentrations at the target site to promote tumor growth inhibition [515].

In another study, Serio et al. developed biocompatible ECM-like NFs composed of PVA/gum arabic (GA) blend for in vitro testing [516]. For this, green-synthesized GA-stabilized AuNPs (GA-AuNPs) were uniformly adsorbed on blended PVA/GA ECM-like NFs and characterized using CLSM, SEM, and high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) (Fig. 53A-C) [516]. CLSM detected intense Rhodamine B isothiocyanate (RBTIC) fluorescence. GA-AuNPs were observed as bright dots on the NFs surface (arrows - Fig. 53B and C), distributed homogeneously along the fibers, corroborating the NFs functionalization with GA-AuNPs. Confocal microscopy confirmed that GA-AuNPs adsorbed onto nanofibers were internalized by B16-F10 melanoma cells within 4 h, with cytoplasmic localization validated by actin/nuclei overlays (Fig. 53D-F) [516]. Prior work established that GA-stabilized AuNPs selectively impair melanoma cell viability and proliferation without affecting non-tumoral cells [517]. At sub-toxic concentrations, GA-AuNPs also reduced metastatic parameters such as invasion and colony formation [517]. As a proof of concept, GA-AuNP-functionalized NFs were applied to evaluate mitochondrial metabolism associated with cell viability (Fig. 54A, B) [516]. Melanoma cells cultured on PVA/GA ECM-like NFs containing 2.44, 24.4, or 244 mg/L GA-AuNPs displayed similar viability patterns to controls, with statistical significance detected only in CHL-1 cells (Fig. 54C) [516]. Meanwhile, BALB/3T3 fibroblasts showed no cytotoxicity or viability changes (Fig. 54D) [516], corroborating earlier findings [517]. These results support advancing GA-AuNPs-decorated ECM-mimetic fibers for melanoma, including migration assays and in vivo validation.

In recent work, PCL nanofibers biofunctionalized with levan and egg lecithin and loaded with tanshinone IIA (Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF) were produced using a factorial design-guided water-in-oil emulsion ES approach [518]. The developed composite NFs exhibited a uniform shape with a mean diameter of 365.5 ± 46.2 nm, along with promising hydrophilicity and tensile strength. Specifically, Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF demonstrated a sustained drug-release profile, achieving complete drug release within 5 days, and providing approximately 50% skin deposition of tanshinone IIA. The anticancer effect was explored in vitro, where significant cytotoxicity of the developed NFs against squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) cells was observed, while maintaining good cytocompatibility with fibroblasts. Moreover, Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF exhibited pronounced apoptotic activity characterized by evident nuclear fragmentation, G2/M phase cell-cycle arrest, and strong antimigratory effects [518]. The in vivo antitumor efficacy of the composite NFs was further evaluated in tumor-bearing mice, in which the composite significantly inhibited tumor progression and reduced relative tumor weight compared with the other treatment groups. Histomorphometric analysis further confirmed the enhanced anticancer potential of the developed NFs [518]. To determine the effect of the developed nanofibers on tumor progression, investigators monitored the tumor growth as a percentage over the study duration and analyzed relative tumor weight normalized to body weight. In the untreated positive control group, tumor volume increased dramatically over the study duration (Fig. 55A), reaching a tumor growth rate of 475.02 ± 35.64% after three weeks (Fig. 55B), along with a relative tumor weight of 5.06 ± 0.006% (Fig. 55C) [518]. In contrast, the NF-treated group showed a significant reduction (p ≤ 0.05) in tumor progression after three weeks, reaching nearly a two-fold reduction compared to the control. Furthermore, this group had the lowest tumor weight (1.25 ± 0.18%) among all treatment groups. Although the remaining treatment groups also reduced tumor progression, their effects were less pronounced than those observed for Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF [518].

To further elucidate the anticancer mechanisms of the developed NFs, the expression levels of VEGF, B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) proteins were analyzed in excised skin tumors collected three weeks after application. VEGF is an important mediator of angiogenesis and plays key roles in tumor growth and cancer progression [519]. VEGF was significantly downregulated in all tested groups by approximately 1.5-fold relative to the untreated control group (Fig. 56A), indicating the antiangiogenic activity of the NFs. Similarly, NF-κB expression, which is closely associated with inflammatory signaling during malignant tumor progression, was markedly reduced in all treated groups (Fig. 56B), confirming the anti-inflammatory effects of the developed formulations [520]. This finding corroborates previous studies demonstrating the anti-inflammatory properties of both tanshinone IIA [521] and levan [522], which may act synergistically to attenuate inflammation in the tumor microenvironment. In addition, the expression of the antiapoptotic protein BCL2 was significantly reduced by nearly two-fold in the Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF and Tan@EL/PCL-NF groups (Fig. 56C), supporting the proapoptotic activity of these formulations. Collectively, these findings suggest that the potent anticancer activity of Tan@Lev/EL/PCL-NF results from the combined effects of proapoptotic, antiangiogenic, and anti-inflammatory mechanisms [518]. Further mechanistic investigation at the gene expression level was conducted using qRT-PCR to evaluate apoptotic caspase-3, the apoptosis-regulating gene BAX, and the proliferation-associated marker MKi67. The developed NF formulation significantly upregulated caspase-3 and BAX expression while markedly suppressing MKi67 expression, with fold differences of 34.3 ± 2.6, 14 ± 1.2, and 6.9 ± 1.6, respectively, compared with control group (Fig. 56D-F). Similar trends were observed for the remaining treatment groups, although to a lesser extent. These findings further confirmed the strong proapoptotic and antiproliferative activities of the developed composite NFs [518]. Table 5 gives an overview of ESNFs utilized in cancer diagnostics and therapy. All these studies have demonstrated suitable in vitro release profiles from drug-loaded ESNFs; however, translating these results into clinical practice remains elusive. The in vivo tumor microenvironment is highly diverse, and various factors, including abnormal vasculature, elevated interstitial fluid pressure, hypoxia, enzymatic activity, and immune-cell interactions can influence it. All these factors can substantially affect the drug's distribution and therapeutic efficacy of the drug. Thus, future studies should compare in vitro release data with in vivo pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic results to better anticipate clinical performance.

Biosensors integrate biorecognition elements with physicochemical transducers, a design that allows precise detection of target analytes while ensuring both high sensitivity and selectivity. These systems translate biomolecular interactions, such as antigen-antibody binding and enzyme-substrate catalysis, into measurable signals, including current, impedance, or fluorescence, thereby playing a crucial role in disease diagnostics and biomedical monitoring. The performance of biosensors largely relies on two key factors: the accuracy of molecular recognition and the efficiency of signal transduction. In this regard, NF-based substrates have emerged as favorable platforms for overcoming the limitations of conventional sensors, particularly in the development of wearable devices and health monitoring [530]. ESNFs are especially attractive because they can optimize the entire sensing cascade, including analyte recognition, signal transduction, and output generation, thereby facilitating the creation of intelligent, very sensitive, and user-friendly sensing systems [530], [531]. Owing to their exceptionally high surface-to-volume ratio, ESNFs provide abundant active sites for analyte interaction and effective immobilization of biorecognition molecules [531]. Moreover, their interconnected porous architecture minimizes diffusion barriers and promotes rapid mass transport toward active sensing regions, ultimately enhancing sensor responsiveness and detection efficiency [532]. Reliable sensing performance, however, requires careful optimization of nanofiber hydrophilicity, mechanical strength, and structural stability by appropriately selecting polymer compositions and ES parameters. To further improve analytical performance, hybrid ESNFs can be fabricated by incorporating nanoscale fillers that serve as catalytic, conductive, or affinity-enhancing components. Commonly employed nanomaterials include metallic NPs, graphene-derived quantum dots (QDs), CNTs, and graphene oxide sheets, all of which contribute to improved mechanical, optical, thermal, and electron-transfer properties while simultaneously providing numerous anchoring sites for sensing probes [533], [534]. In addition, various post-fabrication modification strategies, including LBL assembly, atomic layer deposition, dip-coating, spraying, plasma activation, and annealing, can be applied to tailor interfacial chemistry and construct hierarchical surface structures [535]. Among these techniques, dip-coating and spraying are particularly beneficial because they offer simple and cost-effective methods for decorating ESNFs with 0D-2D nanostructures, thereby enabling synergistic improvements in biosensor sensitivity, signal amplification, and overall analytical performance [536].

Maleki et al. [537] fabricated a biosensor by modifying a carbon screen-printed electrode (SPCE) with ESNFs containing HPMC, eudragit, and zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) NPs for the selective and sensitive electrochemical recognition of mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-MET). The developed Eudragit/HPMC/ZIF-8 NFs, cast onto the SPCE as an effective modifier, enhanced electron transfers at the electrode surface and increased the electroactive surface area, thereby improving the conductivity and stability of the biosensor. Furthermore, the ZIF-8 NPs not only increased the electron transfer rate but also facilitated the stable immobilization of anti-c-MET on the modified electrode. The fabricated biosensor exhibited excellent analytical performance, including a wide detection range from 100 fg mL−1 to 100 ng mL−1, a LOD of ∼1.3 fg mL−1, enhanced selectivity, and long-term stability than the other c-MET biosensors. As a non-invasive sensing platform, this biosensor was effectively tested on human plasma samples. However, its major limitation was the relatively long analysis time [537].

Fu et al. [538] developed a non-enzymatic glucose sensor by decorating carbon NFs with Ni-Co layered double hydroxide (LDH) nanosheets (carbon nanofiber@Ni-Co LDH), resulting in a flake-like LDH shell uniformly grown on the carbon nanofiber backbones, with diameters ranging from 300 to 500 nm. The ES carbon nanofiber network provided a conductive and macroporous scaffold that reduced LDH agglomeration and improved electrolyte accessibility. At the same time, the Ni-Co hydroxide layer supplied abundant redox-active sites for glucose oxidation. Optimization of the Ni:Co ratio to 2:1 yielded the highest catalytic activity, as evidenced by pronounced Ni2+/Ni3+ and Co2+/Co3+ redox peaks and a rapid amperometric response. Under optimized conditions, the sensor revealed a wide linear detection range (1.0-2000 μM), an excellent low LOD of 0.03 μM, and a high sensitivity of 1.47 mA mM−1 cm−2, along with excellent selectivity and stability [538].

In another related study, transparent electrospun nanofibrous hydrogels based on PVA and β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) were prepared and integrated with reverse iontophoresis electrodes to develop a non-invasive biosensing platform for longitudinal glucose monitoring in interstitial fluid [539]. Fig. 57a illustrates the fabrication process of a patch-style glucose sensor based on PVA/1,2,3,4-butanetetracarboxylic acid (BTCA)/β-CD/GOx/AuNP nanofibrous hydrogels and the corresponding sensing mechanism for real-time sweat glucose monitoring. Fig. 57b,c presents the preparation process of the ES solution containing the PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx/AuNP complex, along with optical and SEM micrographs of the resulting transparent nanofibrous structures [539]. The prepared composite hydrogels showed excellent flexibility, biocompatibility, absorptive capacity, mechanical features in both dry and wet states, and high enzyme activity (around 76%). Given the distinct characteristics of the AuNP-incorporated nanofibrous hydrogels, including high permeability to biological molecules and fast electron transfer, the biosensor demonstrated outstanding sensing performance, characterized by a wide linear range, high sensitivity (47.2 μA mM−1), a low detection limit (0.01 mM), and a rapid response time (<15 s). The electrochemical behavior of the GOx-loaded nanofibrous hydrogels hydrated with PBS (pH 7.4) was evaluated by cyclic voltammetry (CV). Fig. 58a shows the CV curves of PVA/BTCA, PVA/BTCA/β-CD, PVA/BTCA/GOx, PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx, and PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx/AuNP hydrogels at a scan rate of 0.1 V s−1. A photograph of the fabricated hydrogel-based non-invasive biosensor patch is presented in Fig. 58b. Electrochemical characterization (Fig. 58c) revealed that the PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx/AuNP hydrogel exhibited quasi-reversible redox peaks at Epa = 0.624 V and Epc = −0.637 V. The AuNP-functionalized hydrogel showed a substantially higher background current than the other hydrogels, consistent with enhanced conductivity [539]. The formal potential was −6.5 mV, and the small ΔEp (∼13 mV) confirmed rapid, quasi-reversible electron transfer. CV measurements in PBS (10 mM, pH 7.4) demonstrated a linear decrease in cathodic peak current with increasing glucose concentrations (0.1-0.5 mM). Chronoamperometric experiments performed with PVA/BTCA/GOx, PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx, and PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx/AuNP hydrogel biosensors at room temperature (Fig. 58d–f) revealed clear differences in sensing behavior among the systems [539]. The resulting current profiles underscored substantial differences in sensing capabilities among the tested membranes. The PVA/BTCA/β-CD/GOx/AuNP hydrogel sensor demonstrated superior accuracy and responsiveness, whereas the PVA/BTCA/GOx hydrogel, which performed poorly due to diminished enzyme activity and stability. A calibration curve of steady-state current versus glucose concentration was constructed for the AuNP-functionalized sensor, further validating its enhanced performance (Fig. 58e, inset). While standard deviation increased with increasing glucose concentration, the sensor maintained strong linearity (R2 = 0.98) and delivered a rapid response time of <15 s. Key performance parameters included a detection limit of 0.01 mM, a linear range spanning 0-0.5 mM, and a sensitivity of 47.2 μA mM−1 [539]. Given its ease of fabrication, scalability, and excellent electrochemical properties, the transparent NF hydrogel biosensing platform represents a promising candidate for wearable monitoring, clinical diagnostics, and diverse biomedical applications [539].

Mondal et al. developed a surface-functionalized, aligned mesoporous anatase TiO2 nanofiber (TiO2 NF) mat that, following oxygen plasma activation and EDC/NHS coupling, enabled the dense and stable attachment of cholesterol esterase (ChEt) and cholesterol oxidase (ChOx) on an indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate for the electrochemical sensing of esterified cholesterol [540]. The ES process and porosity were tuned by incorporating PVP as a sacrificial carrier polymer into the titanium isopropoxide precursor solution. For biofunctionalization, fresh solutions of ChEt and ChOx (1 mg mL−1 each) were mixed at a ratio of 1:1. Subsequently, 10 μL of the enzyme mixture was uniformly deposited onto the oxygen plasma-treated TiO2 nanofiber surface (cTiO2-NF/ITO) via physical adsorption and incubated at 4 °C for 12 h. The functional groups (-COOH, -CHO, and -OH) generated on the cTiO2-NF/ITO surface were used for the covalent immobilization of enzymes through interactions with terminal -NH2 groups, ensuing in the establishment of amide bonds, as shown in Fig. 59 [540]. The high mesoporosity (61%) and small fiber diameter (30-60 nm) significantly increased enzyme loading and facilitated rapid electron transfer, thereby enhancing sensing. As shown in Fig. 60a, CV measurements revealed a clear concentration-dependent increase in anodic peak current with increasing cholesterol oleate concentration from 25 to 400 mg dL−1. The inset highlights the pronounced increase in peak current at lower concentrations. Fig. 60b presents the calibration characteristics of the biosensor. The biosensor demonstrated a wide detection range and a high sensitivity of 181.6 μA mg−1 dL cm−2, which compares favorably with previously reported microfluidic anatase TiO2 nanoparticle-based cholesterol biosensors [541]. The increased analytical parameters can be attributed to the covalent immobilization of enzymes on oxygen-activated TiO2 NFs and to the conductive nanofibrous network, which promotes effective electron transfer between the biorecognition layer and the electrode. In addition, the enhanced sensitivity may be attributed to the formation of TiO2 NFs, which provide efficient pathways for electron transfer between the solution and the surface, thereby improving current density. Similar observations have been reported for aligned carbon nanofiber electrodes, where superior electrochemical performance was attributed to more efficient electron movement from the electroactive species to the signal detector [542]. Therefore, the exceptional charge-transfer characteristics of TiO2 NFs make them ideal for enhanced biosensing performance. Furthermore, the TiO2-NF biosensor achieved a low LOD of 19.3 mg dL−1 and demonstrated excellent selectivity and operational stability. As shown in Fig. 61i, various common interferents, such as ascorbic acid (AA), uric acid (UA), glucose, lactic acid, and urea, generated negligible current responses compared with cholesterol, proving the superior specificity of the sensing platform [540]. Fig. 61(ii) illustrates the reproducibility and stability of the biosensor. Repeated measurements (n = 10) at a cholesterol concentration of 200 mg dL−1 exhibited minimal signal variation, with a relative standard deviation (RSD) of only 3.19%. Moreover, the inset demonstrates consistent current responses over multiple measurement cycles. Collectively, these findings highlight the excellent sensitivity, selectivity, reproducibility, and operational durability of the TiO2 nanofiber-based biosensor for cholesterol detection [540].

Electrospun platforms are also greatly employed in the development of non-enzymatic glucose sensors. Adabi et al. fabricated nickel-modified carbon nanofibers by ES of PAN polymer, followed by stabilization and carbonization to produce carbon nanofibers, and subsequent electrodeposition of Ni onto the nanofiber surface [543]. The average diameter of the fiber declined from 124.4 nm (ES PAN fibers) to 85.3 nm (after carbonization). SEM, EDS, and XRD assessments endorsed the successful and uniform incorporation of Ni into the carbon NF structure. The sensor exhibited a rapid response, a two-concentration-level linear detection range from 2.0 μM to 5.0 mM, a low LOD of 0.57 μM, and excellent stability and selectivity. Furthermore, the sensor demonstrated promising performance in real sample analysis [543]. In a related study, graphene and mixed Co/Mn oxide catalysts were incorporated into composite microfibers to fabricate a high-performance non-enzymatic glucose sensor [544]. Fig. 62a summarizes the synthesis procedure, in which graphene was first dispersed in DMF, followed by the addition of PVP to form a spinnable solution. Subsequently, cobalt and manganese acetates were introduced before ES [544]. The resulting fibers were electrospun under 18 kV applied voltage, a distance of 10 cm (from the collector), and a flow rate of 1 mL h−1. After drying at 75 °C, the fibers were calcined under an argon atmosphere at 650 °C to obtain graphene/metal oxide composite microfibers (GMCFs). Optimization of the operating conditions identified 0.2 M NaOH as the supporting electrolyte, +0.55 V as the working potential, and 4.0 mg mL−1 GMCFs as the optimum catalyst loading. Under these conditions, the GMCF-modified glassy carbon electrode (GCE) exhibited rapid and stable amperometric responses, reaching a steady-state current within 1.5 s following each successive glucose addition, as shown in Fig. 62b [544]. The sensor displayed a linear glucose response over a range of 5.0 nM to 800 μM with a correlation coefficient (R2) of 0.995. In addition, it achieved a high sensitivity of 1.81 mA mM−1 cm−2 and an exceptionally low detection limit of 1.0 nM, as illustrated in Fig. 62c [544].

In another work, enzyme-loaded NFs directly interfaced with microstructured electrodes were fabricated by ES of PVA/PEI/glucose oxidase (PVA/PEI/GOx) blends onto gold microelectrodes, forming a conformal and bioactive nanofibrous coating with high enzyme loading and strong adhesion [545]. The resulting nanostructured gold electrodes were further functionalized using electrospun PVA/PEI/GOx fibers assembled on a 4-aminothiophenol self-assembled monolayer, followed by brief glutaraldehyde crosslinking and decoration with Au NPs to enhance conductivity and catalytic activity [545]. EIS measurements in PBS (0.1 M, pH 5) divulged that the charge-transfer resistance increased with glucose concentration (0-1.0 mM) only in the presence of GOx, whereas enzyme-free controls showed no measurable response. These measurements confirm that the impedance change originates from enzymatic reactions that produce electroactive species such as H2O2 and gluconic acid. Rinsing with PBS restored the baseline signal, indicating reversible interfacial product accumulation and stable immobilization of both GOx and Au NPs [545]. The resulting PVA/PEI/GOx/AuNP nanofiber-modified electrodes exhibited a linear response over 10-200 μM glucose with an LOD of 0.9 μM. The system also demonstrated preserved enzyme activity, good electrode-to-electrode reproducibility, and stable performance under repeated measurements. This study highlights how integration of enzyme-loaded NFs with microstructured gold electrodes, combined with nanoparticle-mediated conductivity enhancement, enables highly sensitive, stable, and miniaturizable electrochemical biosensing platforms [545].

Zhao et al. established a self-powered electrochemical biosensor in which electrospun PAN/carbon nanotube (PAN/CNT) NFs served as a conductive and structural backbone for immobilizing AuNPs and constructing a dual-electrode enzymatic biofuel cell (EBFC) platform for myoglobin (Mb) detection [546]. The system consists of a PAN/CNT-COOH-AuNP-GOx bioanode for glucose oxidation and a PAN/CNT-COOH-AuNP-aptamer biocathode for selective binding of Mb [546]. The ESNFs provide large surface area, adjustable porosity, and outstanding conductivity, while CNT incorporation enhances electron transport and AuNPs improve biocompatibility and enable aptamer immobilization via Au-S chemistry [547], [548]. As illustrated in Fig. 63, the presence of Mb modulates electron flow: in the absence of Mb, electrons generated at the GOx bioanode reduce the [Fe(CN)6]3- redox mediator at the cathode, resulting in a high open-circuit voltage (EOCV). Upon Mb binding, steric hindrance at the aptamer-functionalized cathode impedes electron transfer, resulting in a concentration-dependent decrease in EOCV [546]. This architecture enabled highly sensitive Mb detection over a range of 5.0 ng mL−1 to 5 × 103 ng mL−1, with an ultralow LOD of 0.23 ng mL−1. Polarization studies further showed a decrease in peak power density from 19 μW cm−2 to 3.5 μW cm−2 upon Mb binding, supporting a steric hindrance-based sensing mechanism [546]. Selectivity tests demonstrated negligible interference from BSA, cytochrome c, and sulfite oxidase, even at fivefold higher concentrations (Fig. 64) [546]. Long-term stability studies showed nearly 100% signal retention after 2000 s, while four-day stability tests confirmed consistent EOCV output. Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis further indicated ∼98% AuNP retention [546]. The sensing mechanism is based on strong Au-S bonds that anchor the aptamer to the AuNP-modified cathode. In the absence of Mb, electrons from glucose oxidation at the anode are efficiently transferred to the cathode, where [Fe(CN)6]3- is reduced to [Fe(CN)6]4-, generating a high open-circuit voltage [549]. Upon Mb binding, steric hindrance from the bulky protein structure inhibits electron transfer, resulting in a decreased EOCV [550].

Ozoemena et al. designed an onion-like carbon (OLC)-integrated PAN NFs to enhance spinnability and conductivity for DA detection [551]. Following carbonization, the OLC-carbon nanofibers exhibited an optimized pore structure and increased surface area, enabling efficient DA adsorption and redox cycling. The sensor achieved a sensitivity of 0.31 μA μM−1 and a LOD of 1.42 μM, demonstrating that polymer blending and hybrid carbon architectures can provide adaptable sensing platforms [551]. In another study, Ghorbanizamani et al. developed an electrochemical immunosensor by incorporating aminated MXene nanosheets into polypropylene carbonate (PPC) NFs, which were electrospun directly onto gold screen-printed electrodes, forming a high-surface-area, conductive, and antibody-compatible interface for the detection of synthetic cannabinoids [552]. The MXene-NH2/PPC NFs exhibited a cracked, flake-like morphology, which enhanced electron transfer and facilitated the efficient immobilization of monoclonal anti-K2 antibodies. Optimizing solvent composition, polymer concentration, MXene loading, and ES time yielded a uniform nanofibrous network with increased electroactive surface area and reduced charge-transfer resistance. Using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), the immunosensor demonstrated a suitably wide linear range of 0.6-2000 ng mL−1 for JWH-018 and a LOD of 0.66 ng mL−1 in both PBS and saliva samples. The sensor also exhibited excellent repeatability (CV = 3.66%), reproducibility (CV = 1.25%), high recovery (∼96%), strong selectivity, and long-term stability under vacuum storage conditions [552].

Beyond biomolecular recognition, ESNFs have been combined with molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) to mimic natural receptor-ligand interactions. Compared with biological recognition elements, MIPs offer higher mechanical stability, lower cost, and resistance to harsh conditions; however, challenges such as binding heterogeneity and limited accessibility of recognition sites remain [553]. Incorporating MIPs into nanofibrous architectures mitigates these limitations by increasing the surface-to-volume ratio and improving site accessibility. MIP-nanofiber hybrids can be fabricated via several strategies, including (i) coating preformed NFs with an imprinted layer, (ii) surface imprinting on fibers, (iii) embedding MIP NPs within fibrous networks, and (iv) direct imprinting during ES [553]. For example, Yang et al. created a visible-light-responsive photoelectrochemical (PEC) sensor by integrating ES template-directed molecularly imprinted NFs (MI-ESNFs) with BiOI nanoflake arrays, forming a hierarchical MI-ESNFs@BiOI photoactive electrode [554]. The MIP NFs were prepared by ES using a CS/triphenyl phosphate (CS/TPhP) precursor with TPhP serving as the template. After ES, neutralization, and template removal, the resulting MI-ESNFs contained well-defined recognition cavities complementary to TPhP in size, shape, and functional groups. SEM analysis confirmed the presence of uniform fibers (∼50 nm) intertwined with BiOI nanoflakes, forming a 3D interconnected network that enhanced mass transport and provided abundant active sites. The sensing mechanism is assumed to be that rebinding of TPhP to the imprinted cavities induces steric hindrance, inhibiting the diffusion of electron donor (e.g. AA) and thereby decreasing photocurrent under visible-light irradiation. The resulting MI-ESNFs@BiOI electrode exhibited a linear response from 0.01 to 500 ng mL−1 and an ultralow LOD of 8.0 fg mL−1, outperforming conventional chromatographic methods. The sensor also showed excellent selectivity toward structurally related organophosphate flame retardants (OPFRs), as well as high reproducibility and long-term stability [554].

Enzyme-based assays remain widely used for early disease biomarker detection; however, they are often lengthy, costly, and require specialized laboratory instruments, limiting their application in underdeveloped settings. Accordingly, an increasing need for rapid, compatible, and standardized sensing platforms capable of detecting cancer biomarkers at ultralow concentrations. In this perspective, Tawfik et al. proposed an enzyme-free, cheap assay based on fluorescent molecularly imprinted conjugated polythiophenes (FMICPs) for cancer biomarker detection [555]. Leveraging the high interfacial advantage of NF networks, FMICP-based NFs enabled rapid detection of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) within 15 min. The nanofibrous structure enhanced sensitivity by approximately 80-fold compared with pristine FMICP, achieving LODs of 15 fg mL−1 (AFP) and 3.5 fg mL−1 (CEA), which are several-fold better than those of traditional enzyme-based counterparts. The sensor also demonstrated successful application in clinical liver cancer samples, with results consistent with standard ELISA measurements [555].

Hu et al. fabricated SnO2-doped carbon nanofibers via ES of PAN/SnCl2 precursors followed by stabilization and carbonization, producing uniform fibers (400-500 nm) with well-dispersed SnO2 confirmed by SEM, TEM, EDS, XRD, and XPS [556]. The modified GCE exhibited reduced charge-transfer resistance and enhanced electrocatalytic activity toward p-hydroxyacetophenone (p-HAP) and acetaminophen (APAP). Using DPV, the biosensor showed linear ranges of 0.5-700 μM (APAP) and 0.2-50 μM (p-HAP), with low LODs of 86 nM and 33 nM, respectively. The platform also demonstrated high selectivity, reproducibility, and effectiveness in pharmaceutical and serum samples [556]. Bahrami et al. designed a magnetic nanofiber-based sensor for morphine recognition using electrospun and thermally treated PVA/iron salt precursors, yielding fibers with diameters of 70-120 nm [557]. The resulting composite was mixed with graphite powder and paraffin oil to form a carbon paste electrode (CPE). Structural characterization (FTIR, SEM, and XRD) confirmed material integrity. Electrochemical analysis via CV and DPV revealed a wide linear range (3.3 nM-245 μM) and a LOD of 1.9 nM, demonstrating high sensitivity and reliability [557].

ESNFs have also been widely explored for heavy metal ion sensing. Ehzari et al. developed an aptasensor for Hg2+ detection by integrating electrospun polyethersulfone NFs decorated with CdTe QDs (NFs-QDs) onto a CPE, forming a highly porous electroactive platform that enhanced methylene blue (MB) signal amplification [558]. The sensing mechanism relies on specific T-Hg2+-T coordination, along with additional MB-Hg2+ interactions that increase binding site availability and signal intensity. The composite NFs improved electron transfer kinetics and provided abundant immobilization sites for amine-terminated DNA aptamers. The aptasensor exhibited a wide detection range (0.1-150 nM) and an ultralow LOD of 0.02 nM, with high selectivity against interfering metal ions, excellent reproducibility (RSD 2-3%), and successful application in spiked fruit juice samples [558].

Colorimetric sensing has also benefited from nanofibrous architectures. For instance, a reusable optical sensor based on polyaspartate (PASP) ESNF hydrogel membranes (ENHMs) was developed for the determination of Cu2+ and Fe3+ in aqueous media [559]. The PASP-ENHM sensor demonstrated tremendous sensitivity and selectivity, with visible color changes detectable by the naked eye: white to blue for Cu2+ (LOD = 0.3 mg L−1) and white to yellow for Fe3+ (LOD = 0.1 mg L−1). Desorption processes were also applicable, enabling the reusability of the biosensing platform [559]. Similarly, Tungsombatvisit et al. developed CA nanofiber-based rhodamine B derivative (RBD-CA NF) colorimetric strip for the detection of Cu2+ [560]. Alkaline treatment (0.1 M NaOH) improved wettability and reduced response time from 3300 s to 100 s. Consequently, the sensor demonstrated a detection range of 20-300 ppm, a detection limit of 18 ppm, and optimal performance at pH 6 [560].

In another work, novel Mn2O3-Ag NFs were fabricated via a facile 2-step process involving ES followed by calcination. An amperometric glucose biosensor was created by binding GOx onto highly porous Mn2O3-Ag NFs [561]. The resulting composite NFs exhibited a rough, nanoparticle-assembled morphology with a high surface-to-volume ratio, abundant catalytic sites, and superior electrical properties. Electrochemical studies of the Mn2O3-Ag nanofiber-GOx modified electrode indicated that the highly porous nanofibrous structure provides a favorable microenvironment for enzyme immobilization, stabilizes biological activity, and significantly enhances direct electron transfer (DET). This enhancement arises from the large specific interface, good biocompatibility, and the presence of multiple effective electron passage pathways within the network. The observed DET also suggests close electronic coupling between GOx and the NFs, enabling rapid monitoring of glucose-induced oxygen consumption without significant diffusion-related signal loss. When integrated onto GCE, the Mn2O3-Ag nanofiber matrix enabled efficient electron passage between the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD/FADH2) redox center of GOx and the electrode surface. Operating via an oxygen-reduction transduction mechanism, the biosensor exhibited a fast response time (5-10 s), a high sensitivity of 40.60 μA mM−1 cm−2, and a low LOD of 1.73 μM. It also showed a low apparent Michaelis-Menten constant (2.1 mM), indicating strong enzyme-substrate affinity, along with excellent selectivity against common interferents such as UA and AA. Overall, these results demonstrate that Mn2O3-Ag nanofiber-GOx composites are promising platforms for highly sensitive and selective electrochemical glucose sensing based on oxygen reduction [561].

In another study, Li et al. proposed a sensitive, label-free amperometric immunosensor for AFP using electrospun IrOx NFs engineered into a wire-in-tube architecture [562]. The NFs were synthesized by ES of IrCl3/PVP precursors, followed by controlled annealing, during which calcination at 500 °C produced an optimal Ir/IrO2 mixed-phase structure with increased conductivity, large electroactive interface, and outstanding chemical stability. The resulting IrOx NFs were dispersed in CS and drop-cast onto GCE, enabling efficient attachment of anti-AFP mAb and formation of a stable immunointerface. Stepwise CV and EIS confirmed successful assembly and showed that the wire-in-tube morphology significantly accelerated electron transfer. Under optimized conditions, the immunosensor exhibited a wide detection range between 50 pg mL−1 and 150 ng mL−1 and an ultralow LOD (20 pg mL−1), outperforming many noble-metal-based AFP sensors. The platform also demonstrated strong selectivity, reproducibility, stability, and reliable performance in human serum [562].

Filiz et al. developed crosslinked CS/PVA ESNFs as a stable and biocompatible platform for naked-eye glucose sensing, using a GOx/HRP cascade with o-dianisidine as the chromogenic substrate [563]. The optimized CS/PVA (1:4) blend produced uniform, bead-free NFs (∼378 nm) with high hydrophilicity and mechanical stability, enabling efficient enzyme immobilization and robust operation in aqueous environments. The glucose detection range of 2.7-13.8 mM covers clinically relevant physiological levels, including hypoglycemic, normal fasting, and diabetic conditions [564], [565]. Fig. 65 illustrates spectrophotometric and strip-based validation of the sensing platform [563]. In Fig. 65a, UV-Vis spectra show a monotonic improvement in absorbance at 480 nm with increasing glucose amounts, corresponding to HRP-mediated oxidation of o-dianisidine driven by GOx-generated H2O2. Fig. 65b presents the calibration curve (R2 = 0.9968), confirming excellent linearity across the physiological range. Fig. 65c shows the visual response of the nanofiber strip, which changes from white to brownish-orange as glucose concentration increases, reflecting the enzymatic cascade reaction. Fig. 65d illustrates the underlying mechanism: glucose oxidation by GOx generates H2O2, which is immediately consumed by HRP to oxidize o-dianisidine. This coupled cascade accelerates reaction kinetics and minimizes GOx deactivation by preventing H2O2 accumulation. Overall, the study demonstrates that CS/PVA nanofiber strips operate effectively within the clinically relevant glucose detection window reported for both electrochemical and colorimetric systems (typically 0.001-13 mM) [566], [567], while offering a low-cost, equipment-free, and visually interpretable alternative for glucose monitoring [563].

Wang et al. designed an ESNF-based electrochemiluminescent (ECL) immunosensor for the detection of the tumor suppressor protein p53 (TSP53) by integrating functional NFs with luminescent core-sheath nanocomposites [568]. Multi-walled CNTs (MWCNTs)-doped CS NFs (MWCNTs-CTS) were fabricated via a single-step ES and subsequently decorated in situ with AuNPs by electrodeposition, forming MWCNTs-CTS-AuNP structure for immobilization of capture antibodies (CAb). These NFs provided enhanced loading capacity and improved stability for immobilized biomolecules. Meanwhile, Ru(bpy)32+- and silver-doped silica NPs (RuAg/SiO2 NPs) were created via a water-in-oil microemulsion approach and used as highly luminescent labels for detection antibodies (DAb). During the sandwich immunoassay, CAb-functionalized NFs captured TSP53, while RuAg/SiO2 NPs@DAb conjugates acted as signal probes. The resulting electrode exhibited strong ECL emission intensity due to the synergistic electron-transfer efficiency between the nanofibrous network and the luminescent nanocomposites. As shown in Fig. 66a [568], the fabrication strategy integrates ES, electrodeposition, and antibody conjugation. Selectivity was evaluated using TSP53, hemoglobin, HSA, AFP, and mixed protein samples under identical conditions. As shown in Fig. 66b, only TSP53 produced a significant ECL signal, while the rest exhibited responses comparable to the blank, confirming high selectivity. In addition, the mixed-protein sample generated an ECL response similar to that of pure TSP53, further demonstrating the sensor's strong specificity. The ECL responses of various CAb-TSP53-RuAg/SiO2 NPs@DAb combinations are demonstrated in Fig. 66c [568]. The calibration curve revealed a detection range between 1.0 pg mL−1 and 1.0 ng mL−1 (R2 = 0.9993) and a LOD of 0.5 pg mL−1. These results emphasize the ultrahigh sensitivity, excellent selectivity, and strong reproducibility of the developed ECL immunosensor.

Wang et al. fabricated water-stable electrospun PVA nanofibrous mats decorated with uniformly distributed AuNPs, creating an efficient substrate for HRP-based hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) sensing [569]. An in-situ glutaraldehyde crosslinking method was applied to produce mechanically robust, water-insoluble PVA NFs. At the same time, MPTES functionalization enabled dense Au-S bonding on the NFs, thereby enhancing both conductivity and enzyme loading. As illustrated in Fig. 67, the sensing mechanism relied on the HRP-catalyzed reduction of H2O2, with hydroquinone (HQ) serving as an electron mediator. In this cycle, HRP is oxidized by H2O2, while HQ reduces the oxidized enzyme. Subsequently, benzoquinone is reduced back to HQ, sustaining continuous electron transfer. This catalytic cycle generates a reduction current relative to the H2O2 amounts. The AuNP-PVA nanofibrous network significantly amplifies the electrochemical response by providing a large interfacial area and facilitating rapid electron transfer, resulting in a fast response time, a wide detection range (1.0-500 μM), and an adequate LOD (0.5 μM). Compared with other HRP-based sensing platforms, this nanofibrous system demonstrates both an extended dynamic range and rapid response attributed to the efficient diffusion of H2O2 through the porous AuNP-PVA matrix [569].

A nanofibrous biosensor based on burkholderia cepacia lipase (BCL) immobilized on MOF structures was fabricated using metal-organic NFs (MONFs) synthesized from amino acid and copper nitrate precursors [570]. These MONFs provided high electrochemical activity and chemical robustness, enabling sensitive detection of methyl parathion residues in vegetables. The NFs were integrated with CS as a binder to immobilize BCL@MOF composites onto GCE, resulting in a biosensor with a low LOD of 67 nM and a linear detection range of 0.1-38 μM. The system displayed good selectivity and working stability, highlighting its potential for pesticide monitoring in food matrices [570]. In another investigation, Alim et al. developed a glucose biosensor based on electrospun multiporous SnO2 NFs fabricated from tin-based precursors [571]. The porous nanofibrous architecture facilitated efficient electron transfer between the electrode and the redox-active GOx cluster, thereby enhancing electrochemical communication and catalytic performance. The resulting biosensor displayed a linear amperometric response over 5.0-100 μM, with a LOD of 1.8 μM. In addition, the sensor demonstrated excellent reproducibility and long-term stability, attributed to the ample surface area and excellent conductivity of the SnO2 nanofiber matrix [571].

Similarly, Chauhan et al. reported PAN NFs embedded with magnetic Fe3O4 NPs via ES to form Fe3O4-PAN NFs composites [572]. Nafion was used to improve the adhesion of the NFs onto an ITO substrate. The Fe3O4-PAN NFs/ITO electrode was further functionalized with NaOH to partially convert the nitrile groups in PAN to -COOH and -NH2 groups, providing a suitable microenvironment for anti-vitamin D (Anti-VD) immobilization. BSA was used to block non-specific binding sites on the Anti-VD/Fe3O4-PAN NFs/ITO immunoelectrode. The electrochemical response of the BSA/Anti-VD/Fe3O4-PAN NFs/ITO immunoelectrode toward vitamin D3 (Vit-D3) was investigated using DPV between 10 ng mL−1 and 100 ng mL−1, as shown in Fig. 68. During measurement, the immunoelectrode was incubated with Vit-D3 for approximately 5 min, and a linear increase in signal was observed up to 90 ng mL−1, followed by saturation at higher concentrations (Fig. 68a). This increase in current is attributed to the formation of an immunocomplex (antigen-antibody) at the electrode surface, which facilitates electron passage [572]. Fig. 68b shows the calibration curve of Vit-D3, yielding a sensitivity of 0.90 μA ng−1 mL cm−2 and a correlation coefficient (R2) of 0.98. The LOD was estimated around 0.12 ng mL−1. Furthermore, a Hanes-Woolf plot (Vit-D3 concentration vs. Vit-D3 concentration/peak current), shown in Fig. 68c, was used to determine the association (Ka) and dissociation (Kd) constants, reflecting the kinetics of immunocomplex formation at the electrode surface. The Ka value (74 ng mL−1) was obtained from the reciprocal of the slope, while the Kd value (4.5 ng mL−1) was derived from the product of Ka and the intercept. These results indicate that Fe3O4 NPs within the PAN NFs provide abundant binding sites for antibody immobilization, thereby significantly enhancing biosensing performance [572].

Another notable example of metal-based nanofibrous architectures involves hierarchical NiCo2S4 nanowire arrays grown on electrospun graphite fibers (EGF), as shown in Fig. 69, for glucose biosensing [573]. The EGF substrate was prepared via direct graphitization of electrospun polymeric fibers, followed by hydrothermal growth of NiCo2O4 precursors using Ni2+/Co2+ salts and urea. A subsequent sulfurization step with Na2S converted the oxide into NiCo2S4, forming an interwoven 3D nanowire architecture. The resulting NiCo2S4/EGF composite exhibited excellent mechanical stability and abundant electroactive sites due to its hierarchical core-sheath morphology and high surface area.
