These structural advantages are directly reflected in the amperometric behavior summarized in Fig. 70 [573]. Fig. 70A shows the current-time (I-t) response at low glucose concentrations, where successive additions down to the sub-micromolar level produce immediate and well-defined current steps. The sensor reaches a steady state within 5 s, indicating rapid catalytic kinetics. Fig. 70B extends the response to higher concentrations, demonstrating a wide detection range from 0.5 μM to 3.57 mM, with a proportional increase in current. The inset calibration plot confirms excellent linearity (R2 = 0.995) and a low LOD of 0.167 μM [573]. Comparative analysis shows that the NiCo2S4/EGF-7 configuration outperforms or matches related systems, including NiCo2S4/Pt [574], NiCo2S4/GCE [575], and NiCoO2@CNT [576]. The superior electrochemical performance of NiCo2S4/EGF-7 is attributed to three synergistic factors: (i) the core-sheath NiCo2S4 nanowire structure providing abundant active sites for glucose oxidation; (ii) strong coupling between NiCo2S4 and the conductive EGF backbone, which enhances electron transport and catalytic kinetics; and (iii) uniform nanowire dispersion on the fiber network, which prevents agglomeration and maximizes accessible surface area for charge transfer [573]. Furthermore, interference studies using AA, DA, UA, and common sugars (lactose, xylose, mannose) demonstrated high selectivity, with interference signals below 5% (Fig. 70C) [573]. Operational stability tests showed that the sensor lost 13.8% of its first response after 4600 s of continuous operation, while also exhibiting good storage stability (Fig. 70D) [573]. Overall, these characteristics, combined with rapid response time and enzyme-free selectivity, establish NiCo2S4/EGF-7 as an efficient platform for glucose sensing within physiologically relevant ranges (3.0-8.0 mM in human serum) [577]. In addition to these examples, the literature in this field is extensive, and Table 6 summarizes selected reports on nanofiber-based electrochemical glucose sensors.

Functionalized ESNFs have attracted considerable attention as advanced materials for biomedical applications owing to their tunable porosity, high surface-to-volume ratio, structural versatility, and ability to incorporate, immobilize, or spatially organize bioactive agents. These characteristics have enabled their investigation in DD, wound healing, TE, biosensing, and other therapeutic applications. Despite substantial progress, several challenges remain, including biocompatibility and potential cytotoxicity, controlled-release behavior, mechanical robustness, long-term functional stability, manufacturing scalability, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance. These limitations continue to hinder the broader clinical translation and industrial adoption of functionalized ESNFs. Beyond these challenges, however, recent advances in ES technique have substantially expanded the structural design space of ESNFs, creating new opportunities for the development of next-generation nanofibrous systems with precisely controlled architectures and functions.

sections.title: Structural versatility and emerging electrospinning architectures

paragraphs.en: The development of nanoscale architectures represents an important manifestation of progress in nanoscience and nanotechnology [585]. ES, electrospraying, and electrohydrodynamic jetting/printing are representative electrohydrodynamic fabrication approaches that exploit interactions between working fluids and electrostatic forces to generate micro- and nanoscale structures [586], [587], [588], [589], [590]. Among these approaches, ES is particularly attractive because of its remarkable structural versatility and its ability to generate nanofibrous architectures with controlled composition, spatial organization, and compartmentalization. Depending on the configuration of the ES process and the properties of the working fluids, ES can produce conventional monolithic nanofibers as well as increasingly sophisticated structures, including core–sheath, hollow, Janus, multi-chamber Janus, and hybrid Janus/core–sheath nanofibers [586], [587], [588], [589], [590], [591], [592], [593], [594]. Monolithic nanofibers provide a relatively simple and versatile platform for biomedical applications [586], whereas core–sheath nanofibers enable spatial separation and controlled presentation of different materials, including therapeutic agents and polymers with distinct or gradient distributions [587], [588], [589]. Hollow nanofibers and surface-engineered nanofibrous structures provide additional control over internal morphology and interfacial characteristics [590], [591]. More recently, Janus nanofibers, multi-chamber Janus fibers, and hybrid Janus/core–sheath architectures have further expanded the structural and functional design space of ES [592], [593], [594]. These architectures provide multiple compartments or spatially distinct domains within a single nanofibrous structure, thereby enabling more precise control over drug loading, molecular distribution, interfacial interactions, sequential or differential release, and multifunctional performance [591], [595], [596], [597]. Such advances demonstrate that the progress of ES extends beyond the production of conventional nanoscale fibers toward the rational construction of complex nanostructures with programmed spatial organization and functionality. This structural versatility may be particularly valuable for biomedical applications in which therapeutic agents with different physicochemical properties, release requirements, or biological targets need to be incorporated into a single platform. Nevertheless, increasing structural complexity should be accompanied by careful consideration of fabrication reproducibility, characterization, stability, and manufacturing feasibility. Thus, future development should focus not simply on creating increasingly complex architectures, but on identifying those structural features that provide a clear functional or therapeutic advantage.

sections.title: Scale-up, bulk production, and sustainable manufacturing

paragraphs.en: A critical barrier to the clinical translation and industrial adoption of functionalized ESNFs is the gap between laboratory-scale fabrication and large-scale manufacturing under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-compatible conditions. Translating ESNF systems from laboratory studies to clinically relevant production requires standardized fabrication protocols, batch-to-batch reproducibility, rigorous quality control, and regulatory compliance, all of which can substantially increase process complexity and cost. Conventional needle-based ES provides precise control over fiber formation and functionalization but generally has relatively low productivity, limiting its suitability for large-scale manufacturing. In contrast, NLES, multinozzle systems, and other high-throughput ES approaches offer substantially greater productivity and therefore represent promising routes toward industrial production.

Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of bulk and batch production strategies to increase nanofiber productivity while maintaining appropriate structural and functional characteristics [598], [599]. Such developments are particularly important because industrialization requires not only an increase in fiber yield but also the preservation of critical quality attributes across larger production areas and longer processing periods. During scale-up, changes in electric-field distribution, fluid supply, environmental conditions, jet interactions, and solvent evaporation can influence fiber morphology, diameter distribution, porosity, drug loading, and functional-agent distribution. Consequently, maintaining structural and functional uniformity while increasing productivity remains a major technical challenge.

Future research should therefore place greater emphasis on scalable and continuous manufacturing strategies capable of preserving the sophisticated architectures achieved at laboratory scale. High-throughput electrospinning platforms, multinozzle and needleless systems, automated process control, and real-time monitoring of critical process parameters may facilitate more reproducible production. Integration of ES with established manufacturing technologies and complementary fabrication approaches may provide additional routes toward scalable production and accelerate the industrialization of nanofiber-based drug delivery systems [600]. Importantly, scale-up should be evaluated according to a comprehensive set of critical quality attributes, including fiber diameter and its distribution, porosity, surface chemistry, drug loading, functional-agent distribution, mechanical properties, degradation behavior, and release characteristics. Process analytical technologies and data-driven or machine-learning-assisted optimization may further facilitate the development of robust manufacturing processes.

Sustainability should also become an increasingly important consideration during process development. The large-scale use of organic solvents, energy-intensive processing, and extensive post-fabrication modification may increase the environmental burden of ESNF production. Accordingly, future studies should explore safer and more environmentally compatible solvents, aqueous or solvent-minimized processing where feasible, energy-efficient high-throughput systems, and manufacturing strategies that reduce material waste. Importantly, sustainability should be considered together with product quality, safety, and process performance rather than as an independent criterion. The development of scalable ESNF technologies should therefore aim to achieve an appropriate balance among productivity, structural precision, functional performance, environmental impact, and economic feasibility.

The use of novel crosslinkers, solvents, grafting reagents, and functionalization agents introduces additional considerations regarding toxicity, residual chemicals, degradation products, long-term biocompatibility, and regulatory acceptability. Although functionalization can substantially improve surface bioactivity, drug loading, controlled release, or cell–material interactions, these benefits may be accompanied by changes in mechanical properties, degradation behavior, structural stability, and long-term functional durability. Chemical crosslinking and post-fabrication modification, for example, may improve aqueous stability or functional-agent retention but can introduce residual reagents, additional processing steps, heterogeneous modification, or changes in polymer degradation. Similarly, incorporation of multiple therapeutic or functional agents may enhance biological performance or enable sophisticated release profiles while increasing formulation complexity and potentially compromising reproducibility and stability. These trade-offs become particularly important during scale-up, where increasing material and process complexity may negatively affect batch-to-batch consistency, functional-agent distribution, sterilization, quality control, manufacturing cost, and regulatory evaluation.

Importantly, functionalization should therefore not be considered a universally beneficial modification. Each functionalization strategy should instead be evaluated according to its overall benefit–risk and complexity–performance balance. Increasing functional complexity is justified only when the resulting improvement provides a meaningful and reproducible therapeutic advantage. From a translational perspective, the optimal functionalized ESNF is unlikely to be the system with the highest degree of functionalization or structural complexity. Rather, it is likely to be the system in which each additional functional component or architectural feature provides a clearly demonstrated benefit while maintaining acceptable material stability, safety, manufacturability, and long-term performance.

Long-term stability and biological fate also require greater attention. Although numerous studies have demonstrated improved biological performance following the incorporation or immobilization of peptides, proteins, growth factors, drugs, and other bioactive molecules, relatively limited information is available regarding their long-term stability and preservation of bioactivity under physiological conditions. Changes in surface chemistry, functional-agent conformation, degradation products, and biological interactions over extended periods require systematic investigation. Future studies should therefore establish standardized long-term evaluation protocols and clarify the relationships among ESNF architecture, physicochemical properties, functional-agent presentation, biological response, degradation, and eventual in vivo fate.

sections.title: Clinical translation and emerging research directions

paragraphs.en: Several electrospun biomedical systems have progressed beyond proof-of-concept research and provide useful benchmarks for understanding the factors that may favor clinical translation. One representative example is Restrata®, a synthetic electrospun hybrid-scale fiber matrix composed of polyglactin 910 and polydioxanone, which has received FDA 510(k) clearance for wound management. The use of clinically established, bioresorbable polymers with medical-device precedent, together with a relatively simple nonwoven fiber architecture and a clearly defined therapeutic purpose, has supported its clinical application [601]. Clinical studies have further provided evidence supporting the use of synthetic electrospun fiber matrices in wound management. Another notable example is Spincare™, a portable in situ ES system that directly deposits a nanofibrous matrix onto the wound. Spincare™ has progressed from preclinical development to clinical evaluation in patients with partial-thickness burns and has subsequently been investigated in chronic wound management [602]. These examples illustrate that electrospun systems based on well-characterized materials, relatively simple architectures, and clearly defined therapeutic functions may currently have greater translational potential than highly complex multifunctional systems [603].

Clinical and commercial experience with electrospun components in vascular and cardiovascular devices provides another important translational pathway [604], [605]. In particular, AVflo™ represents an example in which an electrospun nanofabric forms the principal functional structure of a vascular access graft, whereas PK Papyrus represents an alternative strategy in which an electrospun polyurethane layer is integrated into an established cardiovascular stent platform [604], [605]. These examples suggest that electrospinning may reach clinical application through more than one route: either as the primary structural component of a medical device or as a functional component incorporated into a clinically established platform. Although these clinically translated systems do not necessarily incorporate the full range of advanced functionalization strategies discussed in this review, they provide important translational benchmarks for understanding which characteristics of electrospun biomedical systems have already demonstrated clinical feasibility.

From our perspective, the functionalization strategies most likely to achieve clinical translation are those that combine meaningful therapeutic benefits with manufacturing simplicity, reproducibility, and a well-understood safety profile. In particular, surface functionalization using clinically relevant biomolecules, incorporation of established therapeutic agents into well-characterized polymer systems, and relatively simple core–sheath or surface-engineered architectures appear to offer promising translational opportunities. Such strategies can provide controlled presentation or release of therapeutic agents while limiting the number of novel materials and processing steps requiring extensive safety and regulatory evaluation.

Stimuli-responsive, multifunctional, and personalized ESNF systems also represent promising longer-term research directions. However, their clinical potential will depend on demonstrating predictable responses under physiologically relevant conditions, long-term stability, reproducible manufacturing, and adequate control of inter-batch variability. Similarly, complex hierarchical architectures, multiple functionalization agents, poorly characterized crosslinkers, extensive post-fabrication modification, and approaches requiring substantial quantities of non-biocompatible solvents or unstable biological components may face greater barriers to clinical translation. Although these systems can achieve sophisticated functions at the laboratory scale, their increasing structural and compositional complexity may complicate quality control, sterilization, stability assessment, manufacturing, and regulatory evaluation.

Accordingly, future research should increasingly move from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward application-oriented design criteria. Studies should define the specific therapeutic problem to be addressed, identify the minimum level of structural or functional complexity required to solve that problem, and evaluate the resulting system using clinically relevant performance metrics. Standardized characterization protocols and performance benchmarks will also be essential for enabling meaningful comparisons among polymers, functionalization strategies, architectures, and fabrication platforms. Greater integration of materials science, process engineering, pharmacology, toxicology, and regulatory considerations at the early development stage may further accelerate the translation of promising ESNF technologies.

Taken together, recent advances demonstrate that the future of functionalized ESNFs will depend not only on the ability to introduce new functional agents or construct increasingly sophisticated architectures, but also on the ability to translate these innovations into reproducible, scalable, safe, and clinically meaningful products. The capability of ES to construct monolithic, core–sheath, hollow, Janus, multi-chamber, and hybrid architectures provides a powerful foundation for designing nanofibrous systems with precisely programmed functions. However, the most successful candidates for clinical translation are likely to be those in which added architectural or functional complexity produces a clear therapeutic advantage without introducing disproportionate manufacturing, safety, degradation, durability, environmental, or regulatory burdens.

Accordingly, future progress should focus on high-throughput and bulk production, reproducible and sustainable manufacturing, clinically acceptable materials and functionalization strategies, standardized critical quality attributes, long-term safety assessment, and regulatory-aware design. Integration of ES with established manufacturing technologies may further facilitate the transition from laboratory-scale fabrication to clinically and industrially relevant production. At the same time, advanced architectures such as core–sheath, Janus, hollow, and multi-chamber nanofibers should be developed according to application-specific needs rather than structural complexity alone. Ultimately, we envision the field moving toward optimized rather than maximal functionalization and structural complexity, in which each additional functional component or architectural feature is justified by a measurable therapeutic benefit and balanced against its effects on mechanical stability, degradation, long-term durability, manufacturing, sustainability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. This balance between functional sophistication and translational simplicity will be critical for converting promising ESNF concepts into clinically relevant and scalable products.

This review provides an in-depth analysis of recent developments in functionalized ESNFs and their expanding roles across diverse biomedical applications. Emphasis was placed on innovative modification strategies and contemporary techniques to enhance the structural and functional attributes of these nanofibrous scaffolds. Given their unique features, ESNFs demonstrate remarkable appeal across fields such as tissue regeneration, wound healing, targeted DD, and biosensing. Their tunable physicochemical properties and design flexibility further underscore their appeal as multifunctional platforms for both fundamental research and translational biomedical technologies. Nevertheless, fabricating NFs with precisely controlled morphology, superior mechanical and biochemical properties, and high production yield remains a technical challenge. Achieving these goals requires advanced control over the ES process and post-processing functionalization techniques. The use of various functionalization methods, such as plasma treatment, UV irradiation, chemical and biological crosslinking, and LBL deposition, has enabled researchers to tailor the surface chemistry and physico-mechanical properties of NFs to meet specific biomedical requirements. These functionalized NFs can be strategically engineered to direct specific cellular behaviors, including adhesion, proliferation, migration, and differentiation, thereby serving as potent platforms for targeted biomedical interventions. A particularly promising area of application is TE, where NF-based scaffolds are constructed to mimic the architecture and biomechanical characteristics of natural extracellular matrices. These scaffolds support tissue organization in vitro and offer the possibility for in vivo transplantation. ESNFs have also demonstrated potential in facilitating nerve regeneration, bone repair, and VTE and STE. Yet, a key obstacle lies in the tendency of some natural polymer NFs to degrade or lose functional integrity when exposed to physiological conditions, thereby limiting their long-term performance and biocompatibility. As such, identifying novel materials or combining synthetic and natural polymers may offer more reliable alternatives. Despite these advances, significant gaps remain. Most studies to date have used small-animal models, such as rodents, which may not adequately reflect human physiological and immunological conditions. Therefore, validating these findings in larger, clinically relevant animal models is critical before transitioning toward human trials. Furthermore, long-term studies are needed to evaluate the in vivo stability, degradation profiles, immune responses, and therapeutic outcomes of these scaffolds.
